(Photo by Michael Owens/Getty Images) | Getty Images There are NFL teams that would announce firings the morning after a game like the Ravens’ 23-20 loss to the previously-winless Chargers on Monday night. That will not happen in Baltimore. Not from a franchise that has long prioritized continuity and stability, often at significant opportunity costs. It is not the team’s best immediate course of action, either. But gifting Los Angeles their first win of the season should be a wake-up call that echoes through The Castle until the offseason. The Ravens will maintain their stance that they can keep their postseason chances alive until Lamar Jackson comes back – if that even happens. The idea seemed vaguely plausible when he first went down, but still a long shot. Now, it is simply preposterous. Book it: the Ravens will be closer to a top-five draft pick at the end of the season than they will be to the playoffs. (They currently sit at No. 14.) And they have only themselves to blame. Lamenting injuries and refereeing only goes so far. The fact is, the Ravens never should have been in a position for close calls going against them to matter. Monday night put all of Baltimore’s core flaws on display. It started from the very first play from scrimmage – a zero-yard run by Derrick Henry that matched the team’s first-half rushing total. The Ravens openly talked about new quarterback Jacoby Brissett’s ability to push the ball downfield to open up previously-nonexistent rushing lanes for Henry. That only happens if a defense respects the opposing passer’s arm – which can only happen if said passer completes a few throws downfield. Those circumstances would lend themselves to the under-center, play-action look on early downs that have propelled Baltimore’s offense this year. But Declan Doyle rarely pulled that lever on Monday night, and almost never on first down. Instead, he insisted on trying to power through a Chargers defensive line that was having their way in the trenches. The result was a grand total of 16 rushing yards and endless obvious passing situations for Brissett that allowed Los Angeles’ pass rush to tee off on Baltimore’s weak offensive line. He dropped back 51 times with a 35.3% pressure rate ( via PFF’s initial stats ) despite a relatively conservative blitz approach from Chargers defensive coordinator Chris O’Leary. He had no fear of a run on second- and third-and-long, often rolling out dime personnel to lock down passing lanes. Former Raven Del’Shawn Phillips, the Chargers’ No. 2 off-ball linebacker, played just 28 snaps, representing roughly 40% of the team’s defensive total and a massive amount of disrespect for the Ravens’ run game. Despite the negative opportunity set, Brissett found a way to complete 33 of his 49 passes (67.3%) for 340 yards. He somehow managed to take just two sacks, but did throw a crucial interception that set up the Chargers’ second touchdown. Overall, the veteran gunslinger deserves some credit for a decent debut in purple and black after just 10 days in Baltimore. So, too, does Mark Andrews. He has been under siege by Ravens fans this year, but he reeled in all eight of his targets on Monday night for 82 yards and five first downs. ESPN’s broadcast revealed that the veteran tight end was playing through a broken hand earlier this season, explaining his frequent drops but not why he continued to take the field instead of letting it heal. In any event, he gave his best performance since Week 3 of last season and might be able to turn around his fortunes. The rest of the Ravens’ playmakers chipped in, but Zay Flowers struggled to shake loose for his usual explosive gains with a long of 17 yards on the night. He also committed yet another fumble in the worst possible moment, two minutes left, down three points – that sank any chance of a late comeback. Once again, one of Baltimore’s best could not be at their best when their best was needed. The same was true in the Ravens’ other two phases. They allowed the Chargers to rack up 160 rushing yards at 4.7 yards a pop despite an offensive line that featured three rookies. Justin Herbert threw for just 129 yards on the night, but made a number of plays with his legs including a 22-yard touchdown on the Chargers’ opening drive. He was pressured on 59.3%(!) of his dropbacks but took just five hits – one from Mike Green, who had both of Baltimore’s sacks, and two apiece from Trenton Simpson and Calais Campbell. Green is up to 5.5 sacks in his second-year breakout, and Campbell is still chugging away in Year 19. Simpson had another strong game in general, adding to the case that he might be the Ravens’ future at linebacker. But then there are the missing names. Trey Hendrickson. Nnamdi Madubuike. Travis Jones. $66 million worth of pass rushers who could not hit the opposing quarterback. To be fair, Jones was solid against the run and led the trio with five pressures. Hendrickson and Madubuike notched four each – combined, a fine output until Herbert turns the missed sacks into positive plays. This crucial element of the Ravens’ struggles over the last few years has not gotten better despite a heavy investment from the front office and a new defensive brain trust. Not to be outdone, Baltimore’s special teams were a clear negative on the night. Rasheen Ali and Chris Moore struggled with shaky ball-handling and questionable decision-making on kickoffs. LaJohntay Wester largely remained a static centerfielder with three fair catches, at least one of which was returnable. He did rip off a 20-yard return that gave the Ravens their best field position of the night at their own 46. Second-best, though, was Los Angeles gifting Baltimore a touchback on a kickoff to set them up at the 35. Ravens rookie punter Ryan Eckley shanked his first attempt and landed zero inside the opposing 20. The Chargers averaged 15.7 yards per punt return (long of 24) with kickoff returns of 32 and 28 yards. New kicker Riley Patterson was the lone bright spot with a perfect four-for-four night, albeit via two short field goals and two extra points. Baltimore is now 4-6, dropping them to 10th in the AFC standings, two games out of the last wildcard spot and three games out of the divisional lead. Considering everything that has happened this year, that actually could be worse. Now, though, the season seems likely to head in that direction. Monday night’s 23-20 scoreline may help this game look better in the future, but those who watched will know. This is certainly a new low for the 2026 Ravens – could be a new low for the team in the Jackson era. Minter and his players owned the loss, but their words mean less and less as this team falls deeper into the abyss. This offseason should raise plenty of tough decisions for a front office that has too often invested (and even doubled-down) on aging, declining players. Assuming, for a moment, that Eric DeCosta can get Jackson’s extension done, he will still have to navigate a tight cap situation with plenty of holes to fill – a tall task for a general manager who has overseen three straight years of regression. Talk of offseason roster churn will no doubt intensify in the coming days, but the Ravens still have a season to close out. First up is a shortened week before facing an up-and-down Panthers team that can certainly beat this squad. Next is a trip to Houston, where the Texans’ pass rush will be nothing but trouble for the Ravens’ besieged offensive line. One loss would be tank their playoff chances, likely requiring them to win out and pray the tiebreakers break their way. Two would effectively end the season – and render Jackson’s potential return meaningless. The Ravens will continue to hold out hope that their two-time MVP can…
author: Nikhil Mehta

title: Ravens Report Card, Week 10: Poor run defense and costly turnovers doom the Ravens
summary: The Baltimore Ravens dropped their fifth consecutive game on Monday night, losing to the previously winless Los Angeles Chargers by three points (23-20). Here are report card grades for the team’s position groups from another disheartening defeat in Week 10. Quarterback: B- In his debut with the Ravens, Jacoby Brissett wound up airing the ball […]
full_text: BALTIMORE, MARYLAND - NOVEMBER 16: Jacoby Brissett #11 of the Baltimore Ravens looks to pass against the Los Angeles Chargers during the first quarter of the game at M&T Bank Stadium on November 16, 2026 in Baltimore, Maryland. (Photo by Scott Taetsch/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Baltimore Ravens dropped their fifth consecutive game on Monday night, losing to the previously winless Los Angeles Chargers by three points (23-20). Here are report card grades for the team’s position groups from another disheartening defeat in Week 10. Quarterback: B- In his debut with the Ravens, Jacoby Brissett wound up airing the ball out a ton with the team trailing early and the run game ineffective. Brissett threw 47 passes and completed 32 of them for 319 passing yards. He had one interception on an errant throw and a couple other nearly intercepted passes. Otherwise, Brissett did just about all you could ask of him with poor blocking up front and no support from the rushing attack. He was close to leading a potential go-ahead touchdown drive late in the fourth quarter, but a turnover robbed him of the chance to do so. It was a gutsy showing from the veteran signal-caller. Running Back: D Derrick Henry scored both of the offense’s two touchdowns but otherwise had an uneventful performance. Once again, Henry found almost no running room behind the offensive line. He was repeatedly hit at or behind the line of scrimmage. Henry had zero rushing yards in the first half and finished with ___ yards on ___ carries, which unsurprsingly are his lowest totals of the season and in recent memory. Justice Hill broke off one long run, but it was called back due to a penalty. Wide Receiver: C+ Ja’Kobi Lane had the eyes of Brissett all night, receiving a team-high 10 targets. He was only able to catch three passes, though, two of which gained 20+ yards. Lane had a costly drop on third down that would have given the Ravens a first down just one yard outside the end zone. Zay Flowers got going late in the game and finished with six catches for 74 yards, but his production was overshadowed by a back-breaking fumble late in the fourth quarter that effectively ended the game. Had Flowers not fumbled, the Ravens were nearing field goal range with a chance to tie the game at 23-23 or take the lead. Rashod Bateman caught three passes for 42 yards. Tight End: B+ It was a turn-back-the-clock performance for Mark Andrews, who caught all eight of his targets for 82 receiving yards. Andrews had multiple first-down conversions and, most importantly, no drops or penalties. Rookie Josh Cuevas had a trio of receptions and gained 37 yards with some nice production in hurry-up offense mode just before halftime. Matt Hibner has not been involved offensively in recent weeks, but Cuevas continues to show some receiving promise. Offensive Line: D+ It was more of the same for the Ravens’ offensive line, which struggled with penalties, got no push in the running game and surrendered pressure. Ronnie Stanley was once again flagged multiple times and Vega Ioane struggled early before exiting with a pre-existing shoulder injury. The Ravens had a lot of trouble against the Chargers’ interior defensive linemen, who were consistently in the backfield. To only rush for 16 total yards as a team on 15 carries — against any NFL defense — is nothing short of abysmal. Defensive Line: D+ The Chargers had a middle-of-the-pack rushing attack entering this game, but the Ravens had difficulty slowing them down on the ground. Omarion Hampton gained 105 yards on 22 carries and Justin Herbert broke contain several times. Herbert posted 51 rushing yards on seven carries with a 22-yard score in the first quarter. The Ravens had Herbert dead to rights multiple times but did not finish plays with sacks consistently, which has been a recurring trend this season. Calais Campbell had two quarterback hits and Nnamdi Madubuike exited the game early with a hamstring injury. Depth veterans like Broderick Washington and John Jenkins did not make much of an impact. Edge Rusher: C+ Aside from a costly roughing the passer penalty in the second half, Mike Green was wreaking havoc. He had a team-high three quarterback hits along with two sacks and two tackles for loss. It was one of the better games of his young career. Trey Hendrickson’s impact continues to leave much to be desired, as he had just one lone tackle with no sacks nor quarterback hits. Hendrickson has not had a sack since Week 4. Linebacker: C Roquan Smith had one big tackle for loss that forced a fourth down and nearly had a goal-line run stop but was overpowered by an extra Chargers’ blocker. He appeared to get lost in coverage at least once or twice on a long completion. Trenton Simpson made some notable plays, finishing with two quarterback hits and one tackle for loss with eight total tackles. The Ravens’ linebackers have to be knocked for the team’s poor run defense as well. Cornerback: C+ The Ravens were struggling to defend wide receiver Tre Harris early in the game, who quickly caught five passes for 86 yards. He was a non-factor for most of the night after that, though, as was the Chargers’ passing attack as a whole in the second half. No other wideout had more than one catch for the Chargers. Marlon Humphrey forced a fumble that was recovered by Los Angeles, but it was a good play against Hampton nonetheless. Safety: C + Kyle Hamilton had a team-high 10 tackles and was playing clean-up crew against ball-carriers in open space many times. Hamilton was the primary defender on a few completed first-down passes. Malaki Starks appeared to have his snaps reduced. He came up with a big pass breakup on a short pass attempt that would have converted a first down. Keondre Jackson was a bright spot as he played aggressively and made some solid tackles. Special Teams: C In his Ravens debut, kicker Riley Patterson connected on both of his field goal tries and extra points. LaJohntay Wester finally had a long return, taking a punt back for 20 yards. The Ravens’ return coverage has not been great at times this season. The Chargers had a 24-yard punt return tonight and averaged 15.7 yards per return in total.
author: Frank Platko

title: Ravens discussion: instant reactions to loss vs. Chargers
summary: The Baltimore Ravens managed to lose to the NFL’s worst team on Monday night. The Los Angeles Chargers walked into M&T Bank Stadium and controlled the matchup for much of the game before walking out with a 23-20 win. Here are Baltimore Beatdown’s instant reactions; be sure to add yours in the comment section below! […]
full_text: BALTIMORE, MARYLAND - NOVEMBER 16: Justin Herbert #10 of the Los Angeles Chargers celebrates after a touchdown against the Baltimore Ravens during an NFL football game at M&T Bank Stadium on November 16, 2026 in Baltimore, Maryland. (Photo by Michael Owens/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Baltimore Ravens managed to lose to the NFL’s worst team on Monday night. The Los Angeles Chargers walked into M&T Bank Stadium and controlled the matchup for much of the game before walking out with a 23-20 win. Here are Baltimore Beatdown’s instant reactions; be sure to add yours in the comment section below! Nikhil Mehta This morning, I mused that a loss to the winless Chargers could be the worst result in Ravens franchise history. By the time the clock hit 0:00, it certainly felt that way. The 23-20 score will look better in the future, but fans will remember the night Baltimore got beat by a winless team. In all three phases, the Ravens’ coaches and players made repeated mistakes – some physical (poor tackling, turnovers), some mental (clock management, penalties). To give a bit of credit: they did not roll over and die down the stretch like so many other games. But arguably the Ravens’ best, most consistent player this year committing a crucial turnover to lose the game is emblematic of this season. They just can’t get out of their own way. Zach Canter It’s very clear this is simply an awful team. The offensive line isn’t gelling like I hoped it would and now Ioane is hurt once more. They continue to get zero push in the run game. Jacoby Brissett actually played really well despite pressure in his face all night and deliveries strikes despite drops and defenders hitting him all. The defense predictably gave the Chargers offense their best game of the season. It’s awful team. The classic “big game fumble” from Zay Flowers ended the season. I said multiple times the team should have sold at the deadline (Ronnie Stanley, Mark Andrews, Derrick Henry, etc) and it’s looking like they should have. This wasn’t a team worth keeping together and it’s a team that likely could make Eric DeCosta and even Jesse Minter to lose their jobs. Kevin McNelis It’s just like this team to find a way to lose to a previously winless opponent at home in prime time. Officiating didn’t help, but this game shouldn’t have been close and the Ravens got dogwalked in the trenches all night. This is the true point of no return. They should’ve burned it down at the deadline, but this front office watched the same defense we’ve all seen this year and somehow believed this was a team that could stay alive until Lamar came back. That stubbornness probably slowed this franchise’s rebuild by an additional year. Embrace the suck. Tank for your new blindside tackle in this draft. Be ready for the reality that some core pieces might not want to be a part of the rebuilding process. This is the Bad Place. Dustin Cox Any hope that the Ravens could somehow stay alive and save their season for a potential Lamar Jackson return ended tonight. I don’t know what else to say at this point. This is a bad, poorly built, and poorly coached football team that was being propped up by an MVP quarterback. The trenches are weak on both sides of the ball, penalties continue to kill drives, and dumb mistakes happen in the biggest moments. I have to give Jacoby Brissett credit for his performance tonight. It wasn’t flawless by any means, but he led a watchable offense tonight, which is something the Ravens have struggled to do over the past month. Without the ability to run the ball, though, and with weak pass protection, I worry about the offense for the remainder of the season. I think it is fair to begin questioning Jesse Minter at this stage as well. Despite some nice moments tonight, his defense once again allowed an inferior opponent to have their best showing of the season. Losing to this 0-8 Chargers team is simply unacceptable. The offseason cannot get here fast enough. Frank Platko There is no viable excuse for losing this game. The Ravens were absolutely in must-win mode and had 10 days to prepare. Knowing all eyes would be on them in another big primetime home spot, they came out flat and were playing catch-up to a Chargers team that had been dismal and lifeless for much of the season. Giving up 23 points to a bottom-tier offense and only rushing for 16 yards as a team was mightily disappointing. Jacoby Brissett did all he could and, aside from a costly interception, had a gutsy performance. Brissett had the Ravens in position to tie or win the game late before Zay Flowers’ back-breaking fumble. It’s a shame that Flowers, whose been one of the only consistent bright spots this year, once again lost a crucial fumble — but unfortunately this is now a pattern for him. The Ravens did just enough late to reel those still clinging onto hope back in before delivering a crushing blow. That has been the norm for this team in recent memory. This appears to be a lost season now barring an unforeseen winning streak coming up, which seems impossible given how inconsistent, disappointing and poorly coached they’ve been over the past five games.

title: Ravens discussion: loss to Chargers would be most embarrassing since…?
summary: The Ravens have some bad losses on their ledger over the last several years. Some bad losses. But even with all the blown leads and second-half collapses in recent years, falling to the Chargers – the winless Chargers – on Monday night might be a new low. The following is true of Jim Harbaugh’s squad this […]
full_text: Nov 25, 2024; Inglewood, California, USA; Baltimore Ravens running back Derrick Henry (22) carries the ball against Los Angeles Chargers cornerback Kristian Fulton (7) and cornerback Elijah Molden (22) in the second half at SoFi Stadium. Mandatory Credit: Kirby Lee-Imagn Images | USA TODAY Sports via Reuters Con The Ravens have some bad losses on their ledger over the last several years. Some bad losses. But even with all the blown leads and second-half collapses in recent years, falling to the Chargers – the winless Chargers – on Monday night might be a new low. The following is true of Jim Harbaugh’s squad this year: Ranks 32nd in scoring Ranks 28th in points allowed -98 point differential through eight games… …good for a 12.25-point average margin of defeat 18.9% of offensive drives end in a turnover The Chargers will also be without star wide receiver Ladd McConkey on Monday night, while a few other key players are questionable. All of these factors should tip the scales in the Ravens’ direction, even with Jacoby Brissett set to make his debut. But there is a reason winless seasons are rare. This is an Any Given Sunday league, wherein last week’s defeat is forgotten in the fog of a new war. The Chargers are probably going to beat someone eventually. Wouldn’t it be so spot-on for the Ravens’ 2026 season if it happened in Baltimore on Monday night? That would almost certanily be the Ravens’ most embarrassing loss this season. That’s saying something after off three straight defeats of 22 points or more, but those came against three of the best teams in the AFC with a combination of Tyler Huntley and Joe Fagnano under center. Last year’s 44-10 loss to the Texans looms large given the margin, but what more were you expecting from Cooper Rush, a bad O-line against a fiercesome Houston front, and a suddenly banged-up defense? My pick: Week 10 of the 2021 season, a 22-10 loss to the Dolphins. The Ravens had no answers for Brian Flores’ defense. Lamar Jackson could not summon his usual magic to dance away from pressure and make plays downfield, and Baltimore’s offense walked on the field like lambs to the slaughter every drive. A solid showing from the defense – ironically, against Brissett for much of the game – was not enough to rescue one of the worst showings of Jackson’s career. Dishonorable mention: Come to think of it, Week 2 of the 2022 season – Mike Macdonald’s second game as defensive coordinator – was an embarrassing loss, too. The Ravens seem to only throttle the Dolphins or melt down in spectacular fashion.

title: Could Buffalo Bills sign free-agent wide receiver Marquise Brown?
summary: Marquise Brown is now a free agent — will the Buffalo Bills come calling? The veteran wideout was waived by the Eagles over the weekend and has now cleared waivers, making him an unrestricted free agent. Sure, the Bills are probably close to seeing Tyrell Shavers return to the field, which will make for a […]
full_text: Marquise Brown is now a free agent — will the Buffalo Bills come calling? The veteran wideout was waived by the Eagles over the weekend and has now cleared waivers, making him an unrestricted free agent. Sure, the Bills are probably close to seeing Tyrell Shavers return to the field, which will make for a somewhat crowded receiver room. But this article felt necessary due to the team’s perceived past interest in Brown. Back in 2023, Sal Maiorana of the Rochester Democrat & Chronicle selected Brown as a potential trade target for the Bills at the deadline. Brown was not traded then and ended the season with 51 catches for 574 yards with four scores on 69% of Arizona’s offensive snaps. Then, after a season with the Chiefs in 2024, the Buffalo’s supposed interest in Brown was documented in a report from ESPN’s Jeremy Fowler in early February 2025: “Mahomes advocated for signing Brown last year and will likely do so again. Will another star quarterback — like Josh Allen — be next? People with the Chiefs I spoke to this week believe that Allen has long wanted to play with Brown.” Brown ultimately re-signed with the Chiefs and had 49 catches for 587 yards and five touchdowns during the regular season last year, including a two-catch, 73-yard performance against the Bills. His yards-per-route run figure was 1.49, not tremendous but far from a totally brutal figure. If the Bills do sign Brown, it’d hardly be the first time they added a receiver after a stint as a complementary piece in Kansas City (see: Marquez-Valdes Scantling and Mecole Hardman). Brown, 29, was a first-round pick by the Ravens in 2019 and had a 1,000-yard season as a 24 year old in 2021. He was only targeted eight times in 2026 on the Eagles and had five catches for 63 yards on 20.9% of the snaps. There are plenty of charting-based metrics out there today that track how well a receiver gets open, but according to Fantasy Points Data, Browns’ average separation score of +0.053 was the highest among all Eagles receivers. Sample size certainly must be considered here, but that figure would be the third-highest average separation score among Bills receivers to date behind DJ Moore in the top spot at +0.119 and Josh Palmer at +0.118. Brown had at least one 40-plus yard reception in five of six seasons from 2019 through 2025. The Bills currently have six vested veterans on their practice squad, the maximum allowed — Tre’Davious White, Shaq Thompson, Phidarian Mathis, Trent Sherfield, Geno Stone, and Kader Kohou — so if they wanted to add Brown to that level of the roster, they’d need to release one of those players. Do you have any interest in Brown? And do you think the Bills will consider signing him?

title: Bills vs. Dolphins odds: Opening lines for Week 11 matchup
summary: The Buffalo Bills are now 8-1 and remain in first place in the AFC playoff race. The change at head coach hasn’t slowed down Buffalo one bit, thanks in large part to the consistency on offense and the fact that quarterback Josh Allen and running back James Cook III are among the best in the […]
full_text: MIAMI GARDENS, FLORIDA - NOVEMBER 09: Josh Allen #17 of the Buffalo Bills looks to pass during the first half of the game against the Miami Dolphins at Hard Rock Stadium on November 09, 2025 in Miami Gardens, Florida. (Photo by Megan Briggs/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Buffalo Bills are now 8-1 and remain in first place in the AFC playoff race. The change at head coach hasn’t slowed down Buffalo one bit, thanks in large part to the consistency on offense and the fact that quarterback Josh Allen and running back James Cook III are among the best in the NFL. The Bills have a firm hold on the AFC East, and are in prime position to re-claim the division title this season. This, despite a .500 record while having only played two games against division rivals. Week 11 is upon us, and with that comes Buffalo’s first chance to take on the Miami Dolphins in 2026. It’s been another mostly forgettable season for the Dolphins, who will head to Highmark Stadium with a 1-8 record. As might be expected, the Bills enter Week 11 as heavy favorites over the Dolphins. As of publishing, FanDuel Sportsbook listed Buffalo as 16.5-point favorites (-16.5) over Miami , with an over/under set at o/u 45.5. It’s the biggest points spread in NFL action this week. Do the Dolphins have a chance? Buffalo and Miami are two teams headed in very different directions. Though not mathematically eliminated yet, the Dolphins’ chances of making the playoffs are on life support. The team has looked listless much of the season, and now that quarterback Malik Willis is injured, things have been turned over to rookie quarterback Kyle McCord. The Bills-Dolphins rivalry is a heated one that goes back generations, beginning back on September 18, 1966. Miami actually holds the advantage in the all-time series record, 63-61-1, but they’re at real risk of allowing Buffalo to even things up this season. Though one-sided in favor of the Dolphins through the entirety of the 1970s, this series has belonged almost entirely to the Bills since Josh Allen came to Orchard Park, NY. Since 2018, Allen and the Bills are 14-3 (including playoffs). If you were to poll a room of Bills fans, it’s likely that most of them well remember those three losses, which brings us to the last time Buffalo and Miami played. That game was also the most recent loss for the Bills against the Dolphins. During head coach Sean McDermott’s final season with Buffalo, the Bills dropped an uncharacteristic-by-their-standards 30-13 decision in Miami. That ended a seven-game win streak dating back to 2022. Buffalo has its sights set on a major goals in 2026, which includes earning the one seed and a bye to begin the AFC playoff race. title: Buffalo Bills break records in Week 10 win over Jets
summary: Someone once said, “It’s not how you start, it’s how you finish.” Maybe they were previewing the Buffalo Bills’ Week 10 matchup with the New York Jets, because that start was uneventful at best and downright ugly at worst.  But somewhere along the way, the Bills did what the Bills do. They made some big […]
full_text: Someone once said, “It’s not how you start, it’s how you finish.” Maybe they were previewing the Buffalo Bills’ Week 10 matchup with the New York Jets, because that start was uneventful at best and downright ugly at worst. But somewhere along the way, the Bills did what the Bills do. They made some big plays, broke a few records, set some personal bests, and found a way to get the job done. And when it was all over, Buffalo headed back to Western New York with an 8-1 record and gave us plenty to Shout! about along the way. So, let’s hand out some Shout! outs this week. _____________________________________________________________________________ Joe Brady Nine games into his head coaching career, Joe Brady is already keeping some pretty impressive company. And, for the rookie head coach, taking his offense on the road hasn’t been much of a problem, either. Joe Brady is now one of four rookie coaches since 2000 to begin his coaching career with an 8-1 or better record: – 2026: BUF Joe Brady (8-1) – 2022: MIN Kevin O'Connell (8-1) – 2011: SF Jim Harbaugh (8-1) – 2009: IND Jim Caldwell (9-0) https://t.co/LgrLBPi7Bf — Buffalo Bills PR (@BuffaloBillsPR) November 16, 2026 The Bills are averaging 32.0 points per game through the first 5 road games of Joe Brady’s head coaching career, the 9th most PPG by a head coach through 5 road games in NFL history. https://t.co/LgrLBPi7Bf — Buffalo Bills PR (@BuffaloBillsPR) November 15, 2026 _____________________________________________________________________________ Josh Allen Another week, another handful of NFL records for Josh Allen. This time, he’s passing Patrick Mahomes on one list, joining Jalen Hurts on another, and adding two more milestones to a résumé that’s getting pretty crowded. With 96 regular season wins, Josh Allen now surpasses Patrick Mahomes for the second-most regular season wins in their first 9 seasons in NFL history. He trails only Russell Wilson (98). pic.twitter.com/UFP2YLh30E — Buffalo Bills PR (@BuffaloBillsPR) November 15, 2026 Allen has now rushed for 10+ touchdowns in 4 straight seasons, tying Jalen Hurts (2021-24) for the longest streak by a QB in NFL history. https://t.co/hyyiUkRwWj — Buffalo Bills PR (@BuffaloBillsPR) November 15, 2026 Allen also passed Peyton Manning for the most touchdowns in a player’s first 10 seasons and tied Eric Dickerson for 14th on the NFL’s all-time rushing touchdown list . Not a bad afternoon. _____________________________________________________________________________ James Cook James Cook must have decided that one Shout!out wasn’t going to be enough. So, he tied a Hall of Famer, matched his own franchise record, and threw in a career-long touchdown run for good measure. James Cook has now tied LaDainian Tomlinson with 8 straight games of 75+ rushing yards and 1+ touchdown for the longest such streak since 2006. https://t.co/Mg2a1SPtt9 — Buffalo Bills PR (@BuffaloBillsPR) November 15, 2026 With James Cook's 74-yard touchdown run, that was the longest rush of Cook’s NFL career. It is also the longest rushing touchdown for the Bills since LeSean McCoy’s 75-yard rush touchdown on November 27, 2016. pic.twitter.com/Mku2OlAFDg — Buffalo Bills PR (@BuffaloBillsPR) November 15, 2026 _____________________________________________________________________________ DJ Moore DJ Moore is a difference maker when he’s on the field with Buffalo’s offense. His 45-yard touchdown against the Jets was his longest since joining the Bills and one of the longest of his career. DJ Moore's 45-yard receiving TD marked this 9th longest score of his career and his longest since joining the Bills. pic.twitter.com/xqPiEFJJOc — Buffalo Bills PR (@BuffaloBillsPR) November 15, 2026 _____________________________________________________________________________ T.J. Parker How about a little love for the rookie? T.J. Parker got to the Jets quarterback twice on Sunday, putting himself in some pretty good company among recent Bills rookies. T.J. Parker finished the game with 2 sacks on Jets QB Cade Klubnik. Prior to Parker today, the last Bills rookie with 2+ sacks in the same game was Greg Rousseau in 2022 vs. Miami. pic.twitter.com/U44GIVna3W — Buffalo Bills PR (@BuffaloBillsPR) November 15, 2026 _____________________________________________________________________________ Dorian Williams Dorian Williams decided he wanted in on the sack party, too. He brought down Geno Smith for the first sack of his NFL career. Dorian Williams sack of Jets QB Geno Smith marked the first sack of Williams' career. pic.twitter.com/Bp6LdhdTJl — Buffalo Bills PR (@BuffaloBillsPR) November 15, 2026 _____________________________________________________________________________ Buffalo Bills defense And while we’re handing out individual Shout! outs, let’s not forget the entire defense. Buffalo has now gone 28 consecutive defensive drives without surrendering a touchdown, something the Bills haven’t done in more than a quarter-century. The Bills defense has gone 28 consecutive defensive drives without allowing a TD, marking the team's longest streak since not allowing a TD on 38 consecutive drives in 1999. pic.twitter.com/92ejorsSjj — Buffalo Bills PR (@BuffaloBillsPR) November 15, 2026 _____________________________________________________________________________ It wasn’t pretty from start to finish, and there were definitely a few moments that had Bills Mafia yelling at their televisions for all the wrong reasons. But Buffalo found its rhythm, took care of business against a division rival, and added another win to the standings. Now it’s back home to face the Miami Dolphins, with an 8-1 record, a five-game winning streak, and a whole lot of history being made along the way. Plenty of reasons to keep Shout! ing!
author: Rachel Auberger

title: Khalil Shakir should become bigger part of Buffalo Bills passing offense
summary: The Buffalo Bills are leading the NFL in points per game at 31.9, and they’re 8-1 for the first time since 1991, but there’s always room for improvement. And I think said improvement can occur in Buffalo’s pass game if slot receiver Khalil Shakir becomes a focal point. I won’t fault you for questioning why […]
full_text: The Buffalo Bills are leading the NFL in points per game at 31.9, and they’re 8-1 for the first time since 1991, but there’s always room for improvement. And I think said improvement can occur in Buffalo’s pass game if slot receiver Khalil Shakir becomes a focal point. I won’t fault you for questioning why I’m writing this now after Shakir had two catches for 29 yards — along with three “runs” for 26 yards — in the win over the Jets in Week 10. There are a few reasons — it’s a follow from one of my takeaways from Buffalo’s victory in MetLie Stadium, Amon-Ra St. Brown went off for the Lions against the Patriots in Germany, and Parker Washington had the most receiving yards in a game (152) for the Jaguars since 2019. Oh, and now is the ideal time to start incorporating Shakir into a more prominent role, right before the Bills have this five-game stretch during the holiday season — vs. Chiefs, at Patriots, at Packers, vs. Bears, and at Broncos. Let’s start general, with a question — who has been the Bills most reliable receiver for going on four seasons now? Shakir. Even in 2023, his second season as a professional, on a team with Stefon Diggs, Shakir’s yards-per-route run (1.79) rivaled Diggs’ (1.89). His drop rate was drastically lower than Diggs’ 2.0% vs. 6.4%, and he averaged 7.0 yards after contact per reception to Diggs’ 3.9. All those figures are counting the playoffs too. Yes, of course — sample size. Diggs was targeted 175 times to just 56 for Shakir that season. That’s drastic. Speaking of the playoffs… in the two Bills games that postseason, Shakir and Diggs both had 10 grabs. Shakir had slightly more yards 75 vs. 73 and scored two touchdowns to Diggs’ zero. Even if you believed Diggs was more reliable in 2023, from 2024 to the present day, we can all agree the answer to my original question is Shakir, right? And in Allen’s MVP campaign of 2024, Shakir led the team in targets (100), receptions (76), and yards (821) during the regular season. Correlation doesn’t automatically equal causation, but Shakir’s presence as Buffalo’s defacto No. 1 receiver during a season with outrageous efficiency from Buffalo’s offense shouldn’t be ignored. If any receiver has put in the time, paid his dues, and produced to a level that should earn more looks — it’s Shakir! And it’s not as though he’s an overachiever without the physical skills of two of the better slot-based veterans in football. Khalil Shakir Amon-Ra St. Brown * Josh Downs Height / Weight 6’0” / 196 5’11” / 197 5’9” / 171 40-Yard 4.43 4.61 4.48 10-Yard 1.49 1.63 1.49 Vertical 34.5” 38.5” 38.5” Broad 124 127” 131 Three-Cone 7.28 6.9 N/A *testing figures at USC Pro Day Shakir stacks up very favorably with St. Brown and Downs. I didn’t include Washington in that comparison because he didn’t work out before he was selected by Jacksonville in the sixth round of the 2023 NFL Draft. As for this season, Shakir has made a strong case to see the football more based on how effective he’s been accumulating yardage on a relatively low percentage of the team’s targets. Check this graphic, Shakir can be found near Nico Collins just barely in the upper left quadrant, where the under-utilized, above-average producers reside: What can you make of that scatter plot? Shakir has a target share of 18.1% — simply meaning he’s earned 18.1% of Buffalo’s pass targets through nine games — which is the 34th-highest among 71 qualifying wideouts. He’s also 20th in yards per route run (2.00) despite his relatively lower target-share percentage. That disparity is the quantifiable crux of my argument here. In short, Shakir isn’t seeing the football thrown in his direction very much, but he’s still averaging a reasonably high yards-per-route run figure. Note on that graphic too — Washington’s target share is 24.9%, and St. Brown’s is over 30%. Downs’ is almost identical to Shakir’s at 18.0%. Really, there aren’t many other receivers beyond Shakir in the upper-left quadrant either. They are Jameson Williams, Tre Tucker, Caleb Douglas, DeMario Douglas, Rome Odunze, and Collins. Shakir’s average depth of target (aDOT) is currently just 4.7 yards. That is up from a super-gimmicky 3.9 yards a season ago, and not quite to his 5.6 aDOT during the uber-efficient 2024, when his yards-per-route run figure was a hefty 2.15. St. Brown’s aDOT is nearly double Shakir’s at 8.6 yards, and he’s been over 8.0 yards in aDOT in each of the last four seasons. Washington’s aDOT is 13.1 yards, exactly what it was during his breakout year a season ago. And it’s not as though Shakir is incapable of generating big plays or YAC at the rate of the other slot monsters: Khalil Shakir Amon-Ra St. Brown Parker Washington Josh Downs Career YAC / reception 8.1 4.9 4.5 4.5 Career % of 20-plus yard catches 14.7% 14.3% 23.9% 12.7% For as much as usage may contribute to Shakir’s higher YAC here, the same can be said regarding the 20-plus yard reception percentage for Washington relative to the other three wideouts in the table. And heck, Shakir has at least one 50-plus yard reception in each of the last four seasons now. Lastly, if you needed one more piece of persuasion, Shakir is so damn sure-handed. He has a career drop rate of 3.4%. St. Brown’s is 2.9%. Downs’ is 5.2%. Washington’s is 9.0%. Now I’m officially on the record — I believe Shakir should move into a leading role in the Bills passing offense. He deserves it. And Buffalo’s aerial attack would probably be better if he started seeing more than five targets per game.
author: Chris Trapasso

title: Josh Allen ties Eric Dickerson, Curtis Martin at 90 rushing touchdowns
summary: Josh Allen has as many rushing touchdowns as Eric Dickerson. Yes, we’re comparing a quarterback to the guy who ran for 2,105 yards in one season.  Allen scored his 90th career rushing touchdown during Buffalo’s Week 10 game against the New York Jets, tying Dickerson and fellow Hall of Famer Curtis Martin for 14th on […]
full_text: Josh Allen has as many rushing touchdowns as Eric Dickerson. Yes, we’re comparing a quarterback to the guy who ran for 2,105 yards in one season. Josh Allen rushes for his second TD of the day and 90th of his career. Allen is now tied with Eric Dickerson and Curtis Martin (90 rushing TDs) for 14th place on the NFL's all-time list. pic.twitter.com/2JhzOFe2AA — Buffalo Bills PR (@BuffaloBillsPR) November 15, 2026 Allen scored his 90th career rushing touchdown during Buffalo’s Week 10 game against the New York Jets, tying Dickerson and fellow Hall of Famer Curtis Martin for 14th on the NFL’s all-time list. He entered the game with 88. Number 89 came on a one yard run in the first quarter. Number 90 was a two-yard run on the Bills’ first possession of the third quarter. Josh Allen calls his own number. 😤 📺: CBS pic.twitter.com/9Fj8amAJvc — Buffalo Bills (@BuffaloBills) November 15, 2026 Here comes @JoshAllenQB !! 📺: CBS pic.twitter.com/4ZHYqhZ4Ca — Buffalo Bills (@BuffaloBills) November 15, 2026 Dickerson and Martin weren’t running backs who had a few good seasons. Dickerson led the NFL in rushing four times, and nobody has topped his single-season yardage record in more than 40 years. Martin opened his career with 10 straight 1,000-yard seasons, including seven with the New York Jets. Bills fans had plenty of opportunities to get tired of watching him, but now they can celebrate one of their own making what he did look average. Both finished with 90 rushing touchdowns. Allen has matched them in his ninth season while also being responsible for, you know, throwing the football. The quarterback record is already his. It has been for a while. Now Allen has reached the point where we’re comparing his touchdown total to some of the best running backs to ever play, and he could pass a few more before this season is over. One more rushing touchdown would tie Jerome Bettis and Franco Harris for 12th at 91. Barry Sanders is next at 99, followed by Marshall Faulk and Shaun Alexander at 100. Allen would need 10 more to join that pair in ninth place, which is asking a lot. But we’re talking about a quarterback with a chance to finish the season in the NFL’s top 10 for career rushing touchdowns. We can keep asking him to slide, but we shouldn’t expect that he will. Apparently, he has a few more people to catch first.
author: Rachel Auberger

title: Bills news: Recapping win over Jets
summary: The Buffalo Bills (8-1) picked up their first AFC East victory of the year Sunday afternoon, overcoming a sluggish offensive performance in the first half to overwhelm the New York Jets (2-8) by a score of 31-12 at MetLife Stadium in East Rutherford, New Jersey. full_text: The Buffalo Bills (8-1) picked up their first AFC East victory of the year Sunday afternoon, overcoming a sluggish offensive performance in the first half to overwhelm the New York Jets (2-8) by a score of 31-12 at MetLife Stadium in East Rutherford, New Jersey. Bills start slow, pull away from Jets The Buffalo Bills averaged only 4.3 yards per play, put only 10 points on the scoreboard and were clearly frustrated with a first-half effort that resulted in a 10-6 lead after two quarters. Then, Buffalo’s offense came alive, averaging 14.4 yards per play while scoring three touchdowns and compiling four explosive plays of 20+ yards, including three plays that went for 40+ yards, in a dominant second half. We break down how Josh Allen and the Bills offense turned on the afterburners to throttle the Jets in the second half, and praise the running of James Cook, who finished with a season-high 157 yards, the third-highest total of his career, including a 74-yard touchdown run in the fourth quarter. title: Takeaways from Bills win over Jets
summary: The Buffalo Bills beat the Jets 31-12 in Week 10 on inside MetLife Stadium, in a game that went from defensive slugfest in the first two quarters to blowout in the second half. At 8-1, the Bills are out to their best start since 1991. These are my takeaways from Buffalo’s victory. I’m glad we […]
full_text: The Buffalo Bills beat the Jets 31-12 in Week 10 on inside MetLife Stadium, in a game that went from defensive slugfest in the first two quarters to blowout in the second half. At 8-1, the Bills are out to their best start since 1991. These are my takeaways from Buffalo’s victory. I’m glad we saw some pass-game pop within structure During the Bills’ four-game win streak entering this game, which included dominance after the bye week, it felt natural to narrow focus on Buffalo’s entire operation, checking for any component of the team that could improve. And in wins over the Rams, Raiders, Ravens, and Vikings, Buffalo seemingly lacked efficiency from the pass game in a classic sense. You know, Josh Allen standing in the pocket and completing the football to pass catchers within the intended design of the play. It hadn’t happened at the frequency one would expect in games in which the Bills scored 37, 33, 36, and 23 points (against the No. 1 defense in football on the road). But in the second half against the Jets, the Bills demonstrated their ability to move the ball through the air in a normal, rhythmic way… at all levels of the field. And there was an explosive element that’s been mostly missing over the past four outings. For as good as Allen has been creating this season, and for as reliable as Buffalo has been on the ground, this team needs to be able to win with classic dropback passing too, and in the third and fourth quarters against the Jets, the Bills did just that. Defensive depth shines The turf at MetLife Stadium has one of the most notorious reputations in the NFL. And a handful of Bills were dinged with injuries in this game, unsurprisingly. Here’s to hoping the likes of Christian Benford, Dorian Williams, and Dee Alford are OK. In their absence, Buffalo’s defensive depth was immediately tested. And it shined. The Bills defense didn’t skip a beat with Kaleb Elarms-Orr, Jordan Hancock, and Maxwell Hairston on the field. But it wasn’t just that trio making relief appearances for those sidelined in-game with injury. Rookie T.J. Parker played the second-most snaps of his NFL career to date (38) and had five pressures with two sacks on 26 pass-rush snaps. Javon Solomon chipped in 12 snaps and registered a pair of pressures in his two pass-rush opportunities. As we’ve come to know during the Allen era, depth can be vital in the playoffs, and Buffalo’s backups are not only getting a decent amount of run this regular season but they’re playing respectable football. Hats off to Spencer Brown Brown was listed as doubtful going into this game. Ankle injury. He didn’t practice Thursday or Friday. Then he told reporters while warming up pre-game he was going to play. And I don’t think anyone would’ve blamed him if he struggled against surging rookie, No. 2 overall pick David Bailey, on the edge. But that didn’t happen. Per Next Gen Stats , Brown squared off with Bailey 13 times and didn’t allow a single pressure of Allen. He was also the blocker attached to star veteran linebacker DeMario Davis 10 yards downfield on James Cook’s 74-yard touchdown run that put the game away in the fourth quarter. It was such a gutsy performance from Brown, who is still getting better in Year 7 at right tackle. With his height, agility, explosiveness, balance, and power, he’s one of the most unique players at his position in football. And this game was the latest piece of evidence that Brown is incredibly tough too. James Cook is special So maybe not a takeaway just from this game, but I was reminded of just how tremendous of a football player Cook has become in his 157-yard performance in Week 10 that was capped with the long touchdown sprint. Cook isn’t Bijan Robinson or Derrick Henry. He’s not regularly jump-cutting the opponent’s entire linebacker group or running it over. He’s incredibly flexible in his lower half with outstanding vision as he works through blocks from his offensive line and one of the most dynamic open-field running backs in the game. Only Jahmyr Gibbs has more 10-plus yard runs (34) than Cook (27). And Gibbs is the only back in football with more 15-plus yard runs (16) than the Bills feature back (14). Cook is up to 971 yards on the ground this season at 5.2 yards per. He can wear down a defense three or four yards at at time — like vs. Vikings — on 31 carries, or hit explosive plays on the ground like he did against the Jets in this one. Bills linebacker group… a defensive strength? Through the first month of the 2026 campaign, this specific subheading would’ve been insane. But it’s a testament to how things can change for a team — and a position group — throughout a long season in the NFL. Terrel Bernard is 27 years old. Prime of his career. Dorian Williams is playing for a second contract. Elarms-Orr looks as ready to go in Year 1 as a team can expect from a fourth-round pick at linebacker. In this contest, that trio had 19 tackles, two tackles for loss, three total pressures, and a sack without any missed tackles. And it aligned with how the those three have played over the past month or so and certainly since the bye week. And Bernard, Williams, and KEO aren’t simply thriving downhill. In this game, they allowed five catches for 30 yards in their coverage area. And that aligns with how well the group has collectively covered this season.
author: Chris Trapasso

title: Report suggests it’s unlikely Buffalo Bills face Drake Maye vs. Patriots in early December
summary: The Patriots fell to 5-5 in a blowout against the Lions in Germany hours before the Bills moved to 8-1 with a win over the Jets in New Jersey, and in New England’s defeat, quarterback Drake Maye suffered a leg injury. Said injury might be rather serious based on a report from NFL Network insider […]
full_text: The Patriots fell to 5-5 in a blowout against the Lions in Germany hours before the Bills moved to 8-1 with a win over the Jets in New Jersey, and in New England’s defeat, quarterback Drake Maye suffered a leg injury. Said injury might be rather serious based on a report from NFL Network insider Ian Rapoport: Sources: #Patriots QB Drake Maye is believed to have suffered a significant lower leg injury that will keep him out an extended period of time. It’s even possible that Maye will miss the rest of the season. Maye came back from Germany and will seek more medical information. pic.twitter.com/jaOFw9qLGu — Ian Rapoport (@RapSheet) November 16, 2026 Appearing on Get Up on ESPN Monday morning, Adam Schefter reported Maye suffered a fractured ankle and the Patriots are trying to determine if he needs surgery. The Bills play the Patriots in New England on December 6 at 4:25pm ET. The tweet doesn’t make it sound like Maye is likely to be available for that contest. Schefter’s comments make it all but official he won’t play. We’ll continue to monitor this as we get closer to that Week 13 showdown. Suddenly, it feels like there’s a better chance the Bills see Patriots backup Tommy DeVito than Maye in that AFC East clash.

title: Carolina Panthers 2027 NFL Draft Prospect Profile: Ashton Hampton
summary: The 2027 NFL Draft feels like forever away, and we’re all caught up in the NFL season. Regardless, it’s never too early to look ahead to the Draft. This twice weekly series will take a closer look at some of the prospects the Carolina Panthers could select in the 2027 iteration of the Draft. In […]
full_text: CLEMSON, SOUTH CAROLINA - OCTOBER 3: Ashton Hampton #2 of the Clemson Tigers in action during the second half of a college football game against the Miami Hurricanes at Memorial Stadium on October 3, 2026 in Clemson, South Carolina. (Photo by Eston Parker/ISI Photos/ISI Photos via Getty Images) | ISI Photos via Getty Images The 2027 NFL Draft feels like forever away, and we’re all caught up in the NFL season. Regardless, it’s never too early to look ahead to the Draft. This twice weekly series will take a closer look at some of the prospects the Carolina Panthers could select in the 2027 iteration of the Draft. In this series, we’ll only be looking at prospects the Panthers could seriously consider. Today our profile will focus on Clemson Tigers cornerback Ashton Hampton. Bio Hampton (6’2”, 205 lbs.) was a three start recruit out of Tallahassee, FL back in 2024. After signing with Clemson, he saw quite a bit of action as a true freshman, even notching a couple interceptions (with one returned for a touchdown) in a rotational role. Hampton took over the starting role the following season as a sophomore, starting all 13 games making 45 tackles, three tackles for loss, a sack and an interception. With future second-rounder Avieon Terrell on the other side, Hampton got plenty of opportunities to work on his still improving coverage technique. Hampton started off this season hot, leading the nation in passes defended after four weeks. So far, he has only allowed 15 catches on 38 targets this season with two interceptions and 12 pass breakups. Strengths/Weaknesses Hampton has the height, length, and speed that NFL teams look for in a modern cornerback. His coverage skills have improved immensely in his three years at Clemson, and his expansive playing time in those years gives him more experience than most other corners in the Draft, especially the other juniors. He’s a hard worker who Dabo Swinney lauded back in August for his work ethic and how he attacks practice every day. Hampton competes in the run game as well, often fighting through blocks and making stops near the line of scrimmage. Hampton has regressed just a touch in tackling efficiency, already missing five tackles this season. A lot of his negative plays this season came in a single game against Miami. He allowed a touchdown, was flagged twice, and missed three tackles against the Hurricanes. Hampton has the rest of the season to show that that performance was just an outlier against a very good skill position group. Projection Hampton is a modern NFL corner with length, speed, and a willingness to get his nose dirty. Aspects that he struggled with last year have improved this season: he stays in phase on vertical routes, uses his length to finish at the catch point to break up passes, and his eyes have been much more disciplined in zone coverage. Hampton has put together a good season so far with just the one outlier against Miami. He fits the physical mold of what the Panthers like to have at boundary corner regardless of defensive coordinator and seems to have the hardworking mentality that coaches love. Depending on injuries and Mike Jackson’s upcoming free agency, Hampton could start immediately on the outside for the Panthers in 2027 if they take him. What do you think, Panthers fans? If Ashton Hampton is available when the Panthers select in the 2027 NFL Draft, should they take him? Sound off in the comments!
author: Daniel Belton

title: The Optimist: What the Turducken was that, refs?
summary: Despite the closeness of yesterday’s 20-17 victory over the New Orleans Saints, the Panthers established themselves as the team to beat in the NFC South. A dubious honor, to be sure, but it’s where we are now. The Tampa Bay Buccaneers are the only thing that resembles a threat in this division and I’m not […]
full_text: NEW ORLEANS - OCTOBER 07: Quarterback David Carr #8 of the Carolina Panthers successfully argues with referee Gene Steratore #114 and head linesman Paul Weidner #87 after being called for an intentional grounding against the New Orleans Saints at the Superdome on October , 2007 in New Orleans, Louisiana. The Panthers defeated the Saints 16-13. (Photo by Doug Benc/Getty Images) | Getty Images Despite the closeness of yesterday’s 20-17 victory over the New Orleans Saints, the Panthers established themselves as the team to beat in the NFC South. A dubious honor, to be sure, but it’s where we are now. The Tampa Bay Buccaneers are the only thing that resembles a threat in this division and I’m not confident that what we saw against them in Week 7 will happen again in Week 12. I guess we’ll see. The Panthers overcame aggressively one-sided officiated, middling quarterback play from Bryce Young, baffling editorial and marketing decisions by Fox Sports, and inconsistent kicking from Ryan Fitzgerald to do something they couldn’t manage last season: they won a game to take control of the division. They also snapped a three game losing streak, extended their streak of not sending anybody to injured reserve to two weeks, and are set to keep bringing key players back from injuries over the next several weeks. That said, it’s not all sunshine and beignets for the Panthers after conquering the Saints in New Orleans. We can’t pretend like that wasn’t a rough game even outside of the liberal interpretations of several rules that the officials were using. There are four things that need to be addressed coming out of Week 10 that need to be addressed more than anything else if the Panthers want to win any more games this season. Coaching and short yardage situations Play-calling and execution in the red zone and in short yardage situations have been a challenge all season. The Saints opening drive ended with an interception that, after one offensive play, became first and ten at the New Orleans 11 yard line. The Panthers walked away with zero points. They traded three punts with the Saints on subsequent drives before missing a field goal. The Panthers were managed to convert a first down or touchdown on four of eleven attempts with four or fewer yards to gain. On those attempts, they called seven running and four passing plays. That’s a better balance than I thought it was going to be after the game, but the truth remains simple: the Panthers need to find a way to consistently convert in these situations or they are going to have a disappointing end to an already middling season. “Discipline” You’re going to hear the word “discipline” this week as a critique of Dave Canales and his coaching staff about as often as you saw a flag thrown on the field yesterday. There were a couple of false starts and neutral zone infractions that were, indeed, characterized by a lack of discipline. However I would wager that the bulk of the 17 flags thrown for 152 penalty yards (only seventy fewer yards than the Saints total offensive output) were flags that most fans would describe as “bullshit.” When you lose and you point at one sided officiating, it’s called being a sore loser. I guess the Carolina Panthers are in danger of making me a sore winner. Let’s take a moment to consider the penalties that keyed the Saints three scoring drives. 1st & 10 at New Orleans 48, 8:46 3rd quarter , Panthers 7 Saints 0 Quarterback Tyler Shough found a wide open Jordan Tyson for an 18 yard pass. So far so clean. Tyson fell to the ground untouched while making the catch. Panthers linebacker Devin Lloyd fell onto and over Tyson in an effort to make sure he was downed by contact. This was flagged as unnecessary roughness. The NFL rule book, under Rule 12. Section 2. Article 8 states that unnecessary roughness can be defined as the following: running, diving into, or throwing the body against or on any player on the ground either before or after the ball is dead; It’s possible that Lloyd’s momentum qualified under the letter of this law. It is also possible, to revive a quote from last week, that this could have been described as a “bang-bang play.” Unfortunately, that term is not defined in the rule book. The fifteen yards from that penalty, added to the reception, put the Saints into the red zone for the first time in the game. Unlike during the rest of the game, the Saints did proceed to score from there under their own power. 1st & 5 at Carolina 42, 6:18 4th quarter, Panthers 10 Saints 7 Jaelan Phillips, unheld, pursued Shough and brought him down for a 17-yard sack. This should have brought up second & 22 from the Saints’ 39 yard line. Well out of field goal and certainly an uphill climb to get another first down. Instead, a selective interpretation of Rule 12. Section 2. Article 16 was enforced, calling Phillips for a horse-collar tackle and giving the Saints 15 yards instead of them losing 17. The text of the rule is below with one part highlighted for emphasis. No player shall grab the inside collar of the back or the side of the shoulder pads or jersey, or grab the jersey at the name plate or above, and pull the runner toward the ground. This does not apply to a runner who is in the pocket area or in the area defined by close-line play. If his knees are buckled by the action, it is a foul, even if the runner is not pulled completely to the ground. Your next reasonable question is “how does the NFL define the pocket area?”. Fortunately, that is easily answered by Rule 3. Section 25. “Pocket Area”: The pocket area is the area between the outside edges of the normal tackle positions on each side of the center extending backward to the offensive team’s end line. A player who is in possession of the ball is out of the pocket area, and the pocket area no longer exists, if any part of his body or the ball is outside of the pocket area. Where was Shough tackled? Between the inside hip of the right tackle and the center, 17 yards behind where the ball was snapped. Is 17 yards behind the line of scrimmage outside of the pocket area? No, the pocket area extends back to the offensive team’s end line (the back of the end zone, in NFL parlance). Were Shough’s knees buckled by the action? No, he fell to his side. He did not fall directly backwards in the way this rule was meant to penalize and prevent. After this penalty, the Saints ran a total of four plays for an average of 1.2 yards per play. Unfortunately, a poorly timed neutral zone infraction by Trevon Moehrig (five-yard penalty) and a ticky-tack pass interference penalty on Corey Thornton (17-yard penalty, but I couldn’t find a replay last night) added insult and further injury to the pile. Penalties, dubious penalties, accounted for 42 of the Saints 70 yards on this touchdown drive. 2nd & 7 at the New Orleans 37 , 1:10 4th quarter, Panthers 17 Saints 14 Tyler Dodson tackled Jordyn Tyson high. His hand was clearly around the upper chest to neck area of Tyson and replay showed that not even a single finger contacted or snared Tyson’s face mask. Nonetheless, Dodson was flagged for grabbing Tyson’s facemask. We return to Rule 12. Section 2, this time Article 15 holds our answers: If a player grasps an opponent’s facemask or helmet opening, he must immediately release it. He shall not grasp and control, twist, turn, push, or pull the facemask or helmet opening of an opponent in any direction. The only part of the rule that Dodson failed to comply with is that he did not immediately release Tyson’s facemask. That is because he never grabbed it in the first place. He did not grasp and control, twist, turn, push, or pull the facemask or helmet opening of Tyson. So it must be Dodson’s failure to release that which he did not ever grasp that gifted the Saints 15 yards on their tying field goal drive. Keep in mind that the Saints only advanced the ball six yards after this penalty before kicking their 55-yard field goal. Yes, there are legitimate things to…

summary: The Chicago Bears won’t issue an official injury report until Wednesday, but after the bye week, they held an extra practice today at Halas Hall, and several injured players returned to the field. Again, there will be no official practice participation designation until Wednesday, but the Chicago Tribune’s Brad Biggs shared that the “only player […]
full_text: Sep 20, 2026; Chicago, Illinois, USA; Chicago Bears running back Kyle Monangai (25) runs the ball against the Minnesota Vikings during the second half at Soldier Field. Mandatory Credit: Patrick Gorski-Imagn Images | IMAGN IMAGES via Reuters Connect The Chicago Bears won’t issue an official injury report until Wednesday, but after the bye week, they held an extra practice today at Halas Hall, and several injured players returned to the field. Again, there will be no official practice participation designation until Wednesday, but the Chicago Tribune’s Brad Biggs shared that the “only player not spotted during the portion of practice open to media was (cornerback) Kyler Gordon.” Gordon left their win over the Tampa Bay Buccaneers with an undisclosed injury — it looked like a left arm issue after landing awkwardly following a tackle — but returned to finish the game and appeared in 76% of the defensive snaps (57 total). His absence may not be injury-related, but we’ll know more on Wednesday. With Gordon the only Bear missing, that means running back Kyle Monangai (thumb/toe), cornerbacks Malik Muhammad II (toe) and Tyrique Steevenson (hand), and wideout Luther Burden III (concussion) were all on the field. Monangai hasn’t played since Week 4, and Muhammad has been out since Week 7. Stevenson and Burden both exited the Week 9 win over the Bucs. Burden’s participation doesn’t necessarily mean he’s cleared concussion protocol, but we’ll know more on Wednesday. Defensive lineman Dayo Odeyingbo is eligible to come off injured reserve this week, and if he’s ready, the Bears could open his 21-day practice window on Wednesday. The Bears host the New Orleans Saints this Sunday at Noon (CT). Here are a few clips from Halas Hall. title: How the Bears’ offense grades after their bye week
summary: The Bears had their bye week this week, using the weekend to recover and regroup heading into their final eight games of the 2026 season. All told, their 7-2 record is one to be proud of, and a good chunk of that success comes down to how their offense has performed this year. Ben Johnson […]
full_text: CHICAGO, ILLINOIS - NOVEMBER 8: Caleb Williams #18 of the Chicago Bears celebrates after a touchdown against the Tampa Bay Buccaneers during the first quarter at Soldier Field on November 8, 2026 in Chicago, Illinois. (Photo by Todd Rosenberg/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Bears had their bye week this week, using the weekend to recover and regroup heading into their final eight games of the 2026 season. All told, their 7-2 record is one to be proud of, and a good chunk of that success comes down to how their offense has performed this year. Ben Johnson has done a great job in his second year as the Bears’ head coach and their offensive play-caller, and Caleb Williams has led the passing attack to become one of the better units in the league. As the eye test can tell you if you’ve watched enough of this team, the analytics are quite favorable to this offense as it heads out of the Week 10 bye. All year, I’ve been recapping how the Bears have done analytically based on PFN Impact grading . Coming out of the bye week, I wanted to recap how each of their offensive players have ranked at their respective positions throughout the course of the season. Offense Caleb Williams: 82.0 (6th of 36 QBs) D’Andre Swift: 77.9 (12th of 44 RBs) Luther Burden III: 79.1 (17th of 79 WRs) Rome Odunze: 76.2 (25th of 79 WRs) Kalif Raymond: 72.6 (46th of 79 WRs) Colston Loveland: 74.2 (20th of 43 TEs) Theo Benedet: 79.9 (16th of 60 OTs) Joe Thuney: 75.8 (31st of 51 OGs) Garrett Bradbury: 71.5 (23rd of 30 Cs) Jonah Jackson: 87.6 (6th of 51 OGs) Darnell Wright: 88.9 (1st of 60 OTs) As a team, the Bears rank No. 8 in the NFL with an 80.3 PFN Offense Impact grade. Among the categories they rank within the top 10 among offenses include explosive rate, success rate, EPA per play, percentages of drives resulting in a score, and points scored per drive. It’s been a great year for Caleb Williams, who remains highly ranked in spite of his down game against the Buccaneers in Week 10. He ranks fifth in the NFL with a 68.7% completion percentage, and he ranks seventh with 0.19 EPA gained per dropback. His three-game absence due to a hamstring injury hurts his volume statistics, but from an efficiency perspective, he’s been one of the top passers in the league. Williams has been helped by a strong group of weapons and a talented offensive line. Including Williams, seven of the Bears’ 11 offensive starters have graded as above-average starters so far this season. This includes Darnell Wright, who has the highest PFN OL Impact grade of any offensive tackle in the NFL, and Jonah Jackson, who continues to perform at an incredibly high level at right guard. D’Andre Swift’s nose for the end zone has made him a valuable piece of the Bears’ offense, even though his efficiency numbers have dipped slightly without Kyle Monangai healthy. In the passing game, both Luther Burden III and Rome Odunze rank in the top 25, generally indicating they would both be the bonafide WR1s on a handful of teams around the league. Burden has graded higher than the likes of Justin Jefferson, Malik Nabers, and Davante Adams so far this year, cementing himself as one of the top young receivers in the NFL today. Additionally, Kalif Raymond serves as the Bears’ WR3 but has graded as a respectable WR2 by the NFL’s standards, which is always encouraging to see from a contributor. Colston Loveland started off the year slowly but has improved his PFN TE Impact grade over three of his last four games. The Bears’ interior offensive line has seen slight regression this year, as Joe Thuney has fallen from his 91.1 PFN OL Impact grade in 2025, which led all guards that year, to an average starting grade of 75.8. Likewise, Garrett Bradbury has been a considerable drop-off from Drew Dalman, their Pro Bowl center from last year, who retired abruptly this offseason. However, the strong play of Jackson and Wright has kept Chicago’s offensive line afloat, and Theo Benedet has been a pleasant surprise as an above-average starting left tackle this year. In the grand scheme of things, the Bears have one of the most complete offenses in the NFL this season. They face a difficult schedule for the rest of the regular season, but their offense has shown that it can compete with the best of them.
author: Jacob Infante

title: ESPN likes the Bears to repeat as division champs, but it won’t be easy
summary: Well, that division lead was fun while it lasted. The Chicago Bears (7-2), after entering their Week 10 bye at the top of the NFC North, are now suddenly third in the division following Sunday’s games. Minnesota (7-2), who’s beaten Chicago already this year and just dispatched Green Bay (6-4), and Detroit (7-2) now share […]
full_text: CHICAGO, ILLINOIS - NOVEMBER 08: Devin Bush #12 and Tyrique Stevenson Sr. #29 of the Chicago Bears celebrate a fourth down stop against the Tampa Bay Buccaneers during the second quarter at Soldier Field on November 08, 2026 in Chicago, Illinois. (Photo by Geoff Stellfox/Getty Images) | Getty Images Well, that division lead was fun while it lasted. The Chicago Bears (7-2), after entering their Week 10 bye at the top of the NFC North, are now suddenly third in the division following Sunday’s games. Minnesota (7-2), who’s beaten Chicago already this year and just dispatched Green Bay (6-4), and Detroit (7-2) now share the same record as the Bears but own tiebreakers (for now). Still, a number of experts think the Bears remain the best team in the North—or at least they did before the Vikings and their newly re-acquired quarterback Kirk Cousins put the beats on the Packers 30-10 yesterday. In a pre-Week 10 pundit poll of the NFC North’s ESPN beat writers , three of four put the Bears atop their ultimate NFC North rankings. “The Bears’ runway coming out of the bye is favorable with the Saints in Week 11 and the lowly Dolphins in Week 14, but Chicago has four division opponents (after an 0-2 start in NFC North play) and two potential Super Bowl previews with the Jaguars and Bills. Still, the Bears have proved they can win ugly and coach Ben Johnson is 7-0 in November since arriving in Chicago. With the most complete team in the division and an offense scoring 30.7 points per game when Williams has been under center, the Bears are in position to capture the division crown again,” said Courtney Cronin. “The Bears have the most well-rounded team in the division, and maybe the conference, following the trade for Simmons. But the one thing to watch is that both of their losses this season were in the division. That could be detrimental in a division tiebreaker if that is how the season ends,” Kevin Seifert, a Vikings insider, added. Rob Demovsky, notably of the Packers beat, even gave the Bears their props. “The Bears are the best team in the division despite being 0-2. They ran into Minnesota’s red-hot early-season defense in Week 2 and played without their quarterback in Week 5 at Green Bay. They haven’t even played the Lions yet, and Green Bay still has to go to Soldier Field as part of the three-game finishing stretch for the Bears that goes Packers at home, Lions at home and Vikings on the road,” he said. Only Lions writer Eric Woodyard shot down the Bears hype, saying—you guessed it—the Lions were the better squad. “The Bears might be the most well-rounded team in the division, but the Lions beat them twice last season, as Campbell could be one of the few coaches who knows how to counter the attack of Johnson—his former offensive coordinator. The division is certainly up for grabs, but Detroit’s explosive offense could be the game-changer in the division title race,” he wrote. Though this year is not last year, of course, it’s not hard to see how much trouble Detroit has given these Ben Johnson-led Bears. Even with Chicago adding Jeffery Simmons and the Lions now likely to lose Aidan Hutchinson for an extended period of time—maybe even the season—Detroit has been too good to dismiss. And while none of the writers envisioned Cousins putting Minnesota over the top, watching his performance in his first game back with Kevin O’Connell and the Vikings makes one curious. As for the Packers? See you at Soldier Field on Christmas. Payback time. The Bears will have every opportunity to prove those writers right with four division games in the back stretch of their season. If they can so much as break even against their North opponents for the season, it would get them to 10 wins. But who knows? 10 wins might not be enough to keep their crown. Time to see what Johnson, Caleb Williams, and this squad are made of.
