title: Broncos quarterbacks past and present, how does Bo Nix measure up?
summary: As Broncos fans, in our lifetime, we’ve had the absolute privilege of watching some of the best quarterbacks in football play for the Denver Broncos… and the frustration of having to watch the not-so-great struggle. Needless to say, Broncos fans know how to measure quarterback play, both good and bad, when they see it. That’s […]
full_text: DENVER, COLORADO - OCTOBER 15: Bo Nix #10 of the Denver Broncos reacts after winning in overtime against the Seattle Seahawks at Empower Field At Mile High on October 15, 2026 in Denver, Colorado. (Photo by Justin Edmonds/Getty Images) | Getty Images As Broncos fans, in our lifetime, we’ve had the absolute privilege of watching some of the best quarterbacks in football play for the Denver Broncos… and the frustration of having to watch the not-so-great struggle. Needless to say, Broncos fans know how to measure quarterback play, both good and bad, when they see it. That’s what’s so frustrating about the Bo Nix debate that has emerged this season. How could someone be ‘an insult to the quarterback position’ while simultaneously willing his team to victory every single week, breaking and setting records in the process? With the bye week nearly behind Broncos Country, it’s time to take an in-depth at just who Bo Nix is through the lens of Broncos quarterbacks past, the good, the bad, and the universally disliked. John Elway represents the gold standard for quarterback play in Denver. If you need explanation of how fundamentally important he was to the Denver Broncos, I question your Broncos Country citizenship (but welcome you anyway). The best part of Bo Nix just so happens to be the best of John Elway. They both share that ‘never-say-die’, ‘they ain’t licked us yet’, ‘we got them right where we want them’ mentality once the 4th quarter starts. It doesn’t matter what the score is. Call it Mile High Magic , persistence, dedication, or whatever you wish, but when the 4th quarter begins, fans know that the Broncos are never out of it so long as these special quarterbacks were/are under center. It’s hard to come up with a negative for the eternal face of the franchise, but there is one. At the time of his retirement, John Elway had thrown 226 interceptions – bringing him in all-time at 11th in NFL history (currently 17th all time). Bo Nix is different from Elway in that he does a better job of protecting the football. Throughout his young 43-game career, Nix has thrown just 27-interceptions compared to Elway’s 52 over the same number of games. Sure, Nix may throw passes 2 or 3-yards shorter than other quarterbacks, but he he just doesn’t throw the interceptions others do. No fan needs to be told how important limiting turnovers are, so no fan should need to be told how central Bo Nix’s ball control has been to the Broncos recent success. Jake Plummer was the first real spark of hope in the post-Elway era. Sure, Brian Griese had his moments, but not only did Griese never win a playoff game, he never played in one. Plummer was a fan favorite for his explosive plays, crazy beard, and unpredictability that stacked enough wins to go deep into the AFC playoff race during the 2005 season. Like Plummer, Bo Nix was the breath of fresh air after a long period of less-than-stellar Broncos football. Coming after the likes of Gus Ferrotte, Steve Beuerlein, Jarious Jackson, and Bradlee Van Pelt, Broncos Country embraced the confident (and successful!) quarterback that arrived as a free agent from Arizona. Here are two quarterbacks that had/have a deep understanding of what their arrival meant to the Broncos and the city of Denver as a whole. They have both risen to the occasion and grew into leaders that took their teams to AFC Championship games. Because Nix was drafted by the Broncos and not an unrestricted free agent acquisition like Plummer was, Nix benefits from a total franchise buy-in at least for another year (and likely longer). After losing the AFC Championship game in the 2005 season to the Pittsburgh Steelers, coach Mike Shanahan drafted Jay Cutler. Following a miraculous season, Denver suddenly had the supposed ‘quarterback of the future,’ on the bench and it was a fatal blow to Plummer’s security and confidence. Throughout the Bo Nix media saga this year, there has been nothing but unwavering support from inside the Broncos facility. No murmurs. No whispers. No attempts to find someone better. Why would there be? All he does is win. Who knows what the future holds, but it’s hard to not believe in a quarterback who consistently stacks wins like Bo Nix. Jay Cutler is a _________. You fill in the blank. It’s no secret that Broncos Country has intense feelings about him that are anything but positive. Like Jay Cutler, Bo Nix was one of the few Broncos quarterbacks actually drafted by the franchise. Although Cutler didn’t start until the inaugural Thursday Night Football game in 2006 (then on NFL Network), hopes for both quarterbacks’ careers were at the franchise’s highest when they debuted. They both could extend plays with their feet, generate highlight reel passes for touchdowns, and generally invigorated the franchise with the promise of youthful energy. Bo Nix is not like Jay Cutler in that he’s a likable, mature, quarterback who clearly has a desire to win above all else. Cutler, quite frankly, had none of those qualities. His body language would tell anyone all they needed to know about how things were going in Cutler’s head. In the face of adversity, Cutler would pout and mentally check-out when things got tough. When former coach and documented cheater Josh McDaniels took over in 2009, it was the threat of (checks notes) QB Matt Cassell that sent him into a full-blown tantrum, tailspinning him in a trade to the Chicago Bears. Bo Nix has thrown no tantrums. When things are tough, he locks in and, more often than not, finds a way to win. He has the maturity and drive that Jay Cutler never had and, sadly, never will. Peyton Manning is the only quarterback that could ever, or likely will ever, challenge Denver’s devotion to John Elway. In 2013, early in his Broncos career, Manning set records for single-season passing touchdowns (55), single-season passing yards (5,477), single-season passing yards per game (342.3), tied the single-game passing touchdowns record (7), total touchdowns in a season (56), and more. Like Manning, Bo Nix has had his fair share of records set, bested, or broken. Nix has the highest single-game completion percentage by a rookie (89.7%), most home passing touchdowns by a rookie (19), most games with 2+ passing TDs and 0 interceptions as a rookie (7), most games with 300+ passing yards, 4+ passing TDs, and a 140.0+ passer rating by a rookie (2). As for Denver Broncos franchise records, Nix stands alone with the longest rushing touchdown by a quarterback (62-yards), most passing yards by a rookie (3,775), most passing touchdowns by a rookie (29), most completions by a rookie (376), and most wins by a starting rookie QB (10). Before the bye, in the Broncos week 9 victory over the Carolina Panthers, Nix’s Broncos set the record for most consecutive 1-score games in NFL history (16). Unlike Peyton Manning’s time in Denver, Bo Nix has the benefit of youth on his side. The tragedy of the Peyton Manning era, that he didn’t get to Denver sooner. He toiled with the Colts for 14-season before landing in Denver and so, sadly, age and then injury caught up with Peyton after that record-shattering 2013 season. During his final year, the Super Bowl 50 2015 season, Manning missed 6-games to injury. As for Bo Nix, he’s never missed a regular season game due to injury and has only missed that one, crucial AFC Championship start to end last season. While it seems like everyone has been micro-analysing Bo Nix’s performances this season for reasons why he’s not ‘it,’ most people have overlooked the wealth of evidence that he is ‘it.’ Every quarterback that has strapped on the orange and blue has had their talents and their flaws. Never before has there been this level of scrutiny on a Broncos quarterback who has had so much success, especially coming off a decade of embarrassingly awful football in Denver. I’ve said it before and I’ll say it again, don’t be so focused on identifying what Bo Nix isn’t that you miss all that he is . When you look at…

title: Discussion: Which team will win the NFC North?
summary: We’re 10 weeks through the NFL season with eight remaining, and the playoff picture in the NFC North is as tight as ever. While the Detroit Lions technically sit atop the division thanks to a tiebreaker (2-0 in divisional games), it’s essentially a three-way tie between the Lions, Minnesota Vikings, and Chicago Bears—with the Green […]
full_text: DETROIT, MICHIGAN - SEPTEMBER 14: Head coach Ben Johnson of the Chicago Bears and Head coach Dan Campbell of the Detroit Lions shake hands following the game at Ford Field on September 14, 2025 in Detroit, Michigan. (Photo by Gregory Shamus/Getty Images) | Getty Images We’re 10 weeks through the NFL season with eight remaining, and the playoff picture in the NFC North is as tight as ever. While the Detroit Lions technically sit atop the division thanks to a tiebreaker (2-0 in divisional games), it’s essentially a three-way tie between the Lions, Minnesota Vikings, and Chicago Bears—with the Green Bay Packers not that far behind. Here’s a reminder of the standings through Week 10. Lions: 7-2 (2-0 in division) Vikings: 7-2 (3-1) Bears: 7-2 (0-2) Packers: 6-4 (1-3) Each team seemingly has an elite unit, and a significant weakness. The Lions have one of the best offenses in the league (sixth in scoring), but their defense—while improving—remains suspect, especially after the Aidan Hutchinson injury. The Vikings have the best defense in the league, but their offense is still struggling, even with the addition of Kirk Cousins. The Bears may be the most balanced team in the division, but there are some underlying concerns about their defense and they haven’t notched a divisional win yet. The Packers are easily the most inconsistent team in the division, but they’ve shown flashes of excellence on both sides of the ball. So today’s Question of the Day is simple: Who wins the NFC North this year? My answer: I think it’s going to be the Lions or Bears. Detroit has a pretty favorable schedule with games against the Falcons, Titans, and Giants still on the docket. And they’ve played their divisional opponents well. They’re certainly in the driver’s seat. But I do think the Bears are playing better football right now. They’re seventh in points scored and eighth in points allowed. While I think their secondary is very questionable, the addition of defensive tackle Jeffery Simmons helps their pass rush and could mask some of those back-end deficiencies. Ultimately, I think the division will come down to the two remaining games between the Lions and Bears: Thanksgiving and their Week 17 showdown in Chicago. As of right now, I’m taking the Bears. Who do you think will win the NFC North this year after 10 weeks of data? Vote in the poll below and share why in the comment section.

title: Aidan Hutchinson injury update: Detroit Lions DE has torn ACL; ‘no other significant damage’
summary: On Sunday, reports emerged that Detroit Lions defensive end Aidan Hutchinson was feared to have suffered a season-ending knee injury, but the team would continue to do more tests when they arrived back in the United States. Unfortunately, those fears were confirmed back in Michigan, as Hutchinson tore his ACL and will miss the rest […]
full_text: MUNICH, GERMANY - NOVEMBER 15: Aidan Hutchinson of Detroit Lions goes down with an injury while celebrating getting a sack during the NFL match between the New England Patriots and the Detroit Lions at the Allianz Arena on November 15, 2026 in Munich, Germany. (Photo by Sebastian Widmann/Getty Images) | Getty Images On Sunday, reports emerged that Detroit Lions defensive end Aidan Hutchinson was feared to have suffered a season-ending knee injury , but the team would continue to do more tests when they arrived back in the United States. Unfortunately, those fears were confirmed back in Michigan, as Hutchinson tore his ACL and will miss the rest of the Lions’ 2026 season, according to NFL Insider Tom Pelissero. Additional tests today confirmed Lions star DE Aidan Hutchinson suffered a torn ACL, sources tell @ringer @netflixsports . The good news is there’s no other significant damage for Hutchinson, who will now focus on getting ready for 2027. https://t.co/Ya6bNrRYAL pic.twitter.com/72L9nVy7cT — Tom Pelissero (@TomPelissero) November 16, 2026 If there is any positive news to glean from this situation, it is that additional testing revealed no further knee damage, which was also a major concern immediately after the injury. Still, it’s a huge blow to the Lions’ 2026 season, considering Hutchinson was the most disruptive force on the team’s defense. Through 11 games, Hutchinson had amassed 6.0 sacks, one forced fumble, and 52 pressures (trailing only Buffalo EDGE Greg Rousseau). More than that, he was a force multiplier, making his teammates around him better by drawing more attention and bodies away from them. On Sunday night after the Lions’ win over the New England Patriots, coach Dan Campbell noted they’ll need several players to step up if Hutchinson’s absence lasts. “We gotta go. We’ll see where Hutch is at, but we’ve gotta step up now,” Campbell said. “We need some guys to really step up—and if that is the case (with a serious Hutchinson injury), fill that role.” Detroit has been able to put together more of a diverse pass rush this year. Hutchinson has only been responsible for 6.0 of the team’s 32 sacks (he had 14.5 of the team’s 49 last year). The Lions have gotten a fair amount of production from Alim McNeill (6.5 sacks), DJ Wonnum (6.0), Derrick Moore (4.0), and Skyler Gill-Howard (2.0) along their defensive front. “We like ‘em. That’s why we acquired them when we did,” Campbell said of their remaining defensive linemen. “And I know this: Derrick Moore gets better every game. The more reps he gets, he gets better. It was good to get Wonnum back today. We know what Mac [McNeill] is, Sky. So can Tyleik (Williams). And all those guys, even Levi (Onwuzurike), (Tyler) Lacy, they play a different flavor, but they push the pocket; they got movement. But I think the important thing is, man, we knew we had to do to get out of this game with a win. We had to play really good defense.” For Hutchinson, it’s a devastating blow to his career. Just two years ago, he suffered a gruesome broken leg that ended his 2024 season. And while he returned to full health and form in both 2025 and 2026, recovering from a torn ACL brings a whole new set of challenges for Hutchinson.

title: Detroit Lions re-claim EDGE rusher following Aidan Hutchinson injury
summary: For the second time in the last 14 months, the Detroit Lions have claimed edge rusher Tyrus Wheat off waivers from the Dallas Cowboys. In a corresponding move, the Lions released cornerback Nick Whiteside from the 53-man roster. At cutdowns in 2025, the Lions claimed Wheat off waivers and placed him on their active roster. […]
full_text: BALTIMORE, MD - SEPTEMBER 22: Tyrus Wheat #99 of the Detroit Lions rushes the passer during an NFL football game against the Baltimore Ravens at M&T Bank Stadium on September 22, 2025 in Baltimore, Maryland. (Photo by Cooper Neill/Getty Images) | Getty Images For the second time in the last 14 months, the Detroit Lions have claimed edge rusher Tyrus Wheat off waivers from the Dallas Cowboys. In a corresponding move, the Lions released cornerback Nick Whiteside from the 53-man roster. At cutdowns in 2025, the Lions claimed Wheat off waivers and placed him on their active roster. Wheat was active for 15 games, though he was mainly a special teamer, playing 215 snaps in the third phase of the game and only 66 on defense. While his opportunities were minimal, he made the most of them, registering career highs in tackles (15), sacks (1.5), QB Hits (2), and PFF grade (82.3). Wheat left the Lions in free agency to re-join the Cowboys —the team that drafted him—but has been limited to just five games played with minimal production (three tackles). The Cowboys released him on November 14th to make room for defensive lineman Jonathan Bullard, and the Lions—having just lost Aidan Hutchinson to injury—were quick to claim him. With Wheat’s experience as a rush end in the Lions scheme, expectations are that he’ll get up to speed with the playbook quickly and could be incorporated into game action as soon as this weekend. While well-versed in the Lions system, expectations should reflect his involvement from last season: a core special teamer who can, on average, give the Lions 4-5 snaps a game on defense. Whiteside spent most of the season on the Lions’ practice squad but played in the last two games on the 53-man roster. It wouldn’t be surprising to see if the Lions try to re-add Whiteside to the practice squad.

title: Detroit Lions Week 10 snap counts: Derrick Moore steps up after Hutchinson injury
summary: In Week 10, the Detroit Lions moved to 7-2 after beating the New England Patriots in Munich, Germany. The Lions dominated the game in every way, and while key injuries will certainly be prominent storylines, they shouldn’t overshadow the fact that Detroit is playing complementary football right now and looks like it can go head-to-head […]
full_text: Detroit Lions edge rusher Derrick Moore (8) celebrates a sack of Miami Dolphins quarterback Malik Willis (not in the photo) during the second half at Hard Rock Stadium in Miami Gardens on Sunday, Nov. 8, 2026. | USA TODAY Network via Reuters Co In Week 10, the Detroit Lions moved to 7-2 after beating the New England Patriots in Munich, Germany. The Lions dominated the game in every way, and while key injuries will certainly be prominent storylines, they shouldn’t overshadow the fact that Detroit is playing complementary football right now and looks like it can go head-to-head with anyone. Let’s look at the snap counts from this game and see what they mean for the depth chart hierarchy and what we can ascertain moving forward. Quarterback Jared Goff: 61 (86%) Josh Dobbs: 10 (14%) With roughly seven minutes left in the fourth quarter and Detroit up 25 points, the Lions rested their starters, and Goff gave way to Dobbs for the final two possessions. Dobbs handed the ball off to the running backs six times, completed a first-down pass to Isaac TeSlaa, and the team went into victory formation for the final three plays. Running back Jahmyr Gibbs: 49 (69%) Sione Vaki: 18 (25%) — 20 special teams snaps (71%) Jacob Saylors: 6 (8%) — 20 (71%) Gibbs once again put on a show, totaling 252 all-purpose yards and finding the end zone twice—despite only playing three-and-a-half quarters. Before the Lions pulled their starters, Gibbs saw over 80% of offensive snaps, with Vaki taking the RB2 snaps. Vaki also got the first three touches with the reserves, before giving way to Saylors, who closed out the game. Wide receiver Jameson Williams: 56 (79%) Amon-Ra St. Brown: 47 (66%) Isaac TeSlaa: 46 (65%) Tay Martin: 11 (15%) — 20 (71%) DeAndre Carter: 5 (7%) — 11 (39%) The St. Brown storybook game will be talked about for years, and it played out even better than the NFL script writers could have hoped. His overall snaps were very similar to TeSlaa’s in this game, but context matters: St. Brown was pulled with the starters, and TeSlaa stepped into a WR1 role over the final 11 snaps, bringing things statistically closer than they were when the game was on the line. TeSlaa not only made a terrific acrobatic touchdown catch, again, but he also made the final catch of the game to seal the win. Tight end Sam LaPorta: 56 (79%) Brock Wright: 39 (55%) — 9 (32%) Tyler Conklin: 22 (31%) Like the other skill-position groups, the tight end reserves saw a slight uptick in usage after the starters (including LaPorta) were pulled. Not much box-score production from this group—a combined 4 catches for 30 yards—but they were all vital contributors in the run game. Offensive line LG Christian Mahogany: 71 (100%) — 5 (18%) RT Blake Miller: 71 (100%) — 5 (18%) LT Penei Sewell: 61 (86%) RG Tate Ratledge: 61 (86%) — 5 (18%) C Juice Scruggs: 61 (100%) — 5 (18%) LT/6th OL: Larry Borom: 10 (14%) — 5 (18%) LG Miles Frazier: 10 (14%) — 5 (18%) C Seth McLaughlin: 10 (14%) C Cade Mays: Inactive (injury) Absolute dominance up front throughout the day. PFF only faults the Lions for six (!) pressures allowed in this game, and the entire unit was mauling people in the run game. When the starters were pulled, Sewell was swapped out for Borum at LT, Frazier took over for Ratledge at RG, and McLaughlin got reps at center in place of Scruggs. Interior defensive lin e 3T Alim McNeill: 42 (71%) — 2 (7%) 3T Skyler Gill-Howard: 31 (53%) — 3 (11%) DT Tyleik Williams: 19 (32%) — 2 (7%) DL Levi Onwuzurike: 17 (29%) 3T Mekhi Wingo: DNP ( Inactive ) With the Patriots trailing by double digits most of the game, New England needed to pass a lot to stay competitive, and as a result, rookie Gill-Howard saw more snaps than Williams opposite McNeill. This situational rotation has worked all season, and the Lions shouldn’t feel the need to alter it. EDGE Rush End DJ Wonnum: 44 (75%) — 3 (11%) Rush End Derrick Moore: 40 (68%) — 3 (11%) Big End Tyler Lacy: 22 (37%) — 5 (18%) EDGE Aidan Hutchinson: 9 (15%) — INJURY Rush End Eric O’Neill: 7 (12%) — 11 (39%) Big End Ahmed Hassanein: DNP ( Inactive ) Following Hutchinson’s reported season-ending injury , the Lions turned to Wonnum and rookie Moore to step into larger roles. For Wonnum, it was a slight uptick from his typical starting reps, but Moore saw his opportunities increase sharply. Moore rewarded the Lions with four pressures and two sacks. Moore is expected to see his role increase following Hutchinson’s injury, but in the two games where his opportunities increased due to injury, he accounted for nine pressures and four sacks, giving Lions fans some hope he can soften the blow of losing their All-Pro defensive end. Linebacker SAM Derrick Barnes: 59 (100%) — 1 (4%) WILL/MIKE Malcolm Rodriguez: 34 (58%) — 2 (7%) WILL/SAM Trevor Nowaske: 33 (56%) — 22 (79%) MIKE K.J. Britt: 22 (37%) — 17 (61%) MIKE Joe Bachie: 1 (2%) — 20 (71%) WILL Owen Pappoe: 0 (0%) — 20 (71%) WILL Amen Ogbongbemiga: DNP ( Inactive ) Last week, their first without Jack Campbell in the lineup, the Lions leaned on Barnes and Rodriguez to play almost every snap, with Nowaske seeing about half the defensive snaps in a situational LB3 role. This week, Barnes and Nowaske’s roles stayed the same, but Rodriguez saw his snaps reduced in favor of Britt. Rodriguez still played a significant role, but Britt’s inclusion is an interesting wrinkle to keep an eye on. Was Britt’s familiarity with the Patriots the catalyst for this decision (the Lions signed him off New England’s practice squad) or is this a sign of things to come? We’ll have to wait and see. Cornerback CB/NB Roger McCreary: 59 (100%) — 3 (11%) CB Rock Ya-Sin: 55 (93%) — 1 (4%) CB Khalil Dorsey: 21 (36%) — 18 (64%) — INJURED CB Nick Whiteside: 7 (12%) — 3 (11%) CB Ennis Rakestraw: 5 (8%) — 7 (25%) CB D.J. Reed: Inactive (injury) McCreary and Ya-Sin have settled in as starters with Reed out, and both are noticeably more comfortable with the defense now that they’ve scaled up man coverage. When Reed returns, look for Ya-Sin to step back into a CB3 role but still play a significant role in nickel sets. Dorsey was injured in this game, and it’s unclear how that will affect him long-term, but it would be surprising to see the Lions turn to Whiteside or Rakestraw for more snaps, as both have struggled lately. Safet y S Brian Branch: 59 (100%) — 1 (4%) S Chuck Clark: 57 (97%) — 3 (11%) DB Andre Cisco: 5 (8%) — 5 (18%) DB Christian Izien: 1 (2%) — 16 (57%) DB Keith Abney: DNP ( Inactive ) Branch’s return has been felt in the secondary, and with him at a point where he doesn’t need to leave the field, the Lions have options at safety. Cisco played sparingly in his first game with the Lions, and it’s notable that he may have already passed Izien on the depth chart. Specialist s K Jake Bates: 11 (39%) P Jack Fox: 9 (32%) LS Hogan Hatten: 9 (32%) Bates had a kickoff out of bounds that he would like back, but otherwise it was a clean day for the group.

full_text: Detroit Lions defensive coordinator Kelvin Sheppard reacts to a play Miami Dolphins during the first half at Hard Rock Stadium in Miami Gardens on Sunday, Nov. 8, 2026. | USA TODAY Network via Reuters Co The Detroit Lions are 7-2 and in the driver’s seat of the NFC North. They’re on a five-game winning streak; they’ve yet to lose a divisional game despite it being an extremely strong set of teams, and they are in the midst of playing their best football right now. But for the second half of the show, the fellas mostly talk about the Hutchinson injury fallout. Who will need to step up on the defensive line? Who will get more opportunities? What kind of formations and schematic changes will defensive coordinator Kelvin Sheppard consider moving forward? And can the health and improvement of the secondary help mitigate some of the damage? title: Detroit Lions grades vs. Patriots: Team win offers hope despite Hutchinson injury
summary: There was plenty to love about the Detroit Lions’ dominant win over the New England Patriots. And while Aidan Hutchinson’s injury may be the biggest headline from the Munich game, there was plenty from Allianz Arena that should keep Lions fans optimistic about the team moving forward. Here is my Lions Week 10 report card […]
full_text: MUNICH, GERMANY - NOVEMBER 15: Jahmyr Gibbs of Detroit Lions runs with the ball during the NFL match between the New England Patriots and the Detroit Lions at the Allianz Arena on November 15, 2026 in Munich, Germany. (Photo by Sebastian Widmann/Getty Images) | Getty Images There was plenty to love about the Detroit Lions’ dominant win over the New England Patriots. And while Aidan Hutchinson’s injury may be the biggest headline from the Munich game, there was plenty from Allianz Arena that should keep Lions fans optimistic about the team moving forward. Here is my Lions Week 10 report card and positional grades for Detroit’s 35-10 victory. Quarterback: C+ Jared Goff threw two interceptions; both were his fault, and the second was an inexcusable decision that took points directly off the board. Because of those two plays alone, it feels like I can’t give him a grade above C+ in good faith. But the truth is the rest of his day was pretty dang good. I thought he navigated the pocket well, especially on his 50-yard pass to Jahmyr Gibbs. He didn’t make a ton of downfield throws or display any jaw-dropping plays, but he was very efficient, finishing with an electric 9.8 yards per attempt and a 101.9 passer rating. Running backs: A+ Jahmyr Gibbs was incredible all freakin’ day. He finished with 252 scrimmage yards and two touchdowns. The Patriots couldn’t handle his speed, his change-of-direction, or his strength. What was even better about his performance than normal is that the negative plays were almost completely non-existent. He had just one touch that went for negative yards, and only a couple more were stopped for zero yards. Sione Vaki was very efficient, too, earning 28 yards on just six carries (4.7 YPC). Overall, the Lions produced an impressive 55% success rate and +0.21 EPA/play on running plays vs. the Patriots. For comparison’s sake, the Patriots were allowing just a 36.9 success rate going into this game and had produced a negative EPA/run. Tight ends: B I was a little disappointed with Sam LaPorta’s play as a receiver. He didn’t create much separation against the Patriots’ defenders, and he had a touchdown grab knocked out of his hands. He finished with just a single catch for 16 yards on four targets. However, the Lions used a ton of tight ends against the Patriots in the running game, and that played a significant role in Detroit controlling the line of scrimmage. LaPorta (26), Brock Wright (29), and Tyler Conklin (17) all logged over 15 run-blocking snaps on the day. Wide receivers: A+ Amon-Ra St. Brown was seemingly unstoppable on Sunday. It was going to take the entire country of Germany to stop him on both of his long catch-and-run touchdowns, and they certainly weren’t going to do that against their most beloved NFL player. Jameson Williams’ day shouldn’t be overlooked, either. He caught four passes for 50 yards, including an impressive toe-tapping catch on the sidelines. Even Isaac TeSlaa got in on the fun with a highlight-reel touchdown grab. This unit lived up to its full potential for the first time in several weeks. Offensive line: A- Outside of some early pass protection issues, the Lions’ offensive line was nails in Munich. They were getting significant push in the run game, and after settling down, they helped Jared Goff breathe comfortably in the pocket. When the offensive line plays this well, the Lions’ entire offense is as close to unstoppable as we’ve seen. Defensive line: A- While the Lions’ pressure was inconsistent at times without Aidan Hutchinson in the lineup, they still gave the Patriots hell for most of the game. In the run game, the Patriots were unable to do anything. Their running backs combined for 17 carries, 31 yards, and just 1.8 yards per carry. The pass rush generated five total sacks, six quarterback hits, and over a 50 percent pressure rate: Pressure was a problem again for the Patriots today Lions pressured them on 51% of plays (up from 46% season rate, 2nd highest in the NFL). *This is the 5th time this season NE has allowed a pressure on 50% or more of dropbacks* Data: @SumerSports — Lindsay Rhodes (@lindsay_rhodes) November 15, 2026 It will be tough to maintain that without Hutchinson and against a better offensive line, but Derrick Moore, Alim McNeill, DJ Wonnum, and Skyler Gill-Howard have all played some pretty sound football, and all were disruptive on Sunday. Linebackers: B The linebackers deserve a lot of praise for Detroit’s stout run defense, but they were a bit of a liability in the pass game again. It didn’t end up costing the Lions too much in this game, because once Drake Maye went down, it looked like Tommy DeVito just didn’t see the field very well. But coverage against tight ends and running backs continues to be a bit of an issue. Still, this defense continues to play good football without its field general at MIKE linebacker, and that means something. Secondary: A- I thought the safety play was fantastic on Sunday. Brian Branch was all over the place in the run game and the pass game. Chuck Clark flipped a couple Patriots and made the receiving corps pay for every DeVito murderball. I can’t give them an A, though, because of a couple of stupid and costly pass interference flags. It wasn’t a great game for Ennis Rakestraw—who also missed a key tackle—nor Nick Whiteside. But the good news is the top corners in this game—Rock Ya-Sin and Roger McCreary were very, very good. Or, as Dan Campbell said: “I thought the back end played outstanding,” Campbell said. “We played some sticky coverage today, bought us a little bit of time.” Special teams: B Nothing too notable from this group on Sunday. The return team didn’t look particularly good, but coverage was good on both punt and kickoff. Jake Bates is still perfect when Jack Fox isn’t blocking his kicks. He did put a kickoff out of bounds and a touchback in the end zone. Coaching: A This was a tough week for both coaches. Flying across the globe, adjusting to a time zone six hours away, and dealing with all of the crazy logistics of getting ready for Sunday is not easy. It’s clear one team was way more prepared than the other. On top of that, Lions offensive coordinator Drew Petzing is really starting to come into his own, building plays off of previous plays, and seemingly having the right call in the right moment more often than not. As he hits his stride, the Lions offense can carry them a long way. But don’t sleep on the defensive coaching, either. Kelvin Sheppard has had to deal with two emotionally draining injuries to two of their best players. Yet through a heavy rotation at every level of the defense, things have never looked more steady and controlled. Say what you will, facing a beat-up Patriots offense with a backup quarterback leading most of Sunday afternoon, but Detroit used to get beat up by backups all the time. The defense finally feels like it’s coming together.
author: Jeremy Reisman

title: Discussion: Are you confident in the Detroit Lions defense without Aidan Hutchinson?
summary: The Pyrrhic victories are unfortunately mounting for the Detroit Lions. Despite winning five games in a row, they have lost two irreplaceable parts of their team. The Lions have now lost two cornerstone pieces of their defense over the last three weeks. Jack Campbell suffered a scary neck injury and will be sidelined for an […]
full_text: MUNICH, GERMANY - NOVEMBER 15: Aidan Hutchinson of Detroit Lions goes down with an injury while celebrating getting a sack during the NFL match between the New England Patriots and the Detroit Lions at the Allianz Arena on November 15, 2026 in Munich, Germany. (Photo by Sebastian Widmann/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Pyrrhic victories are unfortunately mounting for the Detroit Lions. Despite winning five games in a row, they have lost two irreplaceable parts of their team. The Lions have now lost two cornerstone pieces of their defense over the last three weeks. Jack Campbell suffered a scary neck injury and will be sidelined for an unknown period of time. Against the New England Patriots in Munich, the Lions lost yet another heartbeat of their defense. Aidan Hutchinson suffered a serious knee injury that will likely sideline him for the rest of the 2026 season —and perhaps into the 2027 season as well. The impact Hutchinson has on this team is difficult to quantify. For a team built on grit, Hutchinson exemplified that to a tee. Without Hutchinson, can the Lions defense continue to play at a high level? Today’s Question of the Day is: Are you confident in the Detroit Lions defense without Aidan Hutchinson? My answer: I am cautiously optimistic. Few teams boast a pass rusher like Hutchinson, and he was by far the most potent edge on the Lions’ roster. Hutchinson will finish the season with 52 pressures per PFF, while the next-closest defender is Alim McNeill (36) and the next-closest edge is DJ Wonnum (18)—that’s a significant gap. Without question, the Lions are in a far worse position than they were entering the week. The ceiling for the Lions to be a great defense is gone, in my opinion. However, I think the floor is still intact. When the Lions lost Hutchinson back in 2024, their defense was ill-equipped to handle it. The pass rushing depth was largely just Josh Paschal and Al-Quadin Muhammad and The Lions had to make a deadline deal to acquire Za’Darius Smith. They lost Alim McNeill to a torn ACL in Week 15. By the time they rolled into the postseason, their pass rush was limited. This limitation put a lot of pressure on the secondary, and the defense wound up allowing 45 points to the Commanders. This, in turn, forced the offense to be perfect, and on a day when Jared Goff threw three interceptions, it was not. I think the rest of 2026 will be tough sledding for the defense, but the Lions have some options. For one, Wonnum has been playing very well this season. He is not the game-wrecker that Hutchinson is, but he is a steady presence capable of sound run defense and pass rush. Secondly, rookie Derrick Moore is coming into his own of late, now having four sacks in two games. Refining his skillset is still a priority for him, but it’s not hard to see the potential with him. It might be earlier than expected, but he now has to step into a sizable role on defense. The Lions also have McNeill playing at an All-Pro level, while Tyleik Williams is quietly entrenching himself as a menace up the middle. Sprinkle in guys like Tyler Lacy (another underappreciated player) and Skyler Gill-Howard (the pass-rushing rookie tackle), and the Lions not only have more talent on the defensive line than in 2024, but also more flexibility. The loss of Hutchinson will put more pressure on the secondary to step up. The secondary has been balling as of late, but there will be questions about whether that is a mirage or not. Over the last five games, the defense has played the hapless Arizona Cardinals, the inconsistent Green Bay Packers, the formerly-hapless Minnesota Vikings, the hapless Miami Dolphins, and the Drake Maye-less New England Patriots. You can only play the opponent on the schedule, but concerns about the authenticity of this defensive turnaround are certainly justified—are they actually good now or just benefitting from weak and misfortunate opponents? If the Lions can put up a great defensive showing versus the Chicago Bears on Thanksgiving, then you can squash some of my doubts. What makes me encouraged about the secondary is that they look invigorated. They are intercepting passes. They are batting away balls. They are (mostly) limiting the explosive plays. Whereas the defense looked lost to start the season, they are playing with far more confidence at this point. Getting Brian Branch was certainly a catalyst, and if the Lions can add Kerby Joseph to the mix as well, then the defensive back group suddenly looks far more capable You cannot replace a player like Hutchinson. You will struggle to even recreate him in the aggregate. He is a rarity amongst NFL players, a player with a high level of talent and the motor to back it up. However, I think that the Lions have enough pieces on their defense to weather the storm. If they can be a good defense, that might be enough when paired with this potent offense. Do you have faith in this defense without Hutchinson? Let us know in the comments below.
author: John Whiticar

title: Packers WR clears waivers, set up for practice squad return
summary: On Saturday, the Green Bay Packers waived receiver Coleman Owen from the 53-man roster — in part to make room for the addition of receiver Skyy Moore, who was coming off the injured reserve. Owen, who also returned kicks and punts, directly replaced Moore when Moore went down with an ankle injury. Now, Owen has […]
full_text: (Photo by Michael Owens/Getty Images) | Getty Images On Saturday, the Green Bay Packers waived receiver Coleman Owen from the 53-man roster — in part to make room for the addition of receiver Skyy Moore, who was coming off the injured reserve. Owen, who also returned kicks and punts, directly replaced Moore when Moore went down with an ankle injury. Now, Owen has cleared waivers without being claimed, so he’s free to sign with anyone’s practice squad. Notably, the Packers have an open spot on their practice squad, as the team just released defensive lineman David Blay Jr. from the 17-man unit. Things are lining up so that Green Bay can bring back Owen to the practice squad, based on the team’s actions. If you need a reminder, this is what the Packers’ practice squad currently looks like, with an open spot available: QB: Cam Miller RB: None WR: Isaiah Neyor and Quincy Skinner Jr. TE: Kenny Fletcher Jr. and Drake Dabney OL: Dalton Cooper and Dillon Wade DL: Mazi Smith ED: Nyjalik Kelly, Arron Mosby and D.J. Johnson LB: Jack Dingle CB: Domani Jackson and Elijah Culp S: John Saunders Jr. K: Lenny Krieg (international exemption) P: None LS: None The only players currently on the practice squad who have been elevated for game action this year are Dabney (Weeks 9, 10) and Mosby (Weeks 6-8). Mosby has now exhausted his call-ups this year, while Dabney still has one available. Owen was elevated once as a member of the practice squad before being signed to the 53-man roster, so if the Packers bring him back to the practice squad, he can be elevated two more times in 2026. Former practice squadders Mekhi Becton Sr., Pierre Strong Jr. and Kristian Welch remain on Green Bay’s 53-man active roster. On Monday, head coach Matt LaFleur stated that the team will know more about Moore’s ankle injury on Friday , when players return to the club after a three-day break. If Moore is out, it could open the door for Coleman to be elevated on game days as a returner. The Packers also worked out defensive lineman Haggai Ndubuisi today, a player who would qualify for the international exemption. Currently, that role is filled by kicker Lenny Krieg. Ndubuisi previously has been with the Arizona Cardinals, Denver Broncos, San Antonio Brahmas (UFL), Washington Commanders, New England Patriots, Houston Texans and Tampa Bay Buccaneers. The Nigerian trained in London for six months as a combo offensive lineman and defensive lineman in the NFL’s international program. He began his NFL career in 2022 as an offensive lineman before switching to the defensive line in 2023. His time in Arizona did not overlap with defensive coordinator Jonathan Gannon’s time in Arizona, but he was in New England when DeMarcus Covington, currently the Packers’ outside linebackers coach/run game coordinator/assistant head coach – defense, was the defensive coordinator of the Patriots. Since being let go by the Buccaneers in late July with an injury settlement, Ndubuisi has worked out with the Indianapolis Colts, Minnesota Vikings, Buffalo Bills, Las Vegas Raiders and now the Packers. In-season, Green Bay has only worked out one other international player: Australian edge defender Cruz Smith. title: The Packers’ offensive line regressed against the Vikings
summary: We all saw the Green Bay Packers’ offensive line get pushed around by the Minnesota Vikings on Sunday, but I’m sure some of you are wondering exactly why the team messed up in crucial situations over and over. Hopefully, you’ll learn a little more about the game and the status of the team by the […]
full_text: (Photo by Michael Reaves/Getty Images) | Getty Images We all saw the Green Bay Packers’ offensive line get pushed around by the Minnesota Vikings on Sunday, but I’m sure some of you are wondering exactly why the team messed up in crucial situations over and over. Hopefully, you’ll learn a little more about the game and the status of the team by the end of this article. I want to start with this up front: I don’t think the Packers’ running game was actually that bad on Sunday — at least on the relative scale of Green Bay’s running game. Where I really think the team regressed was in the pass protection department, where they played their worst game since at least the first three weeks of the season. Let’s start with the run game. Running Game Kaleb Johnson carries Counter: +3 Duo: +2 OZ: +1 Counter: +3 Sweep: -2 Counter: +6 Split Zone: +8 Counter: +9 Split Zone: +4 Long Trap: +8 pic.twitter.com/9gPWu2c1xC — Justis Mosqueda (@JuMosq) November 16, 2026 MarShawn Lloyd carries: Counter: +11 Counter: +4 Long trap?: -3 Counter: +1 pic.twitter.com/jJFd9vKZ77 — Justis Mosqueda (@JuMosq) November 16, 2026 Chris Brooks carries: Insert: 0 Counter: +1 pic.twitter.com/Freia8Srpz — Justis Mosqueda (@JuMosq) November 16, 2026 I clipped up all of the runs that the Packers’ running backs had in the tweets above, if you want to check them out. There are a couple of poor calls (like the pin and pull sweep that had no chance because of Minnesota’s defensive call), but for the most part, Green Bay got a hat on a hat against the Vikings, something we can’t say of prior games. Can they move anyone? No! They never have been able. They have one preferred starter on the field. Can they get in front of people, at least on the ground? The last two weeks are probably the Packers’ best back-to-back performances this season. The first big mistake the Packers made was on this duo run. The diagram above is what Green Bay’s offensive line is expecting pre-snap. Because the Vikings stunted their three-technique defensive lineman outside on the play, though, right tackle Anthony Belton never gets off his block, and there’s a free runner when the play should have gotten up to the safety level. It’s the second play in the Johnson cutup . The second big mess-up was on this outside zone toss, where the team handled another stunt poorly. On paper, if everyone stays in the gaps they line up in, the diagram above is what the run should look like. Essentially, offensive linemen try to “scoop” defensive linemen to their play-side, and if there isn’t a defender in that gap, they climb to the second level and try to work on backers and safeties, after first securing that no one stunted in their play-side gap pre-snap. The problem is that the Vikings don’t stay in their gaps, and they slant weak on the play. Because of this, there should be three pass-offs. The Packers don’t execute a single one of them, leading to all three players getting penetration. let's check in on the Packers' run blocking pic.twitter.com/lX7D1OOU2z — Benjamin Solak (@BenjaminSolak) November 16, 2026 It’s the play that you keep seeing screenshots of over and over again. It’s the fourth play in the Johnson cutup. These plays look like crap, but outside of that, the Packers mostly played their rules correctly this week — again, which has not been the case over most of the year. Over the last two weeks, they’ve found something that worked for them: running counter, a play that allows the offensive linemen to get on train tracks and just block downhill instead of worrying about assignments being exchanged by the Vikings’ blitzes and stunts. Everyone makes a wall of down blocks except for a kickout player (either a pulling guard or a tight end) and an insert player (again, either a pulling guard or tight end). As a reminder, the zone plays that didn’t work against Minnesota are what Green Bay ran a lot of in the preseason and through Week 3 of the regular season. They went out of their way to try to get good at what they’re doing the worst this year. I didn't remember the wingback counter coming off Pierre Strong playing QB lol pic.twitter.com/Oi1382F4VV — Justis Mosqueda (@JuMosq) November 10, 2026 On counter and split zone concepts, the Packers had 10 carries for 50 yards (5 yards per carry) on the day. On other concepts, which mostly relied on changing targets post-snap, the Packers were just 6 for 6 (1 YPC). My guess: Green Bay wanted to punish Minnesota with the ground game this week, particularly counter and split zone runs, but the game got out of hand and they had to ditch that script when they were down three scores. The team played a lot of extra tight end looks in this game , allowing the Vikings to get an extra player in the box on defense. Passing Game The passing game is really where the Packers’ line struggled, in part because they were playing these multiple tight end sets that added just another variable for Green Bay’s line to account for. Against Minnesota, the Packers looked completely lost on the interior offensive line, which was made up of Laken Tomlinson, John Williams and Travis Glover (left to right). I thought we were over this. From Weeks 4-9, after the disaster that was the Atlanta Falcons game on Monday Night Football , the Packers had just a 35 pressure rate, good for the 16th-lowest in the NFL over this time. They looked like an average pass-protection unit over the last two months. In the first three weeks of the year, the Packers cracked the 40 percent pressure rate twice, but had done it only once in the past six weeks. It seemed like they turned a corner, but then the Vikings came to town. Yesterday, Minnesota posted a 60 percent pressure rate, the highest number that Green Bay has allowed all season. In Weeks 1-3 and 10, the Packers have allowed a 46 percent pressure rate overall, the highest mark in the league over those four weeks. It’s hard to know what Green Bay’s offensive line will look like moving forward , because we just saw a huge regression after a streak of solid play. Mind you, this all came with Love’s time to throw at just 2.27 seconds against the Vikings, and they still sacked him eight times in this game. For perspective, the average NFL time to throw is around 2.8 seconds, so Love was operating about a half-second faster than the average. And he was still getting popped left and right. Had he held onto the ball at an average rate, the line’s pressure rate would have been even higher. Here are just a few clips of the Packers’ offensive line blowing up plays from essentially the snap of the ball on Sunday, just to show how poor it was: Tight formation allows MIN to get 9 in the box. Dallas Turner is never touched by Mekhi Becton. Love hit blindside pic.twitter.com/XL0DZct61t — Justis Mosqueda (@JuMosq) November 16, 2026 Packers 7 for 5 in protection in this tight 3 TE set (Becton at TE again). Either Becton or Glover doesn't pick up former Packer Eric Wilson on the delayed blitz pic.twitter.com/ZuavJeKvbZ — Justis Mosqueda (@JuMosq) November 16, 2026 Becton is dual reading 61 and 43. Jonnu's chip does nothing. Love has to step up into the guy John Williams lost to one-on-one. pic.twitter.com/lPG55Zpzro — Justis Mosqueda (@JuMosq) November 16, 2026 This tweet is supposed to say Belton, not Becton. I apologize to the Becton family. Belton loses on athleticism (should be a guard in the NFL) and Williams + Becton just blow their blocks. Jordan Love sacked pic.twitter.com/sda9P4MjPe — Justis Mosqueda (@JuMosq) November 16, 2026 John Williams had the best seat in the house to watch the game on Sunday pic.twitter.com/dcIHCNm1np — Justis Mosqueda (@JuMosq) November 16, 2026 Packers iOL is supposed to be 3 for 3 and loses all 3 pic.twitter.com/C6dmWsh2ho — Justis Mosqueda (@JuMosq) November 16, 2026 Lloyd is probably supposed to cross block here (Packers would have still been in a 1 for 2 because they let the Vikings walk up 8 with their formation width) pic.twitter.com/MscsDtPJGP —…

title: Packers Film Room: Long snapping on Kicks in Week 10
summary: In this space, we look at the snap-to-hold operation on field goals and extra points. After seeing seven kicks last week, we only have three this week: two field goals and an extra point. We start by looking at the snap accuracy to the holder. After a nice week last week, what do we have […]
full_text: (Photo by Brooke Sutton/Getty Images) | Getty Images In this space, we look at the snap-to-hold operation on field goals and extra points. After seeing seven kicks last week , we only have three this week: two field goals and an extra point. We start by looking at the snap accuracy to the holder. After a nice week last week, what do we have this week? A big thank you to my assistant (my 8-year-old son) for doing the drawing this week. Last week we started tracking snap-to-holder and snap-to-kick times (in seconds). I don’t have a reliable time for snap-to-holder, but it seems like 0.28-0.34 is about the range we’re looking for. On the snap-to-kick time, we’re looking for something in the 1.2-1.28 second range. Kick 1: 53-yard field goal (Miss) Good snap, slightly into the body of Whelan. Whelan is able to catch the ball by the laces and get the hold down, with the ball tilted slightly forward and away from Smack. Operation looks good, but the kick starts a little off-line to the right and keeps drifting. Snap-to-holder: 0.31 Snap-to-kick: 1.26 Kick 2: Extra Point (Make) Orzech’s worst snap of the day, up at the facemask of Whelan. Whelan is able to corral the ball and get down a nice hold. Good, solid kick from Smack that splits the uprights. Keep an eye on Karl Brooks [94] on the right side. He was good on the previous snap, but this snap sees the old issues rearing their ugly head again. He’s extremely slow out of his stance, allowing the rusher to easily get the edge. If the snap-to-kick time was a tick slower, this would have been blocked. Snap-to-holder: 0.33 Snap-to-kick: 1.28 Kick 3: 40-yard field goal (Make) Nice snap from Orzech, arriving in Whelan’s hands directly over the hold point. Looks like a throw to second to catch a base stealer. Whelan just needs to catch it and guide it down to the snap. Solid kick from Smack that splits the uprights. With fewer rushers on the line, Brooks doesn’t need to worry about anyone from the inside, so he fires out and lets the rusher know that he doesn’t appreciate what happened on the previous play. Snap-to-holder: 0.33 Snap-to-kick: 1.28 Average snap-to-holder: 0.32 Average snap-to-kick: 1.27 Albums listened to: Anberlin – CURRENCY

title: The Packers’ bye week will have a unique structure
summary: The Green Bay Packers will be the first in NFL history to do something. Not only will the team be part of the initial duo to debut the league’s new Thanksgiving Eve window, but they also have to figure out how to do it coming off a bye week. Generally, a bye week is a […]
full_text: (Photo by Ric Tapia/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Green Bay Packers will be the first in NFL history to do something. Not only will the team be part of the initial duo to debut the league’s new Thanksgiving Eve window, but they also have to figure out how to do it coming off a bye week. Generally, a bye week is a vacation for players. They’re given the week off, allowed to travel to wherever they please during that period. For the Packers, though, they’re also getting ready for a game that will kick off on next Wednesday, meaning that they don’t have a full week to give their players. According to Green Bay head coach Matt LaFleur, the solution the team found — after discussing it with management, the team’s players and the NFL Players Association — was to give the players three days off this week, leading up to their matchup against the Los Angeles Rams, and then four days off after the team plays Los Angeles. The Packers’ players were in the building today, so that the team could “flush” the loss to the Minnesota Vikings, according to LaFleur. They’ll have the next three days off, returning on Friday for preparation against the Rams. Green Bay will travel on Tuesday, meaning that we can expect the Packers’ practices this week to be on Saturday, Sunday and Monday. On usual bye weeks, players would be returning to the facility on Tuesday — after the Packers would have concluded their three practices for the Rams game — so you can see how this Sunday game-bye week-Wednesday game schedule presented issues for just about everyone involved. In the media, we’ve already talked about this period as consecutive “mini-byes” for the Packers going into and coming out of the game against Los Angeles. Now we know that Green Bay’s practice schedule and days off will also reflect that.

title: Packers’ Matt LaFleur talks injuries, Micah Parsons’ return
summary: When asked about the status of edge defender Micah Parsons, Green Bay Packers head coach Matt LaFleur stated, “That’s my plan,” when the topic of Parsons playing against the Los Angeles Rams on Thanksgiving Eve was brought up. “I think my plan’s been different than everybody else’s this whole time,” LaFleur joked on Monday about […]
full_text: (Photo by Stacy Revere/Getty Images) | Getty Images When asked about the status of edge defender Micah Parsons, Green Bay Packers head coach Matt LaFleur stated, “That’s my plan,” when the topic of Parsons playing against the Los Angeles Rams on Thanksgiving Eve was brought up. “I think my plan’s been different than everybody else’s this whole time,” LaFleur joked on Monday about Parsons’ ACL and meniscus recovery. When he snapped back into serious answers, LaFleur added, “There’s still a couple more hurdles for him to clear before we can definitively say that he’s a go.” So if you’re tracking at home, the answer is that Parsons will probably make his 2026 debut against the Rams in two weeks, but some progress needs to be made before then. Beyond Parsons, LaFleur also touched on a couple of other injury situations that popped up last week for the Packers. On the offensive line, LaFleur stated that the team was “expecting” Kevin Zeitler to make the start at right guard last week, but he had a “freak thing” happen to his triceps during Thursday’s practice. On whether or not Zeitler will play against the Rams, LaFleur said, “We’ll see where he’s at.” Instead of Zeitler, the starting guards against the Minnesota Vikings were Laken Tomlinson on the left and Travis Glover on the right, with Aaron Banks sidelined with an injury of his own but still healthy enough to be active on game day. When pressed on whether Banks is still in the mix as a starter, LaFleur replied, “He certainly is.” Here’s the short: The Packers’ next game is in late November, and we have no idea which two of the six players that have played guard for Green Bay this year are going to be their long-term options. Expect what amounts to be a position battle to continue when the team returns to practice. There is some good news on the injury front, though. LaFleur stated, “No,” when asked if cornerback Brandon Cisse’s rib injury is going to lead to him missing significant time. He, along with two receivers, dropped out against the Vikings. Receiver Bo Melton will be “alright,” according to LaFleur, while fellow receiver Skyy Moore, who just returned from the injured reserve, “will be closer to the end of the week before we can have any determination about that.” Melton injured his thigh, while Moore injured his ankle. For what it’s worth, Moore’s injury that led to him going on the injured reserve previously was also an ankle issue.

title: Packers By The Numbers: Stats from the Week 10 loss to the Vikings
summary: Did you all know that they keep numbers even in games where your team loses by 20? Feels pretty rude to me. As we do every week in this space, we’re looking at some stats from the Green Bay Packers’ most recent game, courtesy of SumerSports. Today we’re looking at the 30-10 loss to the […]
full_text: (Photo by Todd Rosenberg/Getty Images) | Getty Images Did you all know that they keep numbers even in games where your team loses by 20? Feels pretty rude to me. As we do every week in this space, we’re looking at some stats from the Green Bay Packers’ most recent game, courtesy of SumerSports . Today we’re looking at the 30-10 loss to the Minnesota Vikings in Week 10. Offense The Packers wanted to operate out of a heavy offense this week. Coming into this game, the Packers used 11 personnel (1 RB, 1 TE, 3 WR) on 62.0% of their offensive snaps, the 10th highest rate in the league. They clearly wanted to try to find ways to protect Jordan Love, so they were only in 11 personnel on 35.2% of their snaps. That was their lowest rate of 11 personnel since the 47.8% mark they posted in their Week 1 game against the Vikings. That 5.6% personnel in the “Other” category is their use of a 6th offensive lineman. They hadn’t used that personnel group since their Week 1 game (they had 4 snaps with a 6th offensive lineman in that game). Here’s how they looked in the pass game by Personnel: As I thought when watching live, their pass game looked to be operating best when they were out of 11 personnel. This doesn’t show the breakdown between their tempo and non-tempo snaps, but I would expect their EPA when going tempo out of 11 was their best way to operate. Did going heavier help protect Love? Not really! He was pressured on 56.5% of his dropbacks, despite posting an absurdly quick 2.21 seconds to throw. The Vikings averaged 2.3 seconds to pressure. I did look to see what the pressure rate was when the Packers were in 11 personnel to see if he had any more time. Perhaps that personnel helped to spread out the defense and slightly mitigate the rush. Nope! Love was pressured on 72.2% of those dropbacks with an average time to pressure of 2.25 seconds. The quickest pressure on a snap in 11 personnel was 1.4 seconds, which is insane. So Love seemed to be operating at his best when they could spread-and-shred, but he was under immense fire on those snaps. Matthew Golden had another brutal day in terms of drops, but he was also the most productive receiver for the Packers, posting an EPA of 9.28 on a 31.0% target share. He did some nice work on late downs, posting a +3.6 EPA. He did most of his damage from the outside, with +2.12 EPA when lined up wide and +0.82 when in the slot. Kaleb Johnson continues to show promise as a pure runner. He’s not much of a receiving back, but he shows good burst and power when running as a straight-ahead runner. The main scheme that Johnson had success with was when the Packers were pulling linemen. It’s something we haven’t really seen much from them over the past few weeks, but it worked pretty well for them today when Johnson was running. If he can continue to hold onto the ball, I like what I’ve seen from Johnson this year. Defense The Packers worked hard to get pressure on Kirk Cousins, blitzing on 44.4% of snaps. And it worked when they were able to get pressure, but Cousins was getting rid of the ball quickly (2.35 average time to throw) so the Packers only notched a pressure rate of 30.6%. Here are Cousins’ numbers when pressured: Cousins’ pressure numbers were far worse than Love’s, but his clean numbers were much better. Here are Love’s numbers when pressured & when clean: I’m almost positive at least 2 drops came when Love was clean, so that would certainly impact those numbers. I’m curious to dig into those a little later this week. On the pressure side, Lukas Van Ness led the way, posting a 23.5% pressure rate and an Average Time to Pressure of 2.17 seconds. He also threw a Tackle For Loss into the mix for good measure. Good day for LVN. Albums listened to: Jake Bugg – Alamo

title: The Aaron Banks situation gets worse and worse for the Packers
summary: Aaron Banks, the Packers’ $77 million left guard, played three snaps on Sunday. None were on offense. Exiled from the starting lineup, Banks only appeared on the field for two field goal attempts and the Packers’ lone extra point, lining up at left guard on all three plays. And that’s a fitting fate for Banks, […]
full_text: MINNEAPOLIS, MN - JANUARY 04: Green Bay Packers guard Aaron Banks (65) looks on before the NFL game between the Green Bay Packers and Minnesota Vikings on January 4th, 2026, at U.S. Bank Stadium in Minneapolis, MN. (Photo by Bailey Hillesheim/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images) | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images Aaron Banks, the Packers’ $77 million left guard, played three snaps on Sunday. None were on offense. Exiled from the starting lineup, Banks only appeared on the field for two field goal attempts and the Packers’ lone extra point, lining up at left guard on all three plays. And that’s a fitting fate for Banks, considering how the Packers seem to have evaluated their offensive line heading into this week’s game. Asked in his postgame press conference why Banks was out of the lineup, Packers head coach Matt LaFleur offered a brutal assessment. Simply put, LaFleur and the coaching staff view Laken Tomlinson as the better choice at left guard, and, given the chance to earn reps at right guard with Kevin Zeitler ailing, Banks failed, falling behind Travis Glover. “We were going to shuffle up the o-line a bit. Laken’s been doing a pretty good job and we put him back to his natural position [at left guard], and we were going to let Banks compete at the right guard,” LaFleur said. “He doesn’t have a ton of time on task at that position, so we went the way we did tonight.” To say nothing of the overall state of the Packers’ offensive line, what a catastrophe Banks has been. 20 months after signing a rich free agent deal, Banks finds himself behind a player the Packers plucked from the Dallas Cowboys practice squad in September and unable to outcompete a sixth round pick who, coming into this week, had appeared in 11 total NFL games, counting a disastrous playoff performance in 2024. And presumably he only got the chance to compete because Kevin Zeitler, the player the Packers signed to solidify right guard, was unavailable all week with an ankle injury. And that’s just this week! On the season, Banks has appeared in just four games. In one of those four (this week) he didn’t play on offense. In another, he couldn’t finish out the game. For the millions they’ve spent this year, Banks has given the Packers just 137 offensive snaps. Again, what a catastrophe. This is a player the Packers portrayed as ascending when they signed him. General manager Brian Gutekunst said he was excited to get a player “ in the prime of his career ” when he inked Banks in 2025, making him a centerpiece of an effort to get bigger up front. Instead, the only size-related discussion we’re having related to Banks is the enormity of his failure. Packers fans: Find your community Acme Packing Company is SB Nation’s home for Packers news, analysis, and conversation. Download the app to join Green and Gold diehards and share your take. Download the SB Nation app on iOS or Android . Banks is due a $9.5 million roster bonus on March 15, 2027, but it’s hard to imagine he’s going to see a cent of that. Releasing Banks outright would actually cost the Packers a touch more than keeping him thanks to a contract restructuring last offseason, but there are still mechanisms in place to avoid that payout. Designating Banks as a post-June 1 cut would scuttle that roster bonus and spread Banks’ cap hit over the Packers’ 2027 and 2028 books. And given what the Packers are telling us about their internal assessment of Banks, you can probably go ahead and pencil in Banks for a change of address sometime before March 15 of next year. But that will only finalize what’s already happening. The Packers have functionally moved on from one of their priciest free agent signings in recent years. The only remaining question is why they thought it was a good idea to sign him in the first place.

title: Green Bay Packers News: Back to the drawing board on the Offensive Line
summary: No quarterback — even one who has been playing at an MVP level of late — can sustain an offense when he can’t get the ball out of his hands. Jordan Love is no exception, and Green Bay Packers fans saw the team’s fatal flaw get exploited over and over and over again on Sunday […]
full_text: GREEN BAY, WISCONSIN - NOVEMBER 15: Levi Drake Rodriguez #50 of the Minnesota Vikings sacks Jordan Love #10 of the Green Bay Packers during the second quarter at Lambeau Field on November 15, 2026 in Green Bay, Wisconsin. (Photo by Michael Reaves/Getty Images) | Getty Images No quarterback — even one who has been playing at an MVP level of late — can sustain an offense when he can’t get the ball out of his hands. Jordan Love is no exception, and Green Bay Packers fans saw the team’s fatal flaw get exploited over and over and over again on Sunday afternoon. The Minnesota Vikings defense is a singularly bad matchup for the Packers, who continue to make inexplicable decisions with their personnel on the offensive line. Yes, the team has had a glut of injuries up front, and third-string center John Williams was one of the biggest problems on the line on Sunday, but every single player shared in the blame for the constant and, even more problematic, instant pressure that Love faced all game long. Love couldn’t even get the ball out quickly without players in his face, let alone try to dial up any deep balls, which have been a staple of the team’s recent success. So what is there to do? Is the answer just as simple as “don’t play the Vikings again”? Are there answers on this roster, perhaps on injured reserve (looking at you, Sean Rhyan), who could help get this unit back on track? Maybe this team needs to get back to the drawing board at a more fundamental level when it comes to the offensive line — starting with the position coach and working all the way up. The Packers have a long week to start working on some answers before their next game, which is a week from Wednesday in Los Angeles. They’ve got seven more chances to sort things out and find a way into the postseason. It’s time to get this under control Game recap: 5 takeaways from Packers’ loss to Vikings | Packers.com This was a major missed opportunity to get right back into the thick of the NFC North race. Instead, the Packers are two losses behind each of the other three teams in the division, who are all tied at 7-2. Jordan Love and a true outlier pressure performance from Vikings | Packers Wire Love averaged less than 2.5 seconds in his time to throw, but still was pressured on 21 of his 35 dropbacks. Packers can’t function against Vikings’ blitz barrage | Packersnews.com ($) There are only so many times that Matt LaFleur can say that the offensive line wasn’t coached well enough. Where’s the accountability for those failures? NFL playoff chance tiers: Where all 32 teams fit in 2026 postseason picture | ESPN The Packers fall in the fifth tier here, which is labeled as “on the verge of despair.” Clearly there’s something here that the Packers need to address. It’s not unlike tipping pitches in baseball – you have to make everything look the same until it isn’t. title: Value of Things: In the rearview mirror
summary: There are moments in our life that we know are coming before they happen. For me, this usually happens on the golf course. I come to a particular hole and I know it will at least be a double bogey. Often times it is even worse than that. It gets to the point where I […]
full_text: There are moments in our life that we know are coming before they happen. For me, this usually happens on the golf course. I come to a particular hole and I know it will at least be a double bogey. Often times it is even worse than that. It gets to the point where I would rather just write the six on the card and move on to the next hole. So, the actual end result is not the most maddening part. It is all of the lead up to it. You feel so helpless to prevent it. That’s when I am in charge of my own fate. Imagine watching that on television. That is what watching these Texans is like. It is like watching a car wreck in slow motion. You try to yell but nothing leaves your vocal cords. You just sit there in silence knowing what is going to happen. We have seen this movie before. We have seen it in past seasons and we have seen it several times this season. The Texans have a lead and find some way to fumble it at the end. The only real drama is in the figuring out exactly how it is going to happen. Obviously, we will be looking at the good, bad, and ugly from this game and this one will hit a little closer to home. This felt like the final nail in the Texans coffin. Sure, they have not been mathematically eliminated. They could win eight in a row and close out the season 11-6. However, that would defy any and all logic given what we have seen in the first nine games. If there is a clutch gene, this club does not have it. Key Statistics Total Yards: Texans 63/290, Browns 67/379 Rushing Yards: Texans 24/88, Browns 23/99 Passing Yards: Texans 39/202, Browns 44/280 Third Downs: Texans 3/12, Browns 7/15 Fourth Downs: Texans 0/1, Browns 0/0 Sacks. Texans 4, Browns 1 Turnovers: Texans 1, Browns 1 Penalties: Texans 13/112, Browns 2/47 Time of Possession: Texans 29:38, Browns 30:22 Before anyone goes on an on about how this team blew another game they should have won, they should take a good long look at these numbers. There is very little there that indicates that the Texans should have won the football game. Of course, games don’t happen in the box score and that is why we go through the good, bad, and ugly. The Good For the majority of the game this was actually a good defensive effort. Of course, we will hit more on that in a moment. They did register four sacks and got Watson moving on multiple other plays. In particular, it looked like Jalen Pitre, Kamari Lassiter, Derek Stingley, and Calen Bullock played a lot better than they had on previous afternoons. Of course, there is one more defensive back on the field, but we cannot mention him in this section of the proceedings. The unit was missing Danielle Hunter and Azeez Al-Shaair as well. If they had those two in the lineup I’m sure they get more pressure on Watson and they do a better job on the underneath stuff. The fact is that this team played good enough to win defensively. I will have some targeted negative comments, but as a whole this was a decent enough defensive effort. The Bad This game was a coaching failure top to bottom. The Texans got off to a good start offensively and defensively. They were up 17-0 in the second quarter. They had shut down the Browns on three straight possessions (two of them three and outs) and had scored on three straight possessions. Then, the Browns pivoted. I really am struggling to understand this. Of course they pivoted. That’s what coaches are supposed to do when they are getting their rear ends kicked. This seemed to flummox the Texans and we are looking squarely at the defense in this section. M.J. Stewart might have had his worst game as a Texan. He allowed a couple of big plays and another couple that could have happened if the Browns had been more competent. Commentators as far as the eye can see have talked about how simple this defense is. They expect the front four to get there and if they don’t get there we just shrug and move on our way. They had four sacks on the day, so they did get home on occasion and hurried him a handful of other times. When they didn’t get home they got picked apart. This is nine games now. This is who the Texans are. The coaches can say it’s early, that the field was slick, the other side has a great quarterback, or Uranus is not aligned with Venus and Haley’s comet. It’s been nine games for crying out loud. This is who you are. Make some damn adjustments. This is who you are and you wind up in these holes because it takes you longer than anyone to figure out who you are. The Ugly I’m done with Nick Caley. I’m just done. I’ve massaged the numbers. I’ve squinted from every conceivable angle. I can see where if you don’t watch the games and just look at the numbers then you see a good offense. I get that and have said it in the past. The fact is that when another team stops his first plan or when they adjust he has no second plan. He has no counter. He just sits there like a Judge Judy defendant with his mouth slightly open saying “hummuna hummuna hummuna.” Predictably, the Browns were going to amp up the pressure and clamp down on Nico Collins. See, other teams don’t allow a wide receiver to get 17 catches. They make adjustments before that happens. You see how that works? So, the Browns weren’t going to allow Nico to dominate them all day. They weren’t going to sit back and watch you pick them apart. Most teams have a plan for when the other team makes adjustments. The Texans apparently aren’t most teams. There are things you can do when the other team amps up pressure. You can use motion to confuse them. You can use misdirection like some of the wide receiver runs we have seen at different points of the season. Heck, I have heard a rumor that there is something called a screen play that some teams use to good effect. I certainly haven’t seen it in Houston, so I don’t know if this is really a thing. Obviously, this commentary is dripping with sarcasm because you either laugh or throw your laptop through the window. On two separate occasions the defense gave you the ball back with a 24-20 lead and you sent your fourth string running back straight into the line in a jumbo set where everyone on the planet knew what was coming. It is a set where you came into the game averaging two yards a carry in that formation. It is a formation that you ran out of 90 percent of the time. It needs to go the way of the dodo bird. Not only did you go three and out both times, but you didn’t even gain a yard. If you get even one first down the game likely ends. Plays seemed to be drawn from “Coaching Offense for Dummies” and it is time for Caley to be sent on his way. Focus on Stroud This is one of those games where Caley and his apologists will point to Stroud only being sacked once and say, “see we are doing a good job protecting him.” It’s all complete horse manure. He escaped sure sacks on at least three occasions and it was a minor miracle he escaped. He was under constant pressure in the second half, so I’m not putting this one on Stroud. Even his interception was probably a blown pass interference call from the officials. Yet, that is a different story for a different day. Officially, he was 20 for 38 for 211 yards, three touchdowns, and one interception. He had an 84.4 rating, but this one is on Nick Caley. It is not even a question of whether Stroud deserves an extension at this point. It is whether he wants to commit to Houston. I would demand the coordinator fired and I’d also demand a seat at the table when hiring a new one. He will be on his third offensive coordinator in his fifth year in the league. In spite of that instability, he now has 19 touchdown passes and three interceptions. Shoot that straight into my veins every year. I did feel like the interception was forced, but this is a guy that has been fitting throws into tight windows all season. He did say that he wanted a more diverse route tree and maybe they should run some more motion. He knows this offense is dog excrement. He is the whipped cream on the cow patty. He is the…
