title: Shane Steichen’s offensive game plan continues to raise serious questions despite Colts victory
summary: The Indianapolis Colts finally snapped their five-game losing streak Sunday, escaping with a 24-22 victory over the Miami Dolphins in a game that probably should never have been so close. Despite facing a 1-8 opponent starting a backup quarterback, Indianapolis needed a failed two-point conversion and a pair of missed Miami field goals to secure […]
full_text: INDIANAPOLIS, INDIANA - NOVEMBER 15: Head coach Shane Steichen of the Indianapolis Colts looks on during the fourth quarter against the Miami Dolphins at Lucas Oil Stadium on November 15, 2026 in Indianapolis, Indiana. (Photo by Justin Casterline/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Indianapolis Colts finally snapped their five-game losing streak Sunday, escaping with a 24-22 victory over the Miami Dolphins in a game that probably should never have been so close. Despite facing a 1-8 opponent starting a backup quarterback, Indianapolis needed a failed two-point conversion and a pair of missed Miami field goals to secure its third victory of the season. While a win is certainly welcome following several weeks of embarrassing performances, the offensive struggles that have plagued this team throughout the past month remain as concerning as ever. Daniel Jones completed just 11 of 22 passes for 108 yards, 1 touchdown and 2 interceptions, while the Colts managed only 10 offensive points through the first 59 minutes of the game, with their other 7 coming from a defensive touchdown and 3 from a field goal. Jones’ performance was considered the worst of any quarterback in the NFL this season, according to QBR. Baker Mayfield had a game without a completion that ranked higher than Jones’ performance. Indianapolis had 2 running backs averaging more than 5 yards per carry, one of the league’s most talented young tight ends and an opponent that has struggled defensively throughout the season, yet Shane Steichen once again failed to generate any sort of consistent passing attack. The Colts have already traded several established offensive players and are operating with a significantly weakened receiving corps, so expecting this offense to resemble the unit that performed so well during stretches of 2025 would be unrealistic. However, that is precisely why the coaching staff needs to adjust. Steichen was hired in large part because of his reputation as an offensive innovator, someone capable of designing creative schemes and maximizing the talent available to him. Right now, I have serious questions about whether he is doing either of those things. There are four areas in particular where I believe Steichen’s approach needs to change, and Sunday’s performance against Miami provided further evidence of those concerns. Jonathan Taylor should be dominating the backfield I want to make one thing clear before criticizing the running back rotation: Seth McGowan has been excellent in recent weeks. The rookie has demonstrated impressive explosiveness and physicality, and I genuinely believe he could become a very good rotational running back with legitimate starting potential down the road. His 77 rushing yards and touchdown on 12 carries against Miami were another encouraging sign that Indianapolis may have found a valuable contributor for the future. However, Jonathan Taylor is still on this roster, and there is a substantial difference between being an encouraging young running back and being one of the best players at the position in football. Taylor rushed for 83 yards on 16 carries Sunday, averaging 5.2 yards per attempt, while McGowan received 12 carries and averaged 6.4 yards. Those are excellent numbers for both players, but Taylor finished with just 57 percent of the carries between the 2 running backs, despite being the vastly more accomplished player. He also played approximately 68 percent of Indianapolis’ offensive snaps, a number I believe should be well above 80 percent whenever he is healthy and available. The Colts made a conscious decision to retain Taylor at the trade deadline despite reportedly receiving offers involving second-round draft picks. Indianapolis apparently believes he is worth a first-round selection, and given his continued production, I can understand that valuation. However, if the organization believes Taylor is valuable enough to keep around during a rebuilding season, why isn’t it treating him like the centerpiece of its offense? I understand the argument for limiting his workload, particularly when the Colts are sitting at 3-7 and have little realistic chance of making the playoffs. However, if protecting Taylor’s health and preserving his future trade value are the priorities, Indianapolis should seriously consider shutting him down for the remainder of the season rather than continuing to expose him to injuries while only giving him a portion of the backfield workload. If he is healthy, dressed and the coaching staff is genuinely trying to win football games, he should be receiving the overwhelming majority of the opportunities. McGowan’s development is important, but it should not come at the expense of maximizing Taylor’s impact right now. There are ways to involve the rookie without consistently taking the team’s best offensive player off the field. The Colts need to run the football significantly more With Jones struggling as badly as he has over the past several weeks, I don’t understand why Indianapolis continues asking him to carry so much responsibility in the passing game. Against Miami, he threw the football 22 times, completing only half of his attempts while turning the ball over twice. Meanwhile, Taylor and McGowan combined for 160 rushing yards on 28 carries, averaging approximately 5.7 yards per attempt. The running game was clearly the most productive part of the offense, yet the Colts continued putting Jones in situations where he was required to make difficult throws with an inexperienced receiving corps and a weakened offensive line. At this point, I would build the entire offensive approach around limiting Jones’ responsibilities in the passing game and leaning heavily on the Colts’ productive backfield. Ideally, Indianapolis should be running the football on approximately 2/3 of its offensive plays, leaving the remaining 1/3 for passing situations. In a typical game featuring 60 offensive plays, that would mean roughly 40 rushing attempts and just 20 passes, a much more appropriate balance given the current limitations of the offense. Taylor should be receiving the overwhelming majority of those carries, potentially somewhere around 28 to 30, with McGowan handling the remaining opportunities. Obviously, game situations will sometimes force Indianapolis to throw more frequently, particularly when trailing, but the overall philosophy should be clear: take the ball out of Jones’ hands as much as possible and allow the team’s most productive offensive players to dictate the game. Even if the Colts only manage 30 or 32 rushing attempts between their running backs, Taylor should still receive the overwhelming majority of those opportunities. There is simply no justification for consistently splitting carries almost evenly between an established All-Pro and a rookie, regardless of how promising McGowan has looked. Running the football more frequently would also take pressure off Jones, shorten games and reduce the number of possessions where the offense is forced into obvious passing situations. Indianapolis does not have the personnel to consistently win games by asking Jones to throw 30 or 35 passes, particularly now that Josh Downs and Keenan Allen are gone. The Colts retained their best offensive player at the deadline, and their backup running back is emerging as another productive option. Rather than continuing to rely on a passing attack that has become increasingly dysfunctional, Steichen should be building his game plans around those strengths. And if the Colts intend to maximize their best players, there is another offensive weapon who should be receiving considerably more attention. Tyler Warren’s usage is becoming indefensible Of all the questionable decisions made by Steichen against Miami, the handling of Tyler Warren might have been the most frustrating. The second-year tight end finished with just 2 receptions for 1 yard on 3 targets, with his first official catch not coming until the fourth quarter.…

title: Horsepower or Horseplay? Week 10 individual highlights from Colts’ home win vs. Dolphins
summary: The Indianapolis Colts (3-7) won the ‘battle of bad teams,’ defeating the Miami Dolphins (1-8) 24-22 at home on Sunday, but the latter may have actually won the war, keeping their projected 2027 first rounder as a Top 3 pick. While this felt more like a preseason game in intensity and vibes, with neither team […]
full_text: INDIANAPOLIS, INDIANA - NOVEMBER 15: Justin Walley #27 of the Indianapolis Colts forces a fumble as he sacks Kyle McCord #14 of the Miami Dolphins during an NFL football game at Lucas Oil Stadium on November 15, 2026 in Indianapolis, Indiana. (Photo by Michael Owens/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Indianapolis Colts (3-7) won the ‘battle of bad teams,’ defeating the Miami Dolphins (1-8) 24-22 at home on Sunday, but the latter may have actually won the war, keeping their projected 2027 first rounder as a Top 3 pick. While this felt more like a preseason game in intensity and vibes, with neither team playing all that productive or well executed professional football, it was the Colts who benefitted from struggling Dolphins kicker Zane Gonzalez inexplicably going 1 for 3 from field goal range, as just making one of those two missed field goals was the difference in Miami’s obtaining the victory in this one. Without further ado, let’s get to the individual highlights: Horsepower RB Seth McGowan: The rookie rusher has been an uncovered 7th round gem by this current maligned football operations department (which already saw longtime general manager Chris Ballard fired) and one of the few silver linings of an increasingly disappointing 2026 campaign. Once strictly a change-of-pace option behind star workhorse Jonathan Taylor, it’s now evolved into more of a time-share and running back platoon since Taylor was the subject of recent trade talks, with McGowan rushing for 77 total rushing yards and a rushing touchdown on 12 carries (6.4 ypc. avg.) during Sunday’s home win. Perhaps that’s to keep Taylor fresher and take some mileage off his tires in a lost season, but McGowan runs hard with burst, acceleration, and physicality. If the day comes where the Colts ultimately trade Taylor this offseason, they appear to be in solid hands with McGowan who appears to be both a reliable and viable starting running back option. DT Ade Adebawore: It was “Tomi Time” again, as the recently extended blossoming young defensive tackle continues to make plays. On Sunday, he recovered a Justin Walley strip-sack in the end zone to score a ‘big man’ touchdown . He’s so far filled a lot of the big shoes left by departed veteran DeForest Buckner. NT Grover Stewart: For a longtime veteran, who was also the subject of trade rumors like his ex-teammate Buckner, credit to ‘Big Grove’ for hanging in there with this young defense, getting those “big paws” up, and deflecting three passes in this one, for a typical space eater, who’s more known for his interior run stuffing. LB CJ Allen: It’s hard to believe that Allen was recently a healthy benching to begin the 2026 season because the rookie’s seemingly caught fire in recent weeks. He recorded 9 tackles (3 solo), a crushing sack , 2 tackles for loss, 2 tackles for loss, and a pass defensed ( narrowly missing an interception ) against the Miami offense. He’s consistently been Indy’s best linebacker as of late, routinely bringing impact plays and making his presence felt from the 2nd level, and looks like a building block for this rebuilding Colts defense going forward. CB Justin Walley: Speaking of Walley, after the de facto rookie slot cornerback experienced initial slot growing pains this season, like Allen, he’s clearly settled in as of late. He was a stat-sheet stuffer during Sunday’s win, with 5 tackles, a sack, two tackles for loss, a forced fumble (*which was recovered for a TD), and 2 passes defensed. Walley presents another potential young building block to form a solid foundation for this Colts defense going forward into the future. There’s growing levels of optimism for their young defensive core collectively. Horseplay QB Daniel Jones: The Colts embattled starting quarterback, who was booed by the home crowd during player introductions, continued his brutal stretch of starts. Jones completed 11 of 22 pass attempts for just 108 passing yards, a passing touchdown, an interception, and almost lost a self-induced fumble (pictured above). He recorded a season-low QBR of 1.7, the lowest of any starting NFL QB so far this season . Sure, Colts head coach Shane Steichen appreciates his preparation, but his on-the-field performance has been routinely poor this season. The Jones’ starting era in Indianapolis appears to have long run its course, but Steichen continues to be stubborn and still won’t make a long overdue change in favor of his primary backup Anthony Richardson Sr. TE Tyler Warren: With a Colts wide receiver room that now closely resembles a practice squad, with Alec Pierce remaining on IR and the recent trades of Keenan Allen and Josh Downs, the thought was that Warren, Indy’s sure handed safety valve, may benefit the most as far as receiving targets and touches volume. Instead, Warren had 2 catches for *check notes*, 1 total receiving yard, on only 3 receiving targets on the afternoon. I’m not sure what’s going on with Warren as of late, who’s receiving production has clearly regressed in recent weeks, but either he has to evolve and improve as a more diverse route runner and pass catcher, or Steichen has to be better at scheming his tight end open over the middle of the field. There’s probably blame to go around for both sides.

title: Colts Monday Morning Awards: Week 10 vs. Dolphins
summary: After a five-week winless drought that warranted a month-long hiatus from Monday Morning Awards, the Indianapolis Colts survived a late rally to hold off the Miami Dolphins in Sunday’s 24-22 win.  Here are the Monday Morning Awards from Sunday’s narrow victory. MVP: Justin Walley For the first time this season, there were at least three, […]
full_text: After a five-week winless drought that warranted a month-long hiatus from Monday Morning Awards, the Indianapolis Colts survived a late rally to hold off the Miami Dolphins in Sunday’s 24-22 win. Here are the Monday Morning Awards from Sunday’s narrow victory. MVP: Justin Walley For the first time this season, there were at least three, four, maybe five players that had a case to be named the most valuable player of the game. When the offense looks as bad as it did in the second half, sometimes it takes the defense to put points on the scoreboard. After rewatching the game, it’s definitive that without Justin Walley’s takeaway to start the second half, the Colts do not escape with a win against the Dolphins. For a defense that has struggled to generate takeaways, Walley’s impact, timing and awareness earns him MVP honors. The second-year nickel collected five tackles, a critical sack, and etched career-highs with two pass deflections and two tackles for loss. Walley posted a 91.2 Pro Football Focus defensive grade in Week 10, which led all cornerbacks and was third among all NFL players on Sunday. He allowed just three catches on six targets for a minimal 13 receiving yards. Walley’s 22 defensive stops rank second among all cornerbacks this season. How do you perform after your team holds a fire sale? In the case of @Colts cornerback Justin Walley, you ball out in just about every way possible. pic.twitter.com/E1ElU1FFgg — Doug Farrar ✍ (@NFL_DougFarrar) November 16, 2026 Best Play of the Game: Justin Walley strip-sack, Adetomiwa Adebawore TD On Miami’s first snap of the second half, Walley came flying off the edge and strip-sacked quarterback Kyle McCord near the goal line. Defensive tackle Adetomiwa Adebawore was in the right place at the perfect time to recover the fumble in the end zone for a defensive touchdown. Indy’s offense scored just three points in the second half, so this defensive score gave the Colts enough cushion to not blow the lead. Justin Walley and Adetomiwa Adebawore!!!! 📺 CBS pic.twitter.com/6vRWIgioSk — Indianapolis Colts (@Colts) November 15, 2026 Adebawore is also having a phenomenal breakout season, posting an 84.3 PFF pass rush grade that ranks second among defensive linemen, only behind Cincinnati’s Dexter Lawrence. It’s fitting that Adebawore was ready for the opportunity to score as the football was knocked out of the grasp of McCord. Adebaware emerged as a full-time starter and has already hit career highs with 11 QB hits, four sacks, and three pass deflections. Two weeks ago, the Colts signed the 25-year-old to a two-year, $35 million extension to lock in the centerpiece of their interior defensive front. Dud of the Game: Steichen & Jones co. Daniel Jones is off to the worst start of his career and is statistically the worst QB in the NFL. Jones threw two interceptions, including a pick-six on the very next play after the Dolphins cut into the deficit. He’s lucky his fumble rolled out of bounds before it had a chance to be recovered inside the red zone. It’s beyond irresponsible not to make a change, while Jones has career-lows in completion rate (59%), yards per attempt (5.6), passer rating (67) and QBR (36.4). His 1.7 QBR from Sunday matched his jersey number, with a decimal in between, which was the worst rating of any QB this season. #Colts QB Daniel Jones over the last month: 1. 13-22 (59.1%) 108 pass yards, 1 INT 2. 19-28 (67.9%) 144 pass yards, 1 TD, 2 INTs 3. 20-34 (58.8%) 180 pass yards, 1 TD, 1 INT 4. 11-22 (50%) 108 pass yards, 1 TD, 2 INTs — Noah Compton (@nerlens_) November 15, 2026 Shane Steichen needs to dramatically change the offense to sustain the run game and avoid passing to this batch of receivers until Alec Pierce returns to action. The offense moved the ball a combined 49 yards from where the seven second half possessions started. Steichen must have heard the boos rain down during introductions, after the first fumble, or the six punts. Worst play of the game: Daniel Jones pick-six Despite taking a two-possession lead on the first play of the third quarter, Jones and Drew Ogletree both hand-wrapped a pick-six that allowed the Dolphins a chance to stay within striking distance. After Zane Gonzalez finally connected on a field goal to cut the deficit to 21-10, the Colts next drive lasted for a single play. Jones instantly stumbled, but tried to scramble outside the pocket to keep the play alive and forced a fadeaway throw, which ricocheted off the hands of Ogletree and was picked off by Dolphins cornerback Chris Johnson, who returned it for a 59-yard housecall. To be honest, it’s fair to say the way Jones led the offense in the second half, dared the Dolphins to steal the win. PICK-6 FOR DOLPHINS ROOKIE CB CHRIS JOHNSON MIAvsIND on CBS/Paramount+ Stream on @NFLPlus pic.twitter.com/MK3SVpG6M3 — NFL (@NFL) November 15, 2026 Rookies of the week: C.J. Allen, Seth McGowan Rookie running back Seth McGowan stacked another encouraging performance, rushing for a career-high 77 yards on 12 carries. McGowan punched in his second career touchdown from 4-yards out to give the Colts a lead they never relinquished. McGowan’s physicality and explosiveness gives the Colts a sledgehammer to lean on for the tough gains to get through battle. With Jonathan Taylor still leading the backfield tandem, McGowan is beginning to establish himself as a legitimate complementary piece. Taylor was the main name in headlines before the trade deadline, but the front office decided it was best to keep their star captain around for the rebuild. It was to McGowan’s joy of course, since he mentioned that he even prayed Taylor would remain in Indy. The seventh-round draft pick has scored the first touchdown in each of the last two games, delivering his welcome to the league moments inside Lucas Oil Stadium. Perhaps it was rookie linebacker C.J. Allen who delivered the best overall performance in Sunday’s win. More than one Stampede Blue writer seemed to think so. Allen made his presence felt with a game-high nine tackles and two tackles for loss. His biggest play came late in the fourth quarter when he sacked McCord for a 10-yard loss that speared the Dolphins out of field goal range. With Miami threatening to steal the game in the final minutes, Allen was tasked to be the blitzer. The second-round draft pick has become a reliable presence in the middle of Lou Anarumo’s defense since earning the starting job. His instincts and physicality were put on full display in the critical final drive, which is difficult to ignore. CJ ALLEN INCOMING 📺 CBS pic.twitter.com/7wGDIa7aCO — Indianapolis Colts (@Colts) November 15, 2026 Unsung heroes: Spencer Shrader, A.J. Haulcy When the Colts needed insurance, Spencer Shrader drilled a 51-yard field goal in the third quarter to extend the lead to 24-16. It ultimately proved to be the final points Indianapolis would score in a win that was decided by just two points. Shrader leads the league in made FGs of 50-plus yards, currently an efficient 9-for-10. He’s tied for the NFL lead with 88 total points this season and ranks second among kickers with 23 field goals made out of 25 attempts (92%). With the offense unable to put the game away, Shrader’s long-distance connection became the deciding factor, especially since the Dolphins kicker left seven points off the scoreboard from two missed field goals and a missed extra point, all wide left. Multiple staff writers even comically discussed if Gonzalez were the true MVP of the game decided by two points, because every kick matters. “No Fly Zone”: A.J. Haulcy The Dolphins had a clear opportunity to level the score, but the young defensive back refused to let the lead slither away. After Miami scored a touchdown to cut the deficit to 24-22, rookie safety A.J. Haulcy broke up McCord’s two-point conversion attempt to preserve the lead. Although Walley’s strip-sack and Adebawore’s fumble recovery touchdown proved to be the winning play, it was Haulcy’s…

With the Colts already down starting right tackle […]
full_text: INDIANAPOLIS, INDIANA - DECEMBER 28: Bernhard Raimann #79 of the Indianapolis Colts blocks during the game against the Jacksonville Jaguars at Lucas Oil Stadium on December 28, 2025 in Indianapolis, Indiana. (Photo by Michael Hickey/Getty Images) | Getty Images Indianapolis Colts starting left tackle Bernhard Raimann has officially entered the league’s concussion protocol, after being evaluated and ultimately ruled out with a head injury during Sunday’s home win against the Miami Dolphins: Colts LT Bernhard Raimann in concussion protocol. — Mike Chappell (@mchappell51) November 16, 2026 Raimann suffered the concussion during the first quarter and as mentioned, did not return. With the Colts already down starting right tackle Jalen Travis, backup Luke Tenuta came in at left tackle for Indianapolis—while routine starting right guard Matt Goncalves kicked out to right tackle to begin the game. The 29-year-old Raimann has already suffered three medically documented concussions during his first five NFL seasons, so it is something to monitor going forward for the Colts medically and regarding Raimann’s continued playing career—as we saw former Colts Pro Bowl center (now retired) Ryan Kelly’s playing longevity cut a bit short later in his career because of re-occurring concussions. Raimann had previously started all 10 games for the Colts so far this season. Currently, Raimann is PFF’s 17th best graded offensive tackle with a +74.9 overall grade. In pass protection, he’s allowed 3.0 sacks, 3 QB hits, and 20 total QB pressures during his 356 total pass blocking snaps to-date. Obviously, being down both starting offensive tackles potentially playing the Texans fearsome pass rush of Will Anderson Jr. and Danielle Hunter (albeit, who did miss Sunday’s game) off the edge doesn’t ideally bode well for Indianapolis’ offense and keeping Daniel Jones upright and pass pressure free in the pocket. It’s worth noting that Colts starting cornerback Sauce Gardner left the game in the 3rd quarter due to a re-occurring calf injury and underwent an MRI after the game. It’s the third time since he was acquired last year from the New York Jets that he’s missed time because of the lingering calf injury. Fellow starting cornerback Charvarius Ward also suffered a shin injury and was seen post-game walking around with a single crutch —meaning Indianapolis could be without both of its starting outside corners in a short-week headed in to face the Texans on the road for this week’s Thursday Night Football matchup.

title: Super Bowl Coach Applauds Jaguars’ Jordan Davis, Jessie Bates Trades
summary: When a Super Bowl-winning head coach, with a strength in defense praises your recent defensive roster moves, it’s probably worth paying attention. NBC analyst Mike Tomlin, who won a Super Bowl during his 19 seasons leading the Pittsburgh Steelers, had a few glowing remarks when discussing the Jacksonville Jaguars adding safety Jessie Bates III and […]
full_text: JACKSONVILLE, FLORIDA - NOVEMBER 11: Jordan Davis #90 and head coach Liam Coen of the Jacksonville Jaguars speak during an NFL football practice at the Miller Electric Center on November 11, 2026 in Jacksonville, Florida. (Photo by Logan Bowles/Getty Images) | Getty Images When a Super Bowl-winning head coach, with a strength in defense praises your recent defensive roster moves, it’s probably worth paying attention. NBC analyst Mike Tomlin, who won a Super Bowl during his 19 seasons leading the Pittsburgh Steelers, had a few glowing remarks when discussing the Jacksonville Jaguars adding safety Jessie Bates III and defensive tackle Jordan Davis on last week’s NBC conference call: “I think they helped themselves in two distinct ways from a defensive perspective and so it’s a sign that they’re all in. It’s really impressive and it’s going to be fun to watch.” I fully agree with Tomlin here. The resulting roster outlook following the moves, the clear championship aims from the 7-2 Jaguars, and the limited risk exposure, while improving in two areas of defense turned last week’s trade deadline into clear roster improvements. With the deadline dust now settled, we take a quick look at why the trades make Jacksonville’s second-ranked defense (in points surrendered) significantly better, and why the money behind the moves may be the most underrated part of the story. Jordan Davis: Filling the DHam Void The case for Davis starts with what Jacksonville lost. According to NextGenStats, the Jaguars’ defense allowed 6.9 yards per play in 2026 when Davon Hamilton was off the field and just 3.8 when he was on it. Some of that gap reflects the fact that Hamilton didn’t play on obvious passing downs, but it also shows just how dominant he was against the run. A similar pattern shows up with Ventrell Miller, whose splits are 3.16 yards per carry allowed with him on the field and 5.66 with him off. A 3.1-yard swing in yards per play shows how much Hamilton mattered, and why Jacksonville, with Hamilton hurt for the remainder of the season in Week 8, needed a real replacement to keep its Super Bowl hopes intact. Davis is clearly that replacement. He led the Eagles with a 67.4 percent double-team rate this season while playing mostly on first and second downs, and PFF still graded him as the best defensive tackle in Philadelphia’s group on those downs. Notably, he had only 52 pass-rush snaps over eight games because that was, frankly, not his role. In Anthony Campanile’s defense, the run defense has to be elite: not good and not merely above average. This is a team that wants to play nickel, dime, and three-safety sets, and stopping the run on early downs is what keeps opponents in second and third-and-long. Davis does that, and then some. Limiting opponents on early downs forces them to throw into a defense expecting the pass and gives additional opportunities to a defense that already ranks among the league’s top three in interceptions. It is a scheme with a long track record, one that worked for years for Vic Fangio, with whom Campanile has history. Speaking of interceptions… Jessie Bates: More Than Just a Ballhawk Jacksonville added a magnet for the football to a defense that already ranks among the league’s interception leaders. Bates also forces fumbles at a remarkable rate, with three this season, and he’s scored a defensive touchdown in four straight seasons, including this one. The most important part of his arrival, though, is how he fits Campanile’s love of coverage variety. All offseason, the missing piece for this defense was a rangy, sideline-to-sideline safety who can patrol the middle of the field for Cover 3 and Cover 1, the looks Jacksonville prefers in the red zone. Bates is that player. In many ways, he just turned a top-five red zone defense into a Madden cheat code. With Travis Hunter and Montaric Brown outside, Jarrian Jones and Jourdan Lewis working the slots, and Bates roaming center field, there is potential for even more third-down Cover 1, even outside the red zone. While one defender may occasionally require additional help when playing man outside the red zone, Jacksonville would clearly hold the man-to-man advantage when lining up against most receiving groups. There is also a part of Bates’s game that people have probably not considered. The secondary lost its “Foye Oluokun of the back end” in Eric Murray, the communicator who makes sure everyone lines up correctly and avoids coverage busts. That is also the most underrated part of Bates’s game. He is not only a superior athlete to almost everyone around him. He is a student of the game who communicates and studies tape, something we covered in the 5 Questions About Jessie Bates article with The Falcoholic’s Jeanna Kelley: Jessie Bates is obsessed with film study. He carries two iPads around the facility — one from the team with that week’s game plan information loaded on it, and his personal device for taking notes and looking up specific plays, etc. From Bates, via AtlantaFalcons.com : “Film study has always been my way of separating from other players,” Bates said. “That’s what I love. That’s the part a lot of people don’t see every day – the grind, the amount of time that you put into film to shine and make plays on Sunday.” Easing Them In Neither Bates nor Davis played Sunday against the Tennessee Titans. Following the midweek trades, Jacksonville opted to give both players the week to rest and acclimate. The decision made sense given the circumstances: neither player had a 2026 bye week with his previous team, and Bates had only just returned from Santiago Bernabéu Stadium in Madrid, where Atlanta faced the Cincinnati Bengals. A week to recharge and to continue the crash course into Campanile’s system seems a worthwhile investment with the stretch run still ahead. The Money Made Sense What may get lost in the pick-by-pick conversation is how well the contracts work with Jacksonville’s current limitations. Between the two deals, Jacksonville saves around $25 million over the next two years. In effect, the Jaguars bought two years of salary relief by agreeing to part with higher draft capital to secure top players at their position at a low cost. The Eagles absorbed the $19 million prepaid bonus they had given Davis over two years, and the Falcons paid almost all of the $6.5 million owed to Bates in 2026. That leaves $25 million in immediate funds that Jacksonville can put toward extensions for wide receiver Parker Washington or safety Antonio Johnson, rather than being forced to restructure contracts to create cap space. Jacksonville did not say “F— them picks.” It used picks as currency to buy exactly what it wanted at a discount in salary. Essentially, they used a coupon, and closed that deal while reportedly bidding against the Buffalo Bills for both players. The Bills were aggressive in trying to trade for both Jordan Davis and Jessie Bates before trading for Amani Hooker, per @RapSheet pic.twitter.com/14NNuIT5Ml — Smitty Talks Bills (@NickSmitty3) November 14, 2026 Godchaux & the Comp-Pick Game While not mentioned by Tomlin, the Jaguars also added defensive tackle Davon Godchaux, which gives them more interior depth. The savvy move with Davon is that he allows Jacksonville to play the compensatory pick game, as he’s on an expiring contract. That is similar to what the team did with Greg Newsome in 2025, with Jacksonville likely to receive a sixth-round pick for him in this coming draft. Jacksonville’s conditional 2028 sixth-round pick traded for Godchaux accelerates to a 2027 sixth once awarded to the Jaguars by the NFL. However, if Davon were to perform well, Jacksonville could either re-sign him to an extension or allow him to test free agency, where if he signs a reasonable free-agent deal this offseason, there’s a non-zero chance the compensatory formula rewards Jacksonville with a late-round pick right back. In other words, Jacksonville could trade a 2027 sixth-round…

title: Three reasons why the Jaguars beat the Titans
summary: The Jacksonville Jaguars are beginning to look like a serious problem for the rest of the AFC. Liam Coen’s side traveled to Nashville on Sunday and came away with a convincing 40-23 victory over the Tennessee Titans, extending their winning streak to three games and improving their record to 7-2. With the Houston Texans slipping […]
full_text: NASHVILLE, TENNESSEE - NOVEMBER 15: Trevor Lawrence #16 and Parker Washington #11 of the Jacksonville Jaguars react to a play during the first half of the game against the Tennessee Titans at Nissan Stadium on November 15, 2026 in Nashville, Tennessee. (Photo by Johnnie Izquierdo/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Jacksonville Jaguars are beginning to look like a serious problem for the rest of the AFC. Liam Coen’s side traveled to Nashville on Sunday and came away with a convincing 40-23 victory over the Tennessee Titans , extending their winning streak to three games and improving their record to 7-2. With the Houston Texans slipping up against Cleveland, Jacksonville now holds a commanding four-game advantage at the top of the AFC South. There were plenty of positives for the visitors, but this wasn’t simply a case of taking advantage of a struggling divisional rival. The Jaguars demonstrated why they are becoming one of the most dangerous teams in the conference. Here are three reasons why Jacksonville came away with the victory. Trevor Lawrence is playing at an elite level Trevor Lawrence another ELITE performance 307 Pass Yards 3 Pass TD INT 126.7 Pass Rating pic.twitter.com/I76K6bFOfs — PFF (@PFF) November 15, 2026 There have been plenty of questions about Trevor Lawrence throughout his NFL career. Is he capable of being the franchise quarterback Jacksonville hoped they were getting when they selected him first overall in 2021? Can he consistently deliver the performances expected of a quarterback of his considerable talent? Right now, those questions are looking increasingly redundant. Lawrence was outstanding against Tennessee, completing 23 of 35 passes for 352 yards and three touchdowns. He connected with nine different receivers, demonstrating the sort of command and confidence that makes this Jacksonville offense so difficult to defend. Perhaps most encouragingly, this wasn’t an isolated performance. Lawrence has now surpassed 300 passing yards in three of his last five games, while the Jaguars have scored at least 30 points in four consecutive outings. The connection between Lawrence and head coach Liam Coen is becoming increasingly apparent. The quarterback looks comfortable in the offensive system, understands where his opportunities are coming from, and is playing with the sort of conviction that can elevate an entire offense. Lawrence also reached 20,000 career passing yards against Tennessee, becoming the eighth-youngest player in NFL history to achieve the milestone. Jacksonville has a quarterback playing with genuine confidence, and that could make the Jaguars a very difficult proposition come January. Parker Washington is becoming a serious weapon Parker Washington said gimme that pic.twitter.com/OgvAaEPHxe — Underdog NFL (@UnderdogNFL) November 15, 2026 Trevor Lawrence deserves plenty of the credit, but he also needs players capable of turning opportunities into big plays. Against Tennessee, Parker Washington provided exactly that. The young receiver enjoyed a spectacular afternoon, finishing with 152 receiving yards and a touchdown. Remarkably, he had already accumulated 148 yards by halftime, giving the Titans’ defense all sorts of problems before the interval. Washington’s ability to create separation and generate yards after the catch gives Jacksonville another dimension in the passing game. He isn’t simply a possession receiver waiting for the ball to come to him; he is capable of turning relatively routine completions into substantial gains. His performance also highlights an important development in Jacksonville’s offense. Lawrence isn’t reliant on one individual to produce. Washington, Brenton Strange, and Josh Cameron all found the end zone, while nine different receivers caught passes. That variety makes life considerably harder for opposing defensive coordinators. Concentrate too heavily on one threat and another player is likely to make you pay. With Washington producing performances like this, Jacksonville has another weapon capable of making a significant difference down the stretch. Tennessee’s defense simply couldn’t get off the field Robert Saleh vs Liam Coen in a big spot… WIDE OPEN TOUCHDOWN pic.twitter.com/JwKHTETyQQ — John Frascella (Football) (@NFLFrascella) November 15, 2026 There is no getting away from the fact that Tennessee’s defense had a miserable afternoon. Jacksonville finished with 459 total yards, averaged 6.4 yards per play, and converted seven of its 14 third-down opportunities. The Jaguars also controlled possession for more than 38 minutes, leaving the Titans with precious little opportunity to build any sustained momentum. It wasn’t just Lawrence’s passing that caused problems, either. Jacksonville accumulated 123 rushing yards, with Bhayshul Tuten adding a late six-yard touchdown to put the finishing touches on the victory. The inability to get off the field was particularly damaging. Jacksonville repeatedly extended drives, controlled the tempo, and forced Tennessee’s defense to spend long periods chasing the game. There were mitigating circumstances for Robert Saleh. Tennessee has undergone significant personnel changes, with injuries and trades leaving the defensive unit considerably depleted. But the numbers make for uncomfortable reading regardless. Giving up 40 points and 459 yards is not a recipe for success against an offense with the talent Jacksonville possesses. The Titans managed to stay within touching distance for much of the contest, but their inability to consistently disrupt Lawrence and get the ball back to their own offense ultimately proved costly. Jacksonville is a serious contender There is still plenty of football to be played, but Jacksonville is putting together an impressive body of work. Lawrence is playing with confidence, the receiving corps is developing into a dangerous group, and Coen’s offense is producing points consistently. The Jaguars weren’t perfect against Tennessee, and there are defensive areas they will want to address, but winning on the road by 17 points against a divisional opponent is exactly the sort of business a playoff contender should be taking care of. At 7-2, with a four-game lead in the AFC South, Jacksonville has given itself an excellent platform for the second half of the season. The question is no longer whether the Jaguars can win their division. It’s how far this team can go once the playoffs arrive. DUUUVAL! Join the game-day conversation on the SB Nation app! title: Jaguars Winners & Losers From Week 10: Parker Washington Explodes In Rivalry Win
summary: It certainly wasn’t a blowout, but good teams win and better teams cover. The Jacksonville Jaguars did just that in a 40-23 victory over the Tennessee Titans on Sunday. Despite their record and their roster, the Titans aren’t a completely awful team and showed that a bit on Sunday. The Jags had their hands full […]
full_text: NASHVILLE, TENNESSEE - NOVEMBER 15: Parker Washington #11 of the Jacksonville Jaguars carries the ball against Tony Adams #29 of the Tennessee Titans during the first half at Nissan Stadium on November 15, 2026 in Nashville, Tennessee. (Photo by Justin Ford/Getty Images) | Getty Images It certainly wasn’t a blowout, but good teams win and better teams cover. The Jacksonville Jaguars did just that in a 40-23 victory over the Tennessee Titans on Sunday. Despite their record and their roster, the Titans aren’t a completely awful team and showed that a bit on Sunday. The Jags had their hands full at times but made the plays when it mattered most to improve to 7-2 for the first time since 1998. Jacksonville is rattling off wins towards a potential play at the AFC’s top overall seed and with one of the league’s easiest schedules for the rest of the year, things are looking good in Duval County. There is only one place to start when talking about Jacksonville’s third straight win. It’s with Parker Washington. WINNERS Parker “Parker Washington” Washington Jacksonville chopped plenty of wood and carried buckets of water on the way to victory. It was the Washington show in Nashville as the former Nittany Lion rattled off a career-high 152 receiving yards. Washington was quiet in the second half but it didn’t matter because he did more than enough work in the first half, plucking ball after ball off the heads of hapless Titans defenders. Parker Washington just set a new career high with 152 receiving yards. 7 REC, 152 REC YDS, 1 TD vs Titans. Jacksonville is now 7-2 and looking like a serious Super Bowl contender. https://t.co/kp439ArwK8 pic.twitter.com/JTI8VCBdAm — Football Performances (@NFLPerformances) November 15, 2026 Washington’s big day was part of an even bigger day by quarterback Trevor Lawrence who finished with 352 yards and three touchdowns and eclipsed 20,000 yards passing in Jacksonville. One of those touchdowns came on the first drive of the game where the QB found Washington at the back of the end zone. The only downside of Washington continuing to play so well is that Jacksonville still needs to pay him. As it has after almost every game this season, the price for the third-year receiver has gone up again. A career day for Parker Washington 👏 🏈 1st Jaguars WR with 145+ Rec yds in a half in the last 11 seasons 🏈 First Jaguars WR with 150+ receiving yards since Week 5 of 2019 🏈 Career-high 6th Rec TD of the season pic.twitter.com/4kifL9RKzK — ESPN Insights (@ESPNInsights) November 15, 2026 Josh Cameron Back in 2023, Washington was selected in the sixth round, making his way up to wide receiver one status in Jacksonville. If Josh Cameron keeps it up, a sixth-rounder himself, he could be well on his way to Washington levels of status. The rookie Cameron was second on the Jags in receiving with three catches for 67 yards while catching his third touchdown of the year. Cameron also did decently in the return game once more, collecting 142 total return yards with a long of 32. He did get crushed by Tennessee kicker Joey Slye which resulted in a fumble, but those types of plays are few and far between anyway. There’s no question Jacksonville has a loaded wide receiver room. However, Cameron keeps proving he deserves to be on the field. If Brian Thomas Jr. continues to be up and down, Cameron will continue to reap the benefits. Josh Cameron (good player) with two big catches today. A 3rd down dunk and then a TD to make it a two score game in the 4th. pic.twitter.com/wJTsh3KSMi — Nate Tice (@Nate_Tice) November 15, 2026 Bhayshul Tuten For another Washington comparison: It should really come as no surprise that Bhayshul Tuten had another solid day. The running back had 113 total yards with 88 yards rushing and his fifth score of the year on the ground. Tuten now has touchdowns on the ground in three straight games and has gone over 100 total yards in two of his last three outings. Jacksonville made a great call when it turned over the keys to Tuten. His hard-nosed presence unlocks a nastiness in this offense that gives the Jags an edge anytime the ball is in his hands. In the same mold as Washington, Tuten is trusted to make the plays needed to propel the team to victory. He did so on Broadway. Bhayshul Tuten has reached 600 rushing yards ✅ Season Stats: 122 Car | 609 Rush Yds | 5 Rush TD Season Pace: 230 Car | 1,150 Rush Yds | 9 Rush TD #DUUUVAL pic.twitter.com/othk2X2rNP — PaceBall (@paceball__) November 15, 2026 Cam Little Here is your obligatory Cam Little Rocks section. Little went 4-for-4 on field goals and 4-for-4 on extra points. It’s almost indescribable how important it is to have someone as automatic as Little is. The Jags got points on all but two drives (8-10 overall), largely because once the team crosses the 50, they know they can rely on Little to convert. Liam Coen Much was said about last year’s dustup between then 49ers defensive coordinator Rob Salah and Liam Coen. How sweet must it be for Coen to beat Salah last year, only to turn around and drop 40 in Salah’s home stadium, now the head coach with the Titans? Running Tuten into the end zone with under two minutes to play had to feel damn good. Coen has done a tremendous job with the Jags since taking over. It doesn’t take this column to tell you that. Jacksonville has cut down on penalties (just two Sunday) and overall boneheaded mistakes. That game was one Lawrence batted-ball interception away from being about as good as you could get, at least offensively. Coen has won 20 of his first 26 games, and is just the third coach to do so in the last 15 years. He is tops in terms of winning percentage over those games in the history of the sport. Jacksonville is rolling and the head coach is a huge reason why. Keeping his coordinators in place after last year’s hiring cycle cannot go unnoticed too. This is the year to make a run. There’s no reason to believe right now that Coen isn’t the guy to lead it. “Division win on the road. Doesn’t get better than that.” #DUUUVAL pic.twitter.com/VU3ROQh66p — Jacksonville Jaguars (@Jaguars) November 15, 2026 Jessie Bates Yeah, so that trade for Jessie Bates was a huge one because the safety play in Nashville was subpar. More will be said on the defense below, but Bates proved his worth before ever even taking a snap defensively for Jacksonville. This team needs help on the back end. Luckily, help is ready to play and maybe even sleeping in the facility. Do I have news for you https://t.co/2v4AlmrNWU — Daniel Griffis (@DanDGriffis) November 15, 2026 LOSERS The Defense At Times Does anyone want to talk about that Tony Pollard touchdown ? No? Yes, the Titans aren’t a great offense. Yes, the Jags have a smothering defense typically. But also yes that the Titans are playing well offensively as of late. The Jags got exposed at times by that offense and especially on Pollard’s 32-yard receiving touchdown where he broke through just about the entire Jacksonville defense. Cam Ward and company didn’t light Jacksonville up, but that game wasn’t the pure defensive domination many might have thought was coming. There were some solid individual performances though on defense. Travis Hunter had an incredible leaping interception . Ventrell Miller was crushing guys like usual . Dennis Gardeck even looked pretty solid . But this defense needs the help it acquired at the deadline. Overall, no worries probably. But that was not this unit’s best performance of the year at all. Cam Ward ranks among QBs to play Jaguars defense this season Rank Passing yards: 231 4th Passing tds: 2 2nd Rushing yards: 39 1st Completion %: 71.8%… — Titans Era (@titanserashow) November 15, 2026 Injuries There were no DaVon Hamilton-level injuries following Sunday’s game, but that doesn’t mean the Jags got out of Nashville unscathed. The big injury question mark after that game was with a knee injury to Robert Hainsey. You can make the case that Hainsey maybe shouldn’t even be out there,…

title: Liam Coen: Parker Washington was ‘the best player on the field’ on Sunday
summary: Look. Don’t shoot the messenger. I know you already know this. But as somebody who covers the Jacksonville Jaguars, I wouldn’t be doing my job if I didn’t tell you what I saw when I watched them play. In Week 10 of the 2026 NFL season, like the rest of the football-viewing world, I saw […]
full_text: NASHVILLE, TN - NOVEMBER 15: Jacksonville Jaguars quarterback Trevor Lawrence (16) and Jacksonville Jaguars wide receiver Parker Washington (11) bow to each other in celebration after connecting for a touchdown during a game between the Tennessee Titans and Jacksonville Jaguars, November 15, 2026, at Nissan Stadium in Nashville, Tennessee. (Photo by Matthew Maxey/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images) | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images Look. Don’t shoot the messenger. I know you already know this. But as somebody who covers the Jacksonville Jaguars, I wouldn’t be doing my job if I didn’t tell you what I saw when I watched them play. In Week 10 of the 2026 NFL season, like the rest of the football-viewing world, I saw Randy Moss. The greatest deep threat in football history returned to the gridiron after a 5,000-day absence. Moss’ last official NFL action was on December 30, 2012 — but there was no doubt that the all-time receiver was playing for the Jacksonville Jaguars against the Tennessee Titans. Moss’ first catch of the day capped Jacksonville’s opening drive for a touchdown. Some receivers climb the ladder; this cat broke the stratosphere. Parker Washington has a Jacksonville touchdown! JAXvsTEN on FOX/FOX One Stream on @NFLPlus pic.twitter.com/pUVFGg72PT — NFL (@NFL) November 15, 2026 His 33-yard gain on the ensuing drive was a classic “Moss.” Parker Washington is filthy 🙆‍♂️ pic.twitter.com/U3wh9EzdeA — Fitz (@LaurieFitzptrck) November 15, 2026 Not to mention his 20-yarder the drive after that! Parker Washington is going ballistic today pic.twitter.com/cfK4HQ31w7 — Nate Tice (@Nate_Tice) November 15, 2026 Obviously, the guy I’m talking about is Parker Washington. After flaunting his above-the-rim abilities in the first half, Washington exhibited his route-running savvy with this flifthy 50-yard pickup. Parker Washington turning DBs 360 degrees pic.twitter.com/WOCBpP7b5j — Billy M (@BillyM_91) November 15, 2026 Washington finished with a career-high 152 receiving yards — the most by a Jaguars wide receiver since DJ Chark had 164 yards in Week 5 of 2019 — to help Jacksonville score 40 points on the road over the arch-rival Titans. “He was a man possessed in a lot of ways,” said head coach Liam Coen. “Parker was definitely the best player on the field today.” “Parker’s a baller,” said running back Bhayshul Tuten. “He had some crazy catches today, some contested catches, but he just keeps showing up. And I think that’s Parker’s MO, and he just goes out there, chop wood, carry water. He just goes out there and does him.” “Man, I don’t even get surprised no more,” said wide receiver Brian Thomas Jr. Jacksonville’s offense has been a juggernaut for about a full season now. If you combine the first half of 2026 with the second half of 2025, the Jaguars have the NFL’s best record at 15-2. Trevor Lawrence ranks first in passer rating (105.9) and touchdown-to-interception ratio (40:10) in that span. Lawrence deserves all the credit he’s getting, and then some, yet the same should be said of Washington. He ranks 10th among all NFL wide receivers with 1,195 yards over his last 17 games. For context, the only Jaguars with more receiving yards in a sewason are Thomas (2024), Allen Robinson (2015), Keenan McCardell (2000), and Jimmy Smith (1996-97, 1999-01). So far this season, Jacksonville is 5-0 when Washington scores a touchdown and 2-2 otherwise. He may not be Randy Moss, but the kid can play. You already knew that, though. “Got some good opportunities to make some plays and most importantly we came out with this win, and that’s the plan out there,” said Washington. “Let’s keep it going.” Chop Wood, Carry Water. #DUUUVAL — Parker Washington (@CPW11_) November 15, 2026

title: Kingdom Keys revisited: Chiefs turn two keys in win over Falcons
summary: Every week, “Kingdom Keys” identifies three things the Kansas City Chiefs must accomplish to win their upcoming game. Afterward, we revisit those keys to determine which ones Kansas City actually turned. The Chiefs defeated the Atlanta Falcons 35-13 on Sunday, improving to 7-2 behind five touchdown passes from Patrick Mahomes and another strong defensive performance. […]
full_text: (Photo by Kevin C. Cox/Getty Images) Every week, “ Kingdom Keys ” identifies three things the Kansas City Chiefs must accomplish to win their upcoming game. Afterward, we revisit those keys to determine which ones Kansas City actually turned. The Chiefs defeated the Atlanta Falcons 35-13 on Sunday, improving to 7-2 behind five touchdown passes from Patrick Mahomes and another strong defensive performance. Kansas City clearly accomplished its first two keys. The third requires a little more nuance. Offensive Key: Make Atlanta respect the wide receivers Verdict: Accomplished The offensive key was for Kansas City’s wide receivers to punish Atlanta whenever the Falcons committed additional resources to stopping the run. That mission was accomplished. Chiefs wide receivers combined for 12 receptions, 222 yards and three touchdowns. They accounted for nearly 64% of Mahomes’ 348 passing yards and three of his five touchdown passes. Rashee Rice led the group with five receptions for 82 yards, including a 50-yard completion that helped set up Kansas City’s fourth touchdown. Josh Downs made an immediate impact in his Chiefs debut, catching four passes for 53 yards and a touchdown after having only two full practices with Mahomes. The production extended beyond the top two receivers. Filthy route from Cyrus Allen 😮‍💨 pic.twitter.com/YNh2IdJZjU — NFL (@NFL) November 15, 2026 Rookie Cyrus Allen caught two passes for 44 yards, including a 39-yard touchdown that extended Kansas City’s lead to 21-3. Andrew Armstrong turned his only target into a 43-yard touchdown that put the game away in the fourth quarter. The original goal was for the receivers to combine for at least 150 yards. They surpassed that mark by 72 yards. The Falcons wanted someone other than the Chiefs’ running backs to beat them. Kansas City’s receivers provided a convincing answer. Defensive Key: Contain Bijan Robinson and force third-and-long Verdict: Accomplished Bijan Robinson entered the game averaging more than 125 yards from scrimmage per contest. Kansas City held him to 77. Robinson rushed 16 times for 71 yards and caught four passes for just 6 yards. He scored Atlanta’s only touchdown on a three-yard run in the fourth quarter, but the Chiefs prevented him from controlling the game. Kansas City did allow Robinson to break runs of 17 and 14 yards. Outside those two carries, however, he gained only 40 yards on his other 14 rushing attempts. The Chiefs were especially effective against Robinson as a receiver. His four catches produced only 6 yards, and two receptions lost yardage. Taking away those easy completions forced Michael Penix Jr. to throw elsewhere. Kansas City also consistently put Atlanta behind schedule. The Falcons converted only five of their 16 third-down opportunities, finishing at 31.3%. Using third-and-7 or longer as the definition of third-and-long, Atlanta converted just two of 10 attempts. One conversion came on a third-and-11 completion to Jahan Dotson in the second quarter. The other came when Drake London gained 20 yards on third-and-8 in the third quarter. Otherwise, the Chiefs repeatedly ended Atlanta’s possessions in obvious passing situations. The pressure also returned. Kansas City recorded three sacks, including one from Ashton Gillotte on third-and-7 that forced Atlanta to settle for a field goal. George Karlaftis recorded 1.5 sacks, and Chris Jones shared another. Kansas City didn’t completely eliminate Robinson, but it kept Atlanta’s best offensive player from dictating the game. That was the goal. X-factor: Harrison Butker must make his kicks Verdict: No grade — but encouraging Harrison Butker officially finished without a field-goal attempt, making this key impossible to grade as a success or failure. However, that does not mean the afternoon was meaningless. Late in the second quarter, Butker connected on a 41-yard field goal. Atlanta was called for defensive offside, erasing the attempt from the official statistics and giving Kansas City a first down. Mahomes found Downs for an 18-yard touchdown on the next play. The kick did not count, but it still went through the uprights. Butker also made all five of his extra-point attempts. Those kicks don’t prove his season-long struggles are over, especially since most of his problems have come on field goals of at least 50 yards. Still, cleanly converting six kicks — including the nullified field goal — can help him start rebuilding his rhythm. Butker still needs to prove he can consistently convert field goals under game pressure. Sunday simply did not provide enough official opportunities to make that determination. What it did provide was a small, positive step. The bottom line The Chiefs definitively accomplished two of their three Kingdom Keys against Atlanta. The wide receivers delivered their best collective performance of the season, producing 222 yards and three touchdowns. Defensively, Kansas City held Robinson below 100 scrimmage yards and limited Atlanta to two conversions on 10 third-and-long opportunities. Butker did not record an official field-goal attempt, leaving the third key ungraded. However, making five extra points and watching a 41-yard attempt split the uprights gave him something positive to carry forward. Kingdom Keys final tally: Two accomplished, one ungraded

title: Andy Reid loved the execution of Cyrus Allen’s first career touchdown
summary: There were a lot of firsts during the Kansas City Chiefs’ 35-13 win over the Atlanta Falcons in Week 10. Running back Emmett Johnson’s first start was very memorable and wide receiver Andrew Armstrong scored his first-career touchdown on a long bomb from quarterback Patrick Mahomes. Wide receiver Josh Downs played his first game in […]
full_text: (Photo by Logan Bowles/Getty Images) There were a lot of firsts during the Kansas City Chiefs ’ 35-13 win over the Atlanta Falcons in Week 10. Running back Emmett Johnson’s first start was very memorable and wide receiver Andrew Armstrong scored his first-career touchdown on a long bomb from quarterback Patrick Mahomes. Wide receiver Josh Downs played his first game in a Chiefs uniform. The game also featured rookie wideout Cyrus Allen’s first career touchdown. It came on a 39-yard throw where Allen came wide open down the left sideline. It was a long time coming for Chiefs fans who bought into the Cyrus Allen excitement during training camp. When head coach Andy Reid was asked about the play on Monday, he was fired up about how it went down. “You look at this touchdown, and I love his execution of that, the way he handled it,” Reid said during the video call. Filthy route from Cyrus Allen 😮‍💨 pic.twitter.com/YNh2IdJZjU — NFL (@NFL) November 15, 2026 Reid went into detail on how Allen came open. “They were pressing up on him a little bit; it was a double-move play,” Reid shared. “Sometimes, when you get that press, you just want to take off and run but he actually sold it — aggressively sold it.” Allen has been showing off route-running chops since he was a standout at last year’s Senior Bowl. The Chiefs recognized the talent and selected him in the fifth round, and now, those routes are blending with the chemistry he built with Mahomes over the summer. “[He] was able to stay within the red line on the sideline there, the thing we have on the practice field,” Reid explained. “He was able to stay there and give the quarterback an opportunity to have some space to make the throw. Patrick threw the perfect ball to him, but the execution was great by the kid.” The highlight of Allen’s career is more impressive than anything third-year wideout Xavier Worthy has done in recent memory. When asked about Worthy, Reid pointed to the Falcons’ coverage working to cloud Worthy; he mentioned that “it allowed other guys to be available.” But none of the three passes thrown towards Worthy were completed. Still, Reid says it just wasn’t his day — but pointed to his Week 6 output of 73 yards on seven catches against the Los Angeles Chargers as proof he can be productive. “He just needs to keep doing his thing and working, and he’ll be fine,” Reid said about Worthy. “Some days, it will be his, and some days, it will go to other guys. That’s just how this thing works. We’re spreading it around.” “It’s tough on defenses,” Reid continued. “So everybody is kind of getting a little piece of the pie. You saw when he was only the guy against the Chargers and his production there was great, so it’s not that he’s not capable of that.” As Downs continues to work more in the offense, it will be worth monitoring how the receiver rotation changes. Worthy has led the receiver room in snaps most of the time, but players like Allen — and even Armstrong — are doing more with less time on the field.

title: Patrick Mahomes strengthened his all-time legacy in Week 10
summary: It was a prolific performance by Kansas City Chiefs quarterback Patrick Mahomes in the 35-13 win over the Atlanta Falcons in Week 10. He threw for 348 yards and five touchdowns, firing downfield with authority like it was 2018. He has been writing his name into the NFL’s all-time record books since that first year […]
full_text: (Photo by Logan Bowles/Getty Images) It was a prolific performance by Kansas City Chiefs quarterback Patrick Mahomes in the 35-13 win over the Atlanta Falcons in Week 10. He threw for 348 yards and five touchdowns, firing downfield with authority like it was 2018. He has been writing his name into the NFL’s all-time record books since that first year as a starter, taking home the MVP, but this vintage game etched Mahomes further into them. Including the postseason, Mahomes now has 332 career touchdown passes, which surpassed Pro Football Hall of Famer Peyton Manning (327) for the most touchdown passes by a quarterback in their first 10 seasons. Of course, Mahomes started just one game in his first year, making the accolade all the more impressive. The five-touchdown performance in Atlanta — the seventh of his career — also put him in elite company, making him just the fourth quarterback ever to hit the mark that many times. Mahomes (7) Peyton Manning (9) Tom Brady (9) Drew Brees (11) Patrick Mahomes (10th season) and Josh Allen (9th) are still adding to their totals pic.twitter.com/pqawcLrtwR — PFF (@PFF) November 16, 2026 Of course, Buffalo Bills quarterback Josh Allen made history himself on Sunday by scoring the most total touchdowns (323) over the first 10 regular seasons of an NFL player’s career, passing Manning despite playing in just his ninth season this year. But when it comes to passing touchdowns, Mahomes has stacked them up in bunches more than anybody. He is now the first player in NFL history with at least three touchdown passes in 50 games within the first 10 seasons of his career. He’s also the first quarterback to have 20 games with four or more touchdown passes in that span. Chiefs Kingdom doesn’t usually need reminding that their favorite quarterback is one of the league’s all-time greats, but the numbers keep making that case for Mahomes.

title: Chiefs Week 10 snap count analysis: Ashton Gillotte does it all
summary: Welcome to Arrowhead Pride’s weekly snap-count analysis! Let’s take a closer look at the Kansas City Chiefs’ snap counts in the 35-13 win over the Atlanta Falcons in Week 10. The starting lineups are courtesy of NFL Game Stats and Information, and the snap-count data comes from Pro Football Focus’ premium stats. Starters (offensive): LT Kahlil Benson, […]
full_text: Credit: Brett Davis-Imagn Images | IMAGN IMAGES via Reuters Connect Welcome to Arrowhead Pride’s weekly snap-count analysis! Let’s take a closer look at the Kansas City Chiefs ’ snap counts in the 35-13 win over the Atlanta Falcons in Week 10. The starting lineups are courtesy of NFL Game Stats and Information, and the snap-count data comes from Pro Football Focus’ premium stats. Starters (offensive): LT Kahlil Benson, LG Kingsley Suamataia, C Creed Humphrey, RG Trey Smith, RT Joshua Ezeudu, QB Patrick Mahomes, WR Rashee Rice, WR Xavier Worthy, RB Kenneth Walker, TE Noah Gray and TE Travis Kelce Starters (defensive): DE George Karlaftis, DT Chris Jones, NT Khyiris Tonga, DE Felix Anudike-Uzomah, LB Nick Bolton, LB Drue Tranquill, LB Jack Cochrane, CB Nohl Williams, CB Mansoor Delane, S Alohi Gilman and S Chamarri Conner Did not play: N/A Inactive: QB Garrett Nussmeier (Emergency third QB), RB Kenneth Walker (groin), FB Ben VanSumeren, RB Jaydn Ott (hamstring), DT Peter Woods (neck), CB Melvin Smith Jr. and RT Jaylon Moore (ankle) The big takeaway: Ashton Gillotte is the front seven’s Swiss-Army knife As the season has worn on, defensive end Ashton Gillotte has become an increasingly important part of the defense. He started the season recovering from a plantar fascia injury, and now he’s one of the most versatile players in the defense’s front seven. He has played two-thirds of the defense’s snaps in each of the last three weeks; in Atlanta, he was on the field for 75% of the time the defense was. He didn’t start against the Falcons, but he racked up five tackles, one sack, two tackles for loss and a pass broken up. Pro Football Focus credited Gillotte with six pressures total and led all Chiefs defenders in “Stops” (4), tackles that constitute a failure for the offense. DE Ashton Gillotte is the Swiss-army knife of the Chiefs' front seven Inside pass rusher, off-ball linebacker, edge defender, always playing with his hair on fire pic.twitter.com/Tsj7Ro4Awm — Ron Kopp Jr (@RonOnChiefs) November 16, 2026 He made a big impact while lining up in the B-gap 31 of the 52 times he was on the field; most of that time, he rushed the passer from the inside. He also lined up as an off-ball linebacker on two snaps, giving the Chiefs a unique run-defense look in their base 4-3 formation alongside linebackers Nick Bolton and Drue Tranquill. The Offensive takeaway: Josh Downs plays just 10 snaps In his Chiefs debut, new receiver Josh Downs lined up for just 10 snaps and ran eight routes, totaling 51 yards and a touchdown over four catches. It was clear that Downs will be a key part of the passing game moving forward, so whose snaps are going to be reduced to make room for Downs in future weeks? Xavier Worthy (56 snaps) Rashee Rice (30 snaps) Cyrus Allen (22 snaps) Jalen Royals (19 snaps) Andrew Armstrong (17 snaps) Worthy is the easy answer here, because it’s incredible how little production comes out of leading the receiver room in snaps each week. In Atlanta, he was targeted three times, and none were completed. The Defensive takeaway: R Mason Thomas has empty box score Rookie edge rusher R Mason Thomas played 48 snaps in Atlanta, the second-most snaps in his career. However, Thomas did not register a quarterback pressure over the 39 pass-rush snaps; it’s the first time he was held without a pressure this season. Despite the Chiefs playing with a lead and giving Thomas plenty of opportunity to rush the passer, his impact was not felt. Kansas City generated plenty of pressure, but none came from Thomas, a recent trend: the rookie has only two pressures over the last three games. In the three games between Weeks 4-7, Thomas racked up 14 pressures — but hasn’t reached the same level of impact since. Offensive Snaps Defensive Snaps Special teams snaps

title: 5 things we learned from the Chiefs feasting on Dirty Bird
summary: For most of the first half, it looked like the Kansas City Chiefs were the better team, even if the offense on the field didn’t reflect that. Then, just before halftime, the Chiefs trotted Harrison Butker out to attempt a field goal — and he made it! Harrison Butker actually made a field goal. But […]
full_text: (Photo by Logan Bowles/Getty Images) For most of the first half, it looked like the Kansas City Chiefs were the better team, even if the offense on the field didn’t reflect that. Then, just before halftime, the Chiefs trotted Harrison Butker out to attempt a field goal — and he made it! Harrison Butker actually made a field goal. But a flag was thrown on the play. An Atlanta Falcons player jumped offside. The extra five yards gave the Chiefs a first down. The very next play, quarterback Patrick Mahomes threw a dime to his brand-new target, Josh Downs, who brought in the pass for a touchdown. That was it; the rout was on. Here are five things we learned from the Chiefs’ 35-13 victory over the Falcons. 1. The Chiefs are officially better than they were last season I say this a little tongue-in-cheek. We’ve known this team was better than their 2025 iteration pretty much from the jump. But it’s like they say, you are only as good as your record. And up until now, the Chiefs had not surpassed their disappointing 6-11 record from a year ago. But that was then, and this is now. With this week’s drubbing of the hapless Falcons, the Chiefs have amassed their seventh win of the season, ensuring that no matter what happens the rest of the way out, they’ve locked up a better record than last year. Now, the only question that remains is: how much better are they? A few games better? 11-6 better? 15-2? Only time will tell. 2. The Chiefs’ lack of a deep ball isn’t a Mahomes issue A lot has been said about the decline in the Chiefs’ air yards per attempt in recent years, including their modest 4.15 air yards per attempt over the last four games heading into Atlanta. Over the years, we’ve heard every speculated reason for why the Chiefs couldn’t seem to find success throwing the deep ball. Some said it was because we traded away Tyreek Hill. Some said it was because Mahomes had lost his ability to throw the ball 20+ yards accurately. Some blamed it on coaching and playcalling. Some said it was a deficit of talent at the receiving position. Some said teams adapted to take away the deep ball. Most said it was a combination of all four — but we now have definitive empirical evidence that rules Mahomes out of the equation. On Sunday, Mahomes completed six out of seven passes downfield. Mahomes never lost the ability to throw the ball deep — he just needed the pieces to fall back into place for it to make sense to air it out. Patrick Mahomes threw 2 deep TDs (20+ air yards) against the Falcons, his first game with multiple deep TDs since 2021. Mahomes had thrown just 1 deep TD since the start of 2025 entering Week 10. @KCvsATL | #ChiefsKingdom pic.twitter.com/WwjbciRIF6 — Next Gen Stats (@NextGenStats) November 15, 2026 3. Josh Downs looks like everything we hoped he’d be We knew the Chiefs needed help at wide receiver. We knew that the Chiefs had their eyes set on trading for wide receiver Josh Downs from the Indianapolis Colts . And when they pulled off the trade just before the deadline, we all crossed our fingers and prayed he was the missing piece to this passing attack. And while the jury is still out on whether the issues around this passing attack are fully solved, I think it’s fair to say Downs looks like everything we were hoping for. Sure, it’s a small sample size, and he’s not a superstar. But he’s a good route runner, with great hands, and a smart head on his shoulders. In short, he’s a pro. Something the Chiefs have been missing at wide receiver for the last couple of seasons. The only question now is, just how good is Josh Downs? It’s hard to say, especially when he’s had the likes of Anthony Richardson, Gardner Minshew, and Daniel Jones throwing him the football over the last four seasons. I think the jury is still out. Another thing that the jury is still out on is how much better this team is with Downs on it? Mahomes steps up and drops a dime to Josh Downs for a TD! KCvsATL on CBS/Paramount+ Stream on @NFLPlus pic.twitter.com/dwTMy1qZYC — NFL (@NFL) November 15, 2026 4. Emmett Johnson is the real deal Maybe we already knew this one before this game. But there is a difference between being the change-of-pace back and being the workhorse expected to put the offense on your shoulders and carry it downfield to the promised land. With starting running back Kenneth Walker sidelined with injury, the Chiefs rookie running back got his first chance to be the first man up in the backfield, and boy howdy, he did not disappoint. Fifth round rookie Emmett Johnson just had a breakout performance in his FIRST NFL start. 19 CAR, 93 RUSH YDS, 6 REC, 70 REC YDS, 2 REC TD vs Falcons. The OROY race is wide open. Could Johnson become a serious contender down the stretch? https://t.co/AVdhMhzgcq pic.twitter.com/SRJ2JRdjop — Football Performances (@NFLPerformances) November 15, 2026 This Twitter post sells Johnson short. According to ESPN , Johnson finished the game with 101 rushing yards, 70 receiving yards, and two touchdowns. This kid is a star in the making. I don’t think there is any question that Johnson has been the best rookie running back in the NFL this season. It’s not surprising, considering he was fourth in the nation in rushing last season while playing at Nebraska. A lot will be made this week about the Chiefs rediscovering their deep ball. But none of the above happens without Johnson keeping the defense honest. We obviously want Kenneth Walker III back as soon as possible, but until then, we’ve got E-Money. 5. The Chiefs cannot afford to lose Trey Smith for an extended period of time With the turmoil at the Chiefs’ offensive tackle position this season, Kansas City has at least been able to rest on the fact that when left guard Kingsley Suamataia is not in head coach Andy Reid’s doghouse, the Chiefs have one of the better interior offensive lines in the NFL. So when right guard Trey Smith left the game with a concussion, the Chiefs had no choice but to put Mike Caliendo back in. Look at Caliendo on this play pic.twitter.com/GzpFCGFY5I — NlCKBOLTON (@NICKB0LTON) November 16, 2026 The results were less than inspiring.

George Karlaftis didn’t bite on a play fake and picked up his team-leading fifth sack. Ashton Gillotte’s sack stopped a touchdown drive and the Falcons settled for a field goal. Later, Karlaftis and Chris Jones combined for a sack. If the game had a pivotal play, the defense provided it. Midway through the third quarter, with the Chiefs holding a 14-3 lead, the Falcons faced a fourth-and-4 from midfield. Karlaftis got pressure and forced a quick throw. Kristian Fulton blanketed Kyle Pitts and the ball fell incomplete. A few plays later, the Chiefs opened a three-score lead. 10 Instant Observations From Chiefs’ Dominant Win Over Falcons | Sports Illustrated Cyrus Allen finally has his first big moment Allen was held in the first quarter and had a chance at a one-handed touchdown grab, but he made up for it in the second half. On Mahomes’ first completed pass of 20-plus air yards since Week 4, Allen torched cornerback A.J. Terrell for a 39-yard score to punctuate a quick scoring drive: For an offense that’s struggled with verticality in the passing game in recent weeks, that play was much-needed. The same could be said for the club’s promising young wideout. 2026 NFL season, Week 10: What We Learned from Sunday’s games | NFL.com NFL Research: Patrick Mahomes had five passing touchdowns and no interceptions in Week 10 against the Falcons, his first game with five or more passing touchdowns since Week 1, 2022 against the Cardinals. This was his seventh career game with at least five passing touchdowns, breaking a tie for the fourth-most such games in NFL history. Only Drew Brees (11), Tom Brady (nine) and Peyton Manning (nine) have more than Mahomes. Around the NF L Lions’ Aidan Hutchinson feared to have possible season-ending injury after sack celebration, per report | CBS Sports According to the NFL Network, Hutchinson immediately had an MRI and will get a second opinion, but “there does not appear hope that he returns this season.” In the replay, Hutchinson can be seen jumping in the air after the third-down sack, and his knee appears to buckle when he hits the field. He immediately fell, grabbed his leg and remained on the field for some time. Joe Burrow matches Peyton Manning’s record for consecutive games with at least four TDs | Pro Football Talk With his 4-yard touchdown to Chase Brown in the third quarter, Burrow became the first since Peyton Manning in 2004 to have at least four total touchdowns in five consecutive games, which is the longest streak in NFL history. That score gave the Bengals a commanding 31-3 lead with 4:12 left in the third period. Burrow has been excellent all season, but that’s particularly been the case on Sunday night. So far, he’s completed 32-of-41 passes for 359 yards with four TDs. The one difference between Manning’s streak and Burrow’s is that Manning did it with all passing touchdowns. Between Weeks 8 and 12 in 2004, Manning threw for five, four, five, four, and six TDs with the Colts. Raiders’ Fernando Mendoza vows to learn from first NFL start, a loss to Seahawks | ESPN They punted seven straight times. Mike Macdonald-led defenses have made life difficult for rookie quarterbacks in the past, and Mendoza, who was pressured 19 times and sacked six, became another victim in Las Vegas’ 21-13 loss to Seattle on Sunday. “It’s good to get punched in the face because now it’s a great opportunity to grow and learn and to really unveil all the deficiencies that I have in my game,” said Mendoza, who completed 17 of 29 passes (58.6%) for 143 yards and had a passer rating of 71.5. In case you missed it on Arrowhead Pride Emmett Johnson proves a lot to Chiefs in 100-rushing yard game It speaks to the lack of drop-off from the Chiefs’ offense overall, especially the run game. Johnson had a special performance, and head coach Andy Reid made sure it was as memorable as possible by ensuring he passed the century mark. “Emmett, getting himself over 100 yards there with the help of the offensive line, I thought that was great,” Reid told reporters at the podium after the win. “We left him in there so we could get that, and he took care of business there.” From The Feed Follow Arrowhead Pride on Social Media Facebook: Like our page Instagram: @ArrowheadPride X: Follow @ArrowheadPride AP Staff on X: See complete list
