title: Seahawks-Raiders post-game analysis: One quarter to rule them all
summary: subhead: Seahawks showed us shades of last year’s Super Bowl champions, in spurts. Which we’ll take The 2025 Seahawks have made precious few appearances in 2026. We’ve frequently witnessed the same defense (by some measures even better and more complete!), but only rarely have all three phases partied together to build an early lead and […]
full_text: subhead: Seahawks showed us shades of last year’s Super Bowl champions, in spurts. Which we’ll take The 2025 Seahawks have made precious few appearances in 2026. We’ve frequently witnessed the same defense (by some measures even better and more complete!), but only rarely have all three phases partied together to build an early lead and turn the entire fourth quarter into compost time. Seattle’s Dark Side, special teams and CharboJSNnet offense teased us along those lines today, with a parlay of plays that lasted a quarter. One measly, astonishing, exhilarating, nostalgic, rad quarter of championship-level football. ‘Twas a third quarter sufficient to edge a reeling team who’d just changed quarterbacks. The Seahawks will need more than fifteen minutes of game next time out. In that magical period, though, Seattle balled out. The Hawks: turned a 10-7 deficit into an 11-point lead got an entire game’s worth of production from Jaxon Smith-Njigba, the best offensive player in football forced three (!) three and outs let the Vegas offense run nine plays for a zero percent success rate outgained the Raiders by one eighth of a mile, 223 to minus 2 yards. Yes, one eighth of a mile in a single quarter. And good thing, because those fireworks followed a nightmare first half in which they: fumbled on their opening drive didn’t account for Fernando Mendoza’s legs on third down lost a JSN touchdown to a medium soft offensive pass interference flag found themselves relying on both backup offensive tackles at once lost time of possession 19:25-10:35. Amidst all the slippage (what field was that, RFK?) and injuries (George Holani, Abe Lucas, Jarran Reed, for now), when it came to crunch time in a one-possession affair, the Seahawks were themselves. And by that I mean, they found to time to be the talk of the league for a late-game maneuver that baffled career referees as much as casual fans. Tory Horton’s instant classic Cheathawks play didn’t decide anything — Seattle still wins if it’s deemed illegal or never happens. But for what felt like the first time since K.J. Wright batted a loose ball innocently* out of the end zone to clinch a 2015 victory, officials followed the Rule of Cool and let it stand. *believe that, bridge for sale, brooklyn, yada yada yada The thing that makes Horton’s frantic pointing even better is that he knew, in the moment, he couldn’t pick up the batted ball he had himself batted and return it without drawing a flag. The message got through, Rashid Shaheed came through with twenty emergency yards, and one first down later, it was all over, because Horton’s save knocked out the two-minute warning as a stoppage. The fun fact serving as a cherry on top? It was Horton’s only touch of the day. No targets, no receptions, no returns. Our man put on his combine underwear and showed off that vertical one more time, for the world to see, and also ask, “wait, Tory WHO?” The Raiders were game early on, and for a while, Fernando Mendoza’s mobility plus solid decision-making neutered the sizeable advantage Seattle’s defensive line brought into the contest. For a while. But if we’re comparing quarterbacks for their entire body of work on Sunday, Drew Lock came out rather ahead. A 14-17-240-2-0 day gets added to his ledger, along with another win. Dunno if anyone is going to talk QB controversy (just kidding there’ll be 8,000,000,000 comments on a Field Gulls article later this week) and I’m not really going to participate yet except to drop Lock’s season line right here. 68 for 93, 837 yards, 73.1 completion, 7-0 TD-INT, 9 yards/attempt, five sacks and one fumble we can actually blame him for. With the caveat that he’s faced the Cardinals twice, Lock is quarterbacking the hell out of Darnold, doing a pretty good Safer Sam impression. Now, Darnold has something significant on Lock — he slung the ball as well as Matthew Dang Stafford in the two most recent Rams games, winning both, reaching a level the Seahawks backup simply doesn’t have. I guess what I’m trying to say is, if Lock has to play more this year, that’ll be okay, until it isn’t anymore, and the Seahawks can cross that rickety bridge when it comes. Until then, Seattle will continue to win every game he posts a 158 rating, I’m pretty sure of that. Even the fumbles were somewhat capricious. A failed shovel pass where the ball comes loose, that’s on Drew but bad fortune too. The collision with Charbs goes in the box score officially, but come on, pretty weird and rare to see the running back hit his quarterback’s arm on the way past. By that time, however, the game’s real turning point was in the rear view mirror, also where Jaxon Smith-Njigba usually sees defensive backs. This week, that moment where you knew the Seahawks would emerge with a win came right in the middle of the third quarter tsea-nami. There’s that incessant slipping again, even in the middle of JSN’s weekly magnum opus. Noticed something else on replay: Lock throws across his whole body, falling away the other direction, and swishes the ball into JSN’s hands like a Steph Curry fadeaway three from the logo. To the recap, and birds of prey. Q1: Seahawks 7, Raiders 7 Predator : The mutant creature with guard Spencer Burford’s upper body and Mendoza’s legs. Prey : Another third down, the Raiders’ favorite food group until the Seahawks defense got cooking. How : Burford blocks two men while Mendoza chooses which lane to amble down on his way to six points. Seriously, look at that space. Mike Macdonald’s defense didn’t really account for Mendoza on the ground at first. They paid for it. Fortunately not with a loss this time, because as we’ll see, things got a lot more cramped for the rookie as the game wore on. Recap : So on that first fumble, Lock has to either get the shovel pass out a fraction sooner or take the sack. In between won’t do. Pretend you’re at a four-way stop, Drew. Go or don’t go. But don’t try to do both. Pregame, it was understood Vegas would have trouble moving the ball unless they got help. Don’t give them help! Like starting in plus territory. There’s no shame in immediately allowing Ashton Jeanty to bounce it out for a first down on third and three, and Mendoza can already sneak on 3rd and 1 better than most vets. But his scoring play can easily be chalked up to poor preparation. It’s not like the rookie won last year’s Heisman standing in the pocket a la Peyton Manning. Down seven, the Seahawks remembered who they were and struck back, scoring twice on one drive; if the first one had counted we wouldn’t have had to hear JSN slander for a half. The second touchdown stood and counted extra for Lock especially, who won’t tell you he needed the redemption although it can’t have hurt. To be honest, I’m not convinced Lock couldn’t see the blue line. He can see it, right? That’s why he plants his foot on it and forgets about the elbow tendinitis to find Cooper Kupp forty yards downfield, right? The drive had been vintage Seahawks already: explosive from Charbs, Barner moving the sticks, two more runs, the OPI they only flagged ’cause it’s a point of emphasis now. (Just wait until JSN starts getting the superstar calls due a star of his superitude.) Lock’s masterpiece came on third down, with him on the run. Brian Fleury knows how to deploy his backup now: get him moving. We all learn stuff all the time! The Raiders, undeterred, ended the quarter with a Mendoza third-down scramble again. Hopefully they enjoyed it while it lasted. Q2: Raiders 10, Seahawks 7 Predator : Devon Witherspoon Prey : physics, his former OC, empty space, rookies How: I know we’re in the second quarter, but the view of Spoon’s second sack, that came in the final period, tells the story better. Not only did Spoon allow no completions in the quarter, he contributed a sack right as the Raiders were marching again and made two tackles at the line of scrimmage. It’s likely I said this last week and the week before, but pay him again. Recap :…

title: Seahawks Droppings: Raiders first-round treasure sunk by Seahawks defense
summary: Everybody take a deep breath. Now exhale. Let that relaxation set in for the next two weeks as the Seattle Seahawks head into their bye on a two-game winning streak after coming alive in the second half in a 21-13 win over the Las Vegas Raiders. It was one of those “get it done any […]
full_text: Everybody take a deep breath. Now exhale. Let that relaxation set in for the next two weeks as the Seattle Seahawks head into their bye on a two-game winning streak after coming alive in the second half in a 21-13 win over the Las Vegas Raiders. It was one of those “get it done any way you can” games, with injuries piling up for Seattle. On the other side of the field was the No. 1 overall pick Fernando Mendoza making his first start at quarterback, leading to a suddenly hot ticket in Sin City. Despite more injuries, turnovers, and a missed FG, Seattle found a way to get the win and now get a few weeks to regroup for the stretch run of the season. Seahawks Droppings Seattle’s defense started slow, then exploded. One would think that Mike Macdonald’s defense facing a rookie QB in his first start would mean a very rough day for Mendoza. It didn’t start out that way with two straight scoring drives given up by the Seahawks. Mendoza got the ball out quickly and accurately, and used his legs when needed to extend plays and get into the endzone. After those early drives, the Seahawks defense CLAMPED DOWN. At one point in the fourth quarter, the Raiders had -17 yards of offense in the second half. A stupid 38-yard pass play from Mendoza to Jeanty near the end of the fourth quarter bumped the numbers up for Mendoza, but he still finished with just 143 passing yards. The Seahawks sacked him six times for a staggering 45 yards lost! They also held the Raiders to 65 yards rushing for the game. That equates to 163 total yards for the suffocating Seattle defense. They didn’t force any turnovers, but the Raiders had nowhere to go after those first two drives. Seattle’s offense started slow, then exploded…mostly in the third quarter. Drew Lock was back in at QB, and Seattle had its one-two punch of Zach Charbonnet and Jadarian Price at their disposal once again. Lock “fumbled” on the first offensive drive after it seemed like he was clearly trying to execute a basketball chest pass near a receiver’s feet to avoid a sack. The refs saw it differently, and it was still a poor decision on his part. Jaxon Smith-Njigba had a TD called back on a questionable offensive PI call and had a drop on a later third down. Everything just looked disjointed. Then, on a third and long, Lock rolled out, avoided a sack, stopped just short of the line of scrimmage and threw a long TD pass to Cooper Kupp. There wasn’t much after that until the third quarter where the Seahawks went wild mostly on the back of JSN. Lock found him in another scramble drill for a 71-yard TD, and the Seahawks also scored on Jadarian Price’s first NFL TD showing his burst to the outside. The offense went cold again in the fourth quarter when they had the chance to salt the game away, but Brian Fleury had maybe his best call of the game with the naked bootleg to essentially end the game. Seattle overcame a lot. Lock turned the ball over on the first drive. Abe Lucas got hurt early on leading to Bobby Hart playing RT after Josh Jones was already playing LT for the injured Charles Cross. That’s in addition to Quenton Nelson, Sam Darnold, Leo Williams also on the sidelines. The rest of the games where Seattle played like crap this season, they lost. To find a way to come away with a win when giving the other team extra chances and facing a litany of injuries – on the road no less – shows grit. The Turf Monster was busy. How many times did a Seahawks player eat dirt today after slipping on that terrible field? Charbonnet and Price both went down early multiple times. JSN actually fell down before he got loose for the 71-yard TD. Those are the worst field conditions I can remember seeing in the last number of years. I get it that the players want natural grass, but if that’s going to be the result, count me out. Spoon went blitz-crazy. Devon Witherspoon is a demon blitzing from his CB position. We saw him give Drake Maye fits in the Super Bowl, but he hasn’t been utilized that way as much as I anticipated this season. Until today. Spoon blitzed three times, and came away with 2.0 sacks and a QB hit on the third one. Each time, he hammered Mendoza and I can’t believe that he didn’t cough the ball up. Spoon is such a weapon and brings the juice for the whole defense. Stacking sacks. Spoon had 2.0 sacks, and the Seahawks defensive line added 4 more, one each from Derick Hall, DeMarcus Lawrence, Dante Fowler Jr, and Byron Murphy. They were a key to the second half surge against Mendoza and will look to keep the momentum going after the bye week, hopefully with Leo Williams added back into the mix. JSN. That’s it, I’m honestly running out of adjectives for his tremendous play. What can you say when a guy puts up 144 receiving yards in one quarter?? He finished with 8 catches for 178 yards and a TD. The rest of the team managed 6 catches for 69 yards. Can Seattle find someone else after the bye week to step up and take some pressure off of JSN? The running game is coming around. I shouldn’t have made it this far without mentioning the run game, but here we are. Am I crazy, or does Charbonnet actually look better now than he did before his injury? He runs ANGRY and is displaying great vision. Charbs finished with 20 carries for 94 yards and sent a bunch of dudes to the turf. Price only had 36 yards on 9 carries, yet got loose to the outside for his first TD. I’m still waiting on Price’s breakout game which I do think is coming. Still, with Charbs playing as well as he is, maybe it isn’t needed. Tory Horton made one of the coolest plays ever . Seriously, Horton skying to keep the ball in bounds on the kickoff, which was then returned by Rashid Shaheed to get the ball to the two-minute warning was awesome. It might not seem like a huge deal, but the Raiders weren’t dead at that point and still had 2 timeouts. With the two-minute warning, they could’ve stopped the clock three times and who knows what would’ve happened. Horton’s heady play put more pressure on the Raiders, and the Seahawks ended up icing the game away. Great stuff. With the way the Seahawks season has gone, getting to the bye week at 6-4 with a chance to heal up is just what they needed. We can all sit back and enjoy a stress-free few weeks until Seattle suits up again. Get healthy, continue to run the ball with authority, and play great defense. Everything is still there for Seattle, but it will take hard work and Seahawks Football.

full_text: SANTA CLARA, CA - NOVEMBER 28: Nick Bosa #97 of the San Francisco 49ers sacks Kirk Cousins #8 of the Minnesota Vikings during the game at Levi's Stadium on November 28, 2021 in Santa Clara, California. The 49ers defeated the Vikings 34-26. (Photo by Michael Zagaris/San Francisco 49ers/Getty Images) | Getty Images Kawakami: Kyle Shanahan on QBs — the old Cousins plan and Purdy as an all-timer (paywall) “Shanahan completely agreed, then added a very revealing aspect of this QB/coach relationship: Shanahan just doesn’t feel like he has to keep Purdy away from certain things or that he has to limit his play-calling to make sure the QB isn’t forced to do too much. It’s all open for Purdy. And if you want to read some general thoughts into this about what Shanahan felt he had to do at times when he was calling plays for Garoppolo or Lance (or anybody else), I think it’s pretty fair. “That’s what affects my play-calling,” Shanahan said. “That’s why I don’t mind throwing it a bunch, if that’s what the defense says we should do. I don’t mind getting away from that and running, either. “But I don’t have to feel like I have to protect him that much. Even with the real good guys, you’ve gotta protect guys a lot. And Brock rarely makes me feel like that.” Kyle Shanahan shares 49ers updates during Monday conference call “I think Christian’s the perfect mentor just because even if he doesn’t say anything, just how Christian works every second. Christian’s the most detailed, focused, obsessive player I’ve ever been around. Just watch how he blocks when [WR] Deebo’s [Samuel Sr.] running back and he’s playing receiver and just the technique and the effort he goes through on every single play. Just the way Christian plays football is the best example or mentor to anybody who’s on our team or anybody who wants to watch how a football player goes about his business. I also think Christian really respects Kaelon. I remember Christian telling me right when he got here how much of a pro that guy seemed like and seemed like he was made of the right stuff. It’s because K.B., similar to Christian, he works at everything. He’s very hard on himself. He’s very tough and approaches each day to get better. As talents and as people, I think they pair together very well.” 49ers WR Mike Evans’ Achilles tendinitis injury explained “It’s not necessarily at risk for rupture, but it just means it takes a little bit longer for things to heal. And he’s probably — given the fact that he has been out for a couple weeks now — in that territory…..The biggest risk is really more that you let this thing perpetuate and just not actually cool down. So instead of getting 100% better, you’re 75% better and then you play and now you’re 70% better. That’s the bigger risk…..You don’t just purely shut them down and just have them sit on the couch. There’s a physical therapy component where you’re doing certain types of strengthening and stretching and things like that. You are trying to reduce the inflammation. So that’s anti-inflammatories, that’s cold baths, that’s massage. It’s not that you’re just purely saying, “Don’t play for three weeks and you’ll be fine.” There is an active treatment component to it, but the most important thing is giving the tendon a break.” Why Nick Bosa’s sack-less season so far doesn’t worry 49ers coach Kyle Shanahan “I think Nick is ready to go, and I think he’s definitely affecting the quarterback and doing some good things out there,” Shanahan said. “But Nick’s going to get better, the more he gets back with us.” 49ers put up big numbers vs. Cowboys, tout ‘incredibly dangerous’ offense “Purdy finished 22-of-28 passing for a career-high 389 yards with three touchdowns and no interceptions. Even while under pressure, Purdy found ways to do most of his damage when evading defenders, going 8-of-8 for 175 yards and a touchdown outside the pocket.” 49ers game review: Nick Bosa in career-worst drought. How bad did it look in Dallas? (Paywall) “After reviewing Bosa’s snaps Sunday against the Cowboys, however, some context is required for a performance that wasn’t up to his standards, but also didn’t suggest he’s a shell of himself. Bosa did have four QB pressures — he twice had quick wins against Steele that forced Prescott to scramble — and the Cowboys devoted an extra blocker to Bosa on nine of his 41-pass rush snaps, using a tight end or running back to deliver a chip block on six plays. In the third quarter, two series after Bosa hit Prescott’s arm in mid-throw, Bosa beat Steele with a speed rush, forcing Prescott to step up in the pocket before he fired a deep incompletion on 3rd-and-6. A contributing factor to Bosa’s relatively silent Sunday was the 49ers’ shredded secondary, which routinely failed to hold up in coverage. As a result, Prescott rarely had to hold onto the ball for a few extra beats in a game in which he completed 30 of 51 passes for 343 yards with five touchdowns and an interception and was sacked only once.” 49ers’ lack of a pass rush is becoming hard to ignore, even at 8-1 (paywall) “It didn’t seem like we got there enough, especially at the end when they were coming back,” Shanahan said. “It seems like we got gassed. I could tell how tired we were.” “Usually, when an offense gains 584 yards and scores 46 points, it means the starters on both sides of the ball are watching comfortably from the sideline in the fourth quarter. On Sunday, however, Warner and a few others played all 76 defensive snaps.” 9 Winners, 7 losers, and 1 IDK from the 49ers win over the Cowboys “The Cowboys ran 76 plays. Let’s add some context to the poor play. The defensive line was clearly gassed and running on fumes. With that said, the interior was getting pushed around in the first half, and fortunate Dallas didn’t run the ball on them more. Osa Odighizuwa had three run stops and four pressures. That’s about as well as he can play. DeForest Buckner had three pressures. Sebastian Valdez had two, and James Thompson had one. Pass-rush win rate is a better indicator of how a player performed. Only Odighizuwa was in the double digits. Buckner, who played 55 snaps and 39 pass-rushing snaps, only won on 5.1% of his rushes. He has to be better.”
author: Yinon Raviv

title: NFC Playoff picture: The 49ers are sitting pretty at the top; there’s a new No. 2
summary: The NFC playoff picture is set through ten weeks. The San Francisco 49ers are leading the way with one loss. Let’s take a look at the playoff picture: 1. San Francisco 49ers (8-1) 2. Detroit Lions (7-2, 1-0 vs CHI/MIN, 2-0 NFCN) 3. New York Giants (5-3-1) 4. Carolina Panthers (4-5)5. Minnesota Vikings (7-2, 1-1 […]
full_text: (Photo by Stacy Revere/Getty Images) | Getty Images The NFC playoff picture is set through ten weeks. The San Francisco 49ers are leading the way with one loss. Let’s take a look at the playoff picture: 1. San Francisco 49ers (8-1) 2. Detroit Lions (7-2, 1-0 vs CHI/MIN, 2-0 NFCN) 3. New York Giants (5-3-1) 4. Carolina Panthers (4-5) 5. Minnesota Vikings (7-2, 1-1 vs DET/CHI, win over CHI) 6. Chicago Bears (7-2, 0-2 vs DET/MIN, loss to MIN) 7. Green Bay Packers (6-4) 8. Seattle Seahawks (6-4, 2-1 NFCW) 9. Los Angeles Rams (6-4, 0-2 NFCW) 10. Dallas Cowboys (4-6) 11. Washington Commanders (3-5-1) 12. Tampa Bay Buccaneers (3-6, 3-3 NFC) 13. Arizona Cardinals (3-6, 2-5 NFC) 14. New Orleans Saints (3-6, 1-4 NFC) 15. Atlanta Falcons (3-7) 16. Philadelphia Eagles (2-7) In the NFC North, the three-way tie goes to the Detroit Lions because of their win over the Vikings. They are undefeated in the three-way head-to-head. The Vikings are next because they have a win over Chicago. The Vikings humbled the Packers in Week 10. Staying in the division, we still believe the Lions and Bears are the biggest threats to the 49ers. They have elite offenses, and we saw what happens when the Niners run into an aggressive passing attack. Unlike Dallas, Chicago and Detroit are just as dangerous on the ground as they are through the air. The Rams and Seahawks are still on the outside looking in. Green Bay currently holds the tiebreaker over Seattle based on best win percentage in conference games. It would be hilarious if the reason the reigning Super Bowl champs missed the playoffs was because they lost to Marcus Mariota. Speaking of the Commanders, they just beat the top team in their division. J.J. McCarthy looks lost against a 2-high structure, and their cornerbacks are bound to come back down to earth. A tie may be the reason New York sneaks into the playoffs. There’s a lot of football to be played. Another slip-up by the Giants opens the door for the Cowboys. If you rank the NFC by point differential, here’s how the standings would look: 49ers +85 Rams +61 Lions +58 Bears +57 Vikings +50 Seahawks +48 Buccaneers +24 I think it’d be easier to convince the masses that these are the conference’s seven best teams.
author: Kyle Posey

title: 49ers open up as slight favorites in their Week 11 clash with the Vikings
summary: The San Francisco 49ers are coming off a game in which 86 points were scored. The Niners’ 46 points were more than any total points in a Vikings game since Week 1. The unstoppable force takes on the immovable object. Minnesota is No. 1 defensively in success rate. They’ve allowed six passing touchdowns compared to […]
full_text: (Photo by Adam Bettcher/Getty Images) | Getty Images The San Francisco 49ers are coming off a game in which 86 points were scored. The Niners’ 46 points were more than any total points in a Vikings game since Week 1. Faithful, take 49ers game day wherever you go! Stay connected to the action and share every reaction with fellow 49ers fans on the SB Nation app. Join the live game-day chat Browse with fewer ads Seamlessly jump between communities Enjoy faster commenting and posting Download the SB Nation app on iOS or Android . The unstoppable force takes on the immovable object. Minnesota is No. 1 defensively in success rate. They’ve allowed six passing touchdowns compared to 10 interceptions. They’ve held their opponent to 16 or fewer points in six games this season. If last week was the toughest challenge to date for the 49ers defense, the same is true for Brock Purdy and the offense in Mexico City. Purdy was sacked five times against the Cowboys. The Vikings sacked Jordan Love eight times. Minnesota is the only team in the NFL with a double-digit sack percentage. Their blitz rate has dipped over the past month. Brian Flores now blitzes only 69% of the time. Purdy’s completion percentage dips 16% while his yards per attempt drops about a yard when he’s under pressure compared to when he’s kept clean. It’s a different story against the blitz. Purdy’s completion percentage drops from 71 to 69 percent, but he has a 12-to-2 touchdown-to-interception ratio and an outrageous 11.6 yards per attempt. Purdy is a big play hunter and will fight pressure with pressure, making for a fascinating matchup. The Vikings scored 30 points against Green Bay in Kirk Cousins’ first start, but he threw a boneheaded interception and avoided another after his knee was down. The Vikings only averaged 4.8 yards per play and went 1-for-4 in the red zone. But eight sacks and four turnovers make it nearly impossible to lose. My gut feeling says the Vikings are frauds. Cousins raises the ceiling infinitely, but they have more holes on both sides of the ball than their record suggests. Minnesota is also expected to be without Jordan Addison this week. The 49ers are 3-point favorites on FanDuel Sportsbook , with the total on the game set at 45.5 — 10 points lower than the Niners and Cowboys total.
author: Nicholas McGee

title: ‘The sky is the limit’ – 49ers don’t see an offensive ceiling after record-setting explosion
summary: For the rest of the NFL, the scary thing about the 49ers’ dominant offensive performance against the Dallas Cowboys will not be the numbers they put up, but that they did so while missing one of the most integral pieces of their passing game. San Francisco’s attack was remarkable in the Niners’ 46-40 shootout win […]
full_text: ARLINGTON, TX - NOVEMBER 15: San Francisco 49ers wide receiver Deebo Samuel Sr. celebrates with San Francisco 49ers guard Dominick Puni after scoring a touchdown during the NFL game between the San Francisco 49ers and the Dallas Cowboys on November 15, 2026 at AT&T Stadium in Arlington, Texas. (Photo by Brian Rothmuller/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images) | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images For the rest of the NFL, the scary thing about the 49ers’ dominant offensive performance against the Dallas Cowboys will not be the numbers they put up, but that they did so while missing one of the most integral pieces of their passing game. San Francisco’s attack was remarkable in the Niners’ 46-40 shootout win over the Cowboys on Sunday, racking up 584 yards, the most Dallas has ever given up at home. Quarterback Brock Purdy threw for 389 yards and three touchdowns in a game that marked another stunning display of his playmaking ability, while Christian McCaffrey had 223 scrimmage yards (161 receiving, 62 rushing). He scored on receptions of 74 and 66 yards and also found the endzone on a 16-yard fourth-quarter rush. McCaffrey became the first running back in NFL history with multiple receiving touchdowns of at least 65 yards in one game, and the first player in the league history to have 160 receiving yards, two touchdown receptions, 60 rushing yards and a rushing touchdown in the same game. Those numbers reflect a performance that was McCaffrey the receiver at his most devastating — though he was aided by one particularly favorable assignment on his third and final score — and yet, even after a game in which the San Francisco’s main focal point exploded for the most scrimmage yards he has recorded as a 49er — there was consensus in the Niners’ locker room that they have room to hit even greater heights. This was the 49ers’ third successive game without top receiver Mike Evans, with the future Hall of Famer still battling an Achilles issue. Though the Niners’ effort against the Cowboys showed there is no reason to rush Evans back, his prospective return is something tight end George Kittle is relishing. “When you add Mike Evans to it, when Mike Evans is on the field and the threat that he poses, I don’t get to get covered by corners anymore and that’s all Mike Evans,” Kittle told his postgame press conference. “So it makes my life easier, it makes Christian’s life easier. “Everybody on the field, their live is easier because of how good he is and how much of a threat he is. So I’ve actually never been more confident in an offense when I look out and I see Mike Evans and he just has a go ball. It’s like sick. So I’m excited to get Mike back, hopefully.” McCaffrey, though, is less focused on what the 49ers could achieve offensively, and more on the frame of mind that has allowed them to continue delivering outstanding production regardless of who is in the lineup, with Keenan Allen putting up 61 yards on five catches on his debut. “I don’t know I don’t focus on any of that,” McCaffrey said when asked about the offense’s ceiling. “All I know is we got the right mindset. We got the right group of guys. We have a lot of guys. It’s cool because we’re a very veteran run offense. We’ve had a lot of guys who have had a lot of success, but we really love each other. I think that shows in practice, that shows in the game. “I think everybody just wants to win no matter how it is. And I think that’s what makes it really cool. Guys like Mike, guys like Keenan, we come here and just do your job, do it really well, help the team win however you can and let’s see where we can go. But the standard’s really high. We got the right guys in the locker room and it’s a fun team to be a part of.” Of course, the enjoyment factor is heightened when the offense can score as easily as the Niners did in moving to 8-1. “The ceiling is high as we set it,” Deebo Samuel said after a two-touchdown display. “We got a lot of playmakers on both sides of the ball and we go out there and put up 40 points. It just shows you what we’re capable of on offense.” That sentiment was echoed by future Hall of Fame left tackle Trent Williams, who believes the 49er attack does not have a ceiling when the group delivers the kind of execution he displayed with his downfield blocking on several key plays. “I think we can be as good as we allow ourselves to be,” Williams said. “As long as we execute, we play together. “We got to cut down on the penalties and shooting ourselves in the foot. But when we execute, I think the sky’s the limit for us.”
author: Nicholas McGee

title: We’re Firemen: The 49ers don’t need more; they need to stay who they are
summary: In November 2015, Teddy Atlas leaned into Timothy Bradley’s corner between the 7th and 8th rounds against Brandon Rios and gave a speech fight fans still quote. “We’re firemen,” he told him. Other people panic in the heat. Firemen walk into it, because that’s the job. Most people assume a speech like that comes when […]
full_text: (Photo by Ron Jenkins/Getty Images) In November 2015, Teddy Atlas leaned into Timothy Bradley’s corner between the 7th and 8th rounds against Brandon Rios and gave a speech fight fans still quote. “We’re firemen,” he told him. Other people panic in the heat. Firemen walk into it, because that’s the job. Most people assume a speech like that comes when your fighter is losing. Bradley wasn’t losing. He was winning, clearly in control. Atlas spoke up because he saw slippage. Rios was finding his confidence, and Bradley had started changing who he was, as if he needed something different to finish the job. He didn’t. Atlas wasn’t asking him for more. He was reminding him of who he already was. Bradley went back out and stopped Rios in the 9th. Sunday in Arlington, the San Francisco 49ers lived that whole fight in one afternoon. In the first half, they weren’t themselves. They dropped back 22 times and ran it only 11, against a Dallas run defense that came in ranked 31st. Kaelon Black got 1 carry. Brock Purdy took 4 sacks. The 49ers went into the locker room up 17-16, mostly because Christian McCaffrey turned a short throw into a 74-yard touchdown. In the second half, they remembered who they were. 16 designed runs, 169 rushing yards, 9.9 a carry. Black got 10 carries, and on his 25-yard touchdown he went through Caleb Downs like Downs owed him money. Deebo Samuel took a reverse for 70 yards. McCaffrey scored from 16. Brock went 10 of 11 and was sacked once. They scored 29 points and led 38-19 with 11:26 left. Then came the slippage. Up big, the defense sat back and started giving away yards. And the refs didn’t do us any favors. The 49ers were flagged 11 times for 100 yards, 7 of them judgment calls, including a roughing on the 2nd snap of the game, a hold that wiped out a Mykel Williams strip-sack, and a pass interference that set Dallas up at the 1. Thirty of Dallas’s 40 points came on drives those flags extended or set up. Some of that is on the stripes. 3 Nick Bosa offsides are on us. Either way, Dallas scored 21 in the 4th quarter and got the ball back down 6 with 43 seconds left. The 49ers weren’t losing. They were winning and drifting, just like Bradley. The fix isn’t more. The front office already settled that at the deadline. They went and got Keenan Allen for a 6th and DeForest Buckner for a 4th, and that conversation is over. This is an older team, and it’s the team they’re riding: Trent Williams, George Kittle, McCaffrey and Kyle Juszczyk all past 30, Allen at 34, Buckner 2 games into his 49ers return. What it does need is to get healthy and to get better. Some of the guys who are back aren’t all the way back. Deommodore Lenoir battled a bad foot all week and still broke up 4 passes, but he isn’t the same corner at less than 100%, and Dallas knew it on the final drive. Bosa is working his way back and played like it: 0 tackles, 1 QB hit. Deebo is fresh off a hamstring, Renardo Green left with his back, and Mike Evans still can’t get on the field. Being on the active roster isn’t the same as being in game shape. Teams build toward a peak in December and January. The 49ers are still a ways from theirs, but Sunday’s 2nd half was a glimpse of what it looks like. The test comes immediately, and it comes in thin air. Minnesota, 7-2, in Mexico City, more than 7,000 feet above sea level, where every snap costs a little more breath than it should. Brian Flores’ defense is built on the hunt. It blitzes on 75.3% of snaps, the most extreme rate in at least 25 years, and 87.5% of the time when the quarterback is under center. It allows a league-low 14.5 points a game and has the NFL’s best sack rate. And it isn’t hiding weak corners: Byron Murphy, Isaiah Rodgers and James Pierre have allowed 0 touchdowns and picked off 7 passes between them. This is a pack that circles, closes in, and takes down quarterbacks. Ask Jordan Love. Green Bay ran it 17 times and dropped back 37, and Minnesota sacked him 8 times. The Packers ran from the hunt and got caught in the open. The 49ers know this pack. Flores’ Vikings have beaten Purdy both times they’ve seen him, 22-17 in 2023 and 23-17 in 2024, and after the 2nd one Purdy walked up to Flores and told him his scheme was crazy. This isn’t a defense that has to figure the 49ers out. It already has. So what is all that aggression really about? A defense that sends 5 every snap is either supremely confident or doesn’t trust what it looks like when it sends 4. Maybe it’s a weapon. Maybe it’s a bully’s habit, hitting first so nobody finds out what happens when someone hits back. Buffalo found out. The Bills didn’t try to outsmart the blitz; they leaned into it. James Cook carried it 31 times, the most by any back in a game this season. He averaged only 3.5 a carry, and it didn’t matter. Buffalo kept handing it to him, snap after snap, and held the ball for 42:32. Minnesota’s offense saw the field for 46 plays and scored 6 points. It wasn’t pretty. It was a labor of love, and it broke them. That’s the blueprint, and it’s the 49ers’ native language. A blitz can’t cover every gap. When 5 and 6 rushers are flying upfield, someone has vacated a run fit, and that’s where inside zone, outside zone, duo, and the off-tackle runs live. Catch them with their pants down. And when it is 3rd down, and the pressure is coming, the 49ers finally have a receiver built for that exact moment. Allen beat Dallas for 23 yards on 3rd and 12 and moved the chains again on 3rd and 6, winning on footwork and timing, not speed. Against an all-out blitz, that’s the guy who sits down in the hole the rusher just left. Then there’s the air. The hunt runs on energy: 5 and 6 men sprinting upfield on almost every snap, play after play. That’s a lot to ask at 7,000 feet. Can Minnesota play at that speed for 4 quarters in Mexico City without fading? The best way to find out is to make them chase McCaffrey and Black for 60 minutes. Make the hunter turn around and defend his own ground, then make him do it again on the next snap, and the one after that, until his legs answer the question for him. With Evans out and Allen only 1 game into his 49ers career, the conversation all week has been about the receivers. It shouldn’t be. Minnesota predicates itself on being the physical team. If they’re asking for a fight, the 49ers have to give them one: hand it to McCaffrey and Black, give Deebo the ball in space, take the quick throws, and make that defense tackle for 4 quarters. I’m breaking down exactly how on the channel this week. A 19-point lead that turned into a 6-point finish invites cynicism. But Atlas’s words ring truer for this team right now than ever. You were winning. Don’t change who you are because the other guy found a little confidence. This is the fire you’ve been waiting for, and everything you need is already in you. Remember, Faithful, pressure is the privilege. We’re firemen. Mexico City is the next fire, and the last thing this team can afford is to be afraid of the flame.
author: The Coach

title: 9 Winners, 7 losers, and 1 IDK from the 49ers win over the Cowboys
summary: The San Francisco 49ers and Dallas Cowboys came close to reaching 100 points in Week 10. It was a game where defense was optional. The offenses had their way. Big plays were the norm, and two of the league’s most potent offenses didn’t disappoint. Let’s get into the Winners and Losers from Week 10. Winners […]
full_text: (Photo by Stacy Revere/Getty Images) | Getty Images The San Francisco 49ers and Dallas Cowboys came close to reaching 100 points in Week 10. It was a game where defense was optional. The offenses had their way. Big plays were the norm, and two of the league’s most potent offenses didn’t disappoint. Let’s get into the Winners and Losers from Week 10. Winners Brock Purdy We try to stay away from listing core players in this section. Even Purdy’s biggest naysayers can’t use this performance or “it’s the Cowboys’ defense” against him. Purdy led all quarterbacks in Week 10 with a 0.77 EPA per pass. Second-place Matthew Stafford was 0.63. Purdy had the second-highest passing success rate at 63.6%. He completed nearly 80% of his passes and threw for three touchdowns. Sprinkle in a couple of much-needed scrambles, and it was your typical ho-hum performance from Purdy this season. Five sacks may be alarming — you could argue only one was on the offensive line — but those were offset by 3 completions of 20+ yards in the air. A couple of improv plays off-script where Purdy manipulated the pocket around him, made unblocked defenders miss, and created first downs (one was a touchdown) when nothing was there. There’s more evidence that shows Purdy’s excellence from Sunday. The offense averaged 0.48 EPA per play, the highest of any offense this season. Purdy sliced and diced the Cowboys against man coverage. He completed 12 of 16 passes against man coverage for 273 yards and three touchdowns. That was the most yards in a game facing man coverage by any player since 2021. When Purdy scrambled, he was 4-for-4 for 135 yards and a touchdown. That number ties Patrick Mahomes (W4 2018) and Josh Allen (W15 2024) for the most scramble passing yards in a game since 2018. Against the blitz, Purdy went 6-for-6 for 197 yards and two scores. Christian McCaffrey McCaffrey topped 20 mph on his 66-yard touchdown. He did a fantastic job making himself available and getting into Purdy’s line of sight on the 74-yard touchdown. Surprisingly, McCaffrey had a rushing success rate of only 23.1%. But he made several impact plays on those carries, gained 35 yards after contact, forced two missed tackles, and had two 10+ yard runs, including a 16-yard touchdown. CMC is here because of his work through the air. He had a third-down target where he beat Caleb Downs for a much-needed first down. McCaffrey came through in the clutch when the offense needed a big play. McCaffrey became the first running back in NFL history with multiple 65+ yard touchdown receptions in the same game. He had the most receiving yards by a running back since Jamaal Charles’s 195 yards in Week 15 of 2013. Kaelon Black Welcome to the show, rook. Black forced three missed tackles — two of them on one play. He had 53 rush yards, 44 of which came after contact. Again, the success rate was below average (27.3%), but the big plays more than make up for it. Black contributed 13 yards through the air, but he’s here for running over a first-down and finishing in the end zone. Deebo Samuel Deebo had a 70-yard touchdown on a play where Cowboys defenders didn’t figure out he had the ball until he was 20 yards downfield. Samuel had two other carries for four yards. He caught a screen for a touchdown. He had two other catches for 20 yards. He was efficient, effective, and electric. Samuel ran just under 20 miles per hour on his touchdown run. Keenan Allen I’d argue that Allen helped get the offense off the mat. The player who wasn’t on the roster this time last week had the second-most targets. Allen caught five passes for 61 yards. He had a 25% target share — which is Mike Evans territory. Four of Allen’s receptions resulted in a first down, and he should’ve had five if Purdy didn’t miss him toward the end of the game. We expected Allen to be impactful underneath, but he showed that he can create separation at the intermediate level of the field, both on in- and out-breaking routes. Jordan Watkins Watkins kicked things off with a 22-yard reception. He had a 27-yarder where Purdy bought time, waiting for someone to get open, while Watkins picked himself up off the ground and made himself available. It was only two catches, but Watkins has proven to be a big-play threat. Watkins had a couple of blocks that helped spring plays for the offense. He’s developing nicely and rounding into a complete player. George Kittle Kittle had a 20+ yard screen pass. He had four first-down receptions on nine targets. Every time he touched the ball, it felt like an impact play. Kittle caught three of his four contested targets, something he struggled with over the past couple of games. He had 46 yards after the catch. It wasn’t a vintage Kittle day, but if 74 yards feels like an off day, you know you’re dealing with a star. Losers Connor Colby Of the 115 offensive linemen to play at least 50 snaps in Week 10, Colby ranked 112th with a 17.1% pressure rate allowed. He had six pressures. Usually, Colby makes up for it in the run game. That was not the case on Sunday. You try to give the seventh-rounder some grace, especially going against Quinnen Williams. But you have to be competitive, and Colby simply was not. His lows are in the basement, and teams will start going out of their way to stress Colby. Deommodore Lenoir Lenoir was targeted 17 times against Dallas. That is not a typo. Over half of those came in the first half. That’s the third-most targets for a cornerback in a game since 2022. Coming into the game, Renardo Green was up against CeeDee Lamb, and Lenoir was up against George Pickens. On the surface, it makes sense. Put your better corner on their best receiver, and try to minimize the damage. Lenoir broke up the first two passes his way on the first drive, and you thought, ‘OK, he’s confident, and will hold his own.‘ Dallas completed the next five passes his way. We’ll talk ad nauseam about the pass rush, but the coverage was worse, and Lenoir is leading the charge. It’s 46-32. 1:56 remains. Keion White beats his man cleanly. Dak Prescott gets hit at the top of his drop. Lenoir allows an 11-yard curl to Pickens. First down. Far too many occurrences where there was pressure, but the coverage wasn’t in a position to contest the throw. Despite all those targets, Lenoir forced tight-window throws only 25% of the time. That’s not competitive. You don’t have a chance to survive. Interior line play The Cowboys ran 76 plays. Let’s add some context to the poor play. The defensive line was clearly gassed and running on fumes. With that said, the interior was getting pushed around in the first half, and fortunate Dallas didn’t run the ball on them more. Osa Odighizuwa had three run stops and four pressures. That’s about as well as he can play. DeForest Buckner had three pressures. Sebastian Valdez had two, and James Thompson had one. Pass-rush win rate is a better indicator of how a player performed. Only Odighizuwa was in the double digits. Buckner, who played 55 snaps and 39 pass-rushing snaps, only won on 5.1% of his rushes. He has to be better. Epeshians Prysock A tough spot for a rookie to get extended action. Prysock went in for Renardo Green after Green left with a back injury. Prysock played 28 snaps. He allowed all three of his targets to be completed for 28 yards, including a touchdown. He also missed a tackle. Prysock didn’t need to grab the receiver in the end zone, since he was already in position. That penalty nearly cost the Niners the game. Penalties The 49ers have been sloppy for three weeks now, and the penalties are starting to add up. They had 11 against Dallas, giving the Cowboys a full football field (100 yards) of penalties. The Cowboys had four first downs from penalties. The operation was smooth for the first month and a half of the season, but the Niners have been trending in the wrong direction with the zebras. The refs Bring on the robots. It’s time. Malik Mustapha had a picture-perfect hit. The refs huddled up, talked…

title: We watched vintage Deebo Samuel in the 49ers’ win over the Cowboys
summary: If I told you the San Francisco 49ers offense rode Deebo Samuel and Christian McCaffrey en route to a win, you’d probably assume I was talking about the 2023 season. Unfortunately for the Dallas Cowboys, it happened on Sunday, and the 49ers needed every bit of McCaffrey and Samuel, helping the 49ers edge Dallas in […]
full_text: (Photo by Brian Rothmuller/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images) | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images If I told you the San Francisco 49ers offense rode Deebo Samuel and Christian McCaffrey en route to a win, you’d probably assume I was talking about the 2023 season. Unfortunately for the Dallas Cowboys, it happened on Sunday, and the 49ers needed every bit of McCaffrey and Samuel, helping the 49ers edge Dallas in a 46-40 slobberknocker. It looked for a bit like the 49ers would run away with things on Sunday, but a 21-point fourth quarter allowed by the 49ers’ defense kept things closer than they needed. At the end of the day, the 49ers offense outpaced the defense. With the offense outplaying the defense, it makes sense all three stars are from that side of the ball: 3rd star: WR Deebo Samuel Sunday was as vintage of a game as you can get from Samuel. Samuel opened the scoring for the 49ers in typical Samuel fashion: a quick screen going untouched for a touchdown. With San Francisco chasing an early field goal, the offense went to work for the first time, putting together an eight-play, 78-yard drive ending with Purdy swinging a pass out to Samuel, who used some blocks from Colton McKivitz and Dominick Puni to walk into the endzone to put the 49ers up 7-3. His next score would be on the ground and might become one of the most memorable play calls of the Kyle Shanahan era. With the 49ers clinging to a five-point lead early in the third quarter, San Francisco took advantage of another massive play. On the third play of the drive, Shanahan reached into his bag of tricks and pulled out a reverse. Kaelon Black would take a toss to the right, but pitch it to Samuel going right-to-left. As Tom Brady pointed out on the broadcast, when Samuel had the ball going to the left, ten Cowboys defenders were still following Black in the opposite direction. With all the space in the world and a couple blockers in front of him, Samuel played the sideline perfectly, tight-roping his way for a 70-yard score. With the two scores on top of 109 total yards, Samuel is deserving of Sunday’s No. 3 star. 2nd star: RB Christian McCaffrey It took McCaffrey a while to get things going in the run game on Sunday. However, with just the performance he put together in the passing game, his rushing wasn’t really relevant. McCaffrey led all pass-catchers with 161 yards on four catches, with two game-breaking scores to swing momentum the 49ers’ way. The first one we will get into more detail with our No. 1 star, but McCaffrey was the beneficiary of the play. With the 49ers facing a third-and-8 late in the third quarter, Purdy hit McCaffrey, who had plenty of space to take the short pass 74 yards to put the 49ers up one. His second receiving touchdown wasn’t as long, but it won the 49ers the game. Dallas cut what was a 38-19 San Francisco lead to 38-32 in the span of eight minutes. With the 49ers clinging to the six-point lead, Purdy again would find McCaffrey with an entire field’s worth of space in front of him, and this time McCaffrey would go 66 yards to put the 49ers up 14 and put the game out of reach. McCaffrey sandwiched a rushing touchdown between his receiving scores, finishing with three total touchdowns 1st star: QB Brock Purdy Without Purdy, there is no Samuel or McCaffrey performance on Sunday. Purdy earned Sunday’s No. 1 star with the play that completely swung momentum the Niners way, but it was his whole performance that stole the show. The quarterback used both of McCaffrey’s big plays with a few others to throw for a career-high 389 yards with three touchdowns and no interceptions. And not only did Purdy have a career day, but he may have made the best play of his already impressive highlight reel. With Dallas taking a 16-10 lead in the second quarter, San Francisco’s following drive got off to a less than ideal start. Purdy was sacked to lose six yards but would cancel it out with an eight-yard pass to Kittle to set up a third-and-8. That’s when Purdy magic struck. Purdy started the play by avoiding a Caleb Downs sack and rolled right. The quarterback might have had the angle to scramble for the first down with Shemar James bearing down. Instead, Purdy pulled up and found a wide-open McCaffrey 10 yards in front of him, and McCaffrey did the rest to give the 49ers a 17-16 lead. Oh, you thought that was the highlight play I was referencing? Not at all. The highlight I was talking about was Samuel’s 70-yard end-around. One of those blockers ahead of Samuel was none other than Purdy. The 49ers quarterback kept with the play the whole way, joining Trent Williams and Jordan Watkins as part of the convoy. It was actually Purdy who made the last “block” (more like got in the way) 40 yards downfield to give Samuel the space to finish the run. After a few weeks of his play stabilizing after a hot start, Purdy put together an MVP-level performance when the 49ers needed it the most. Throughout the season, we will track the three stars of the season by tallying points for each star award using a complex scoring system: three points for being the first star, two for the second, and one for the third. Through Week 10, the standings are: QB Brock Purdy – 10 points WR Mike Evans – 8 points RB Christian McCaffrey – 7 points

title: NFC West Recap: 49ers hang 46 on Dallas; Rams rout Cardinals, Seahawks win
summary: The San Francisco 49ers put up the most points and yards in franchise history for a road game, which is also the most yards the Dallas Cowboys have given up at home. I’m just getting started on stats. We’ll begin with the 49ers averaging 9.4 yards per play. That do anything for you? How about […]
full_text: ATLANTA, GA - OCTOBER 25: Head Coach Kyle Shanahan of the San Francisco 49ers in the locker room before the game against the Atlanta Falcons at Mercedes-Benz Stadium on October 25, 2026 in Atlanta, Georgia. The Falcons defeated the 49ers 29-20. (Photo by Michael Zagaris/San Francisco 49ers/Getty Images) | Getty Images The San Francisco 49ers put up t he most points and yards in franchise history for a road game , which is also the most yards the Dallas Cowboys have given up at home. I’m just getting started on stats. We’ll begin with the 49ers averaging 9.4 yards per play. That do anything for you? How about Brock Purdy going 22-of-28 for 389 yards passing and three touchdowns, finishing with a passer rating of 154.5. Then there’s running back Christian McCaffrey, who had 223 yards from scrimmage and three scores. And yet, they still, STILL had to recover an onside kick to win the game. Cowboys quarterback Dak Prescott threw five touchdown passes, while cornerback Deommodore Lenoir spent most of the afternoon chasing Cowboys wide receiver George Pickens. Renardo Green left with the same back injury he dealt with all week. There hasn’t been much about Green’s status for next week as of this writing, but Kyle Shanahan said he was already playing hurt . It was 38-32 in the fourth quarter. All points were by the offense. No sacks (well, there was one, but I wouldn’t call it “legitimate” outside of the stat sheet), and the Cowboys were coming back. Then this happened: CMC FOR THREE 🔥 No one can stop Christian McCaffrey in Dallas 😤 (via @NFL ) pic.twitter.com/V9bJjR6slr — SportsCenter (@SportsCenter) November 16, 2026 And even then, this thing wasn’t over until the most entertaining fumbleroosky play in recent memory as the clock ticked to zero: Final Play: #Cowboys come up short. 90 yards to go passing it backward isn’t a great idea #49ers hold out pic.twitter.com/4u95SfL2GR — FirstDownMedia (@FirstDownMediaa) November 16, 2026 Regardless of whether we want to be optimistic or skeptical, the 49ers stay the NFC’s No. 1 seed, a game ahead of the 7-2 pack of the Detroit Lions, Minnesota Vikings and Chicago Bears. The Seahawks and Rams both won, so the division lead stays at 2.5 games. The 49ers face a tough gauntlet, starting with the Vikings. Any questions you have about this team are about to be answered over the next four games. Seattle Seahawks (6-4) After trading quarterback Kirk Cousins to the Vikings on Tuesday, the Las Vegas Raiders gave Fernando Mendoza his first NFL start. At first it looked like an upset, but then the Seahawks had to spoil the party. There were moments, however. On Seahawks quarterback Drew Lock’s first dropback, he tried to shovel the ball away to avoid a sack and fumbled. Mendoza scored on a quarterback draw a few plays later, and the Raiders led 10-7 at halftime. The second half belonged to the Seahawks, with highlights like rookie running back Jadarian Price scoring his first career touchdown to take the lead, and a 71-yard Jaxon Smith-Njigba score. Final: 21-13. Smith-Njigba had 144 of his 171 yards receiving in the third quarter alone. Just like against the 49ers last week, the Raiders had a terrible second half with negative yards until their final possession. Mendoza took six sacks as well. The score could have been worse. Lock lost a second fumble when Zach Charbonnet ran into him on a play-action fake, and Jason Myers missed a 44-yarder. Right tackle Abe Lucas left with an ankle injury, which is worth watching before Seattle comes to Levi’s Stadium in Week 12. It was a lot of Seattle things, and then a lot of Raider-ing. Unfortunately, Seattle things usually don’t end in losses the way Raider-ing does. Los Angeles Rams (6-4)/Arizona Cardinals (3-7) Minshew Magic is gone to IR. That led us to Carson Beck starting for Arizona. A rookie, Carson Beck. So what happens? The Cardinals tried doing what worked last time they played the Rams: field-goal-ing them to death. This time, it wasn’t as successful, as they managed only six points throughout the game. Besides Matthew Stafford’s early-game interception to linebacker Cody Simon, it was all Los Angeles. Beck threw an interception just before halftime, and the Rams turned it into a 17-6 lead at the break. Final: 34-6 in Glendale, the Rams’ fourth straight win. Arizona finished with 123 yards of total offense: 89 net passing and 34 rushing. Beck was sacked five times, 1.5 of them by Aaron Donald. Stafford threw three touchdown passes. The Cardinals need to get through 2026 and make a football team next year. Credit where it’s due: the Rams look like a team again. They’re 1-2 in the division, and their bye week comes before a Thanksgiving Eve game against the Packers. No credit is given to them for getting a team like the Cardinals, a team that beat them solely on field goals a few weeks back. Luckily, the Rams also have a tough stretch coming up: the Green Bay Packers and the Kansas City Chiefs. Good luck. Onto Week 11 The 49ers “host” the Minnesota Vikings (7-2) at Estadio Banorte in Mexico City on Sunday Night Football. The Vikings traded a 2027 third-round pick for Cousins , and he went 21-of-31 for 207 yards passing and two touchdowns in a 30-10 win at Lambeau . So they got the offense figured out; what about the defense? Well, they sacked Jordan Love eight times. Just a reminder, that’s not the Cowboys defense: Dallas sacked Purdy five times, and the 49ers still scored 46. This time the 49ers’ defense has to carry its share. The No. 1 seed is on the line, and Minnesota won the last two meetings. Cousins also became the first quarterback since at least 1950 to start for two different teams in consecutive weeks , and last week’s start was against the 49ers, when Jaden Dugger returned his pass for a touchdown. At least the game isn’t in Minnesota. The Rams and Seahawks are on bye. So, bye. The Cardinals visit the Kansas City Chiefs, who beat Atlanta 35-13 behind five Patrick Mahomes touchdown passes. Gotta love it when the 49ers get Atlanta’s best, but then they go back to doing Falcons things. 1st: San Francisco 49ers ; Next: vs. Minnesota Vikings (NFL Mexico City Game) TIE-2nd: Seattle Seahawks ; Next: BYE TIE-2nd: Los Angeles Rams ; Next: BYE 4th: Arizona Cardinals ; Next: at Kansas City Chiefs

title: Should Baker Mayfield sit if he’s hurt?
summary: Tampa Bay fans caught wind of a story line they have become all too familiar with in 2026— Baker Mayfield is hurt. Even worse than Mayfield being injured, the injury does have the potential to make him miss time, namely this week’s game against the Detroit Lions. Mayfield did take an awkward hit in last […]
full_text: TAMPA, FL - SEPTEMBER 27: Tampa Bay Buccaneers Quarterback Baker Mayfield (6) holds his right hand as he walks off the field during the regular season game between the Minnesota Vikings and the Tampa Bay Buccaneers on September 27, 2026 at Raymond James Stadium in Tampa, Florida.(Photo by Cliff Welch/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images) | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images Tampa Bay fans caught wind of a story line they have become all too familiar with in 2026— Baker Mayfield is hurt . Even worse than Mayfield being injured, the injury does have the potential to make him miss time, namely this week’s game against the Detroit Lions. Mayfield did take an awkward hit in last week’s prime time showdown with the Chicago Bears and while he limped around the field the injury wasn’t given a significant level of credence, as limping around a football field is in part, Baker Mayfield’s way. Mayfield’s injury may be serious enough to take this scenario off the board completely, however, the question is — If Mayfield can play, should he? Mayfield has a long history of playing through injuries. The former number one overall pick made a choice to play through a torn labrum during his time with the Cleveland Browns. That decision was admirable, Mayfield gritted his way through pain and put his body on line for the team. Commendable, still, that decision cost Mayfield millions of dollars, his career in Cleveland, and a good bit of his reputation. Tampa has been lucky in the sense that Mayfield was able to suit for every start prior to his time missed earlier this season. Baker Mayfield has played mostly good football during his Tampa Bay tenure, but throughout last season the hits mounted, the physical style of play that fans adore so much from their quarterback caught up to him, which left Mayfield battered and bruised. Down the stretch in 2025, Baker Mayfield was battling injuries as much as he was battling defenses and his play reflecting that fight. In the first 10 games of last season, the Bucs’ passing game was humming— Chef Mayfield was cheffing it up. he had 17 touchdowns and only three interceptions. That highly impressive touchdown to interception ratio (better than 5:1) dipped drastically in the latter half of the year. Mayfield’s final seven games were messy. He tossed nine touchdowns alongside seven interceptions. In the back half of last season Mayfield was consistently trying to play despite being both injured and at times hampered significantly. The effectiveness of the Buccaneers’ passing attack dwindled, Mayfield’s success sunk swiftly, and the Bucs’ season began to spiral— A spiral they arguably still have not gotten out of yet, a year later. Would the season have turned out better if the Bucs elected to sit Baker Mayfield and allow to heal rather than just placing their quarterback out on the field at half mast to hoist the sails? That’s as unclear as murky water in a swamp, but their are good vat of facts to support the notion that a hurt Baker Mayfield is not a great Baker Mayfield. The Bucs had a chance to make a similar decision this year already— They made the very same choice that they did a year ago. Against the Minnesota Vikings, in week three, Mayfield got dinged— His thumb on his throwing hand, a fairly serious injury for a quarterback. Tampa’s tough guy was given a three-seven week timeline. Mayfield, being the fighter that he is, missed three games and was back in action— Three games of Jalon Daniels and Baker Mayfield was back on the field. The issue with his recovery timeline is Mayfield wasn’t all the way back. He got away with throwing 11 passes against the Carolina Panthers— The Bucs won and Mayfield was back at again next week. He snuck by throwing just three more passes and not earning a single completion— Tampa beat the Atlanta Falcons to get to 2-0 in the division and everything was unicorns and rainbows. Last week, Baker Mayfield finally threw (32 times) and it did not look good. Save one beautiful, perfectly uncorked deep ball to Tez Johnson, last Sunday was not Mayfield’s day— 18-32, no touchdowns, two picks. Mayfield playing through injury, is, has been, and always will be laudable. The fulcrum of the conversation has to be, just because something is honorable does not mean it is what is best and sometimes players need to be saved from themselves. Mayfield is currently listed as questionable, so the decision may be made for Tampa Bay. Either way, the Buccaneers will find themselves in an extremely important game this Sunday. They’ll be squaring off the with Detroit Lions, a team that is far outperforming them this season. The Lions are not a divisional opponent and the game likely won’t have any tie-breaking ramifications for the postseason, however, half of the NFC South lost last week. The Atlanta Falcons were blown out by the Kansas City Chiefs and dropped to 3-7 (last place in the division). The New Orleans Saints are right beside them, as their loss to Carolina leaves them at 3-6. Tampa is also 3-6 and they will by no means be out of the race for the division crown if they were to lose Sunday, but as the season trudges forward keeping pace with Carolina becomes more and more important. The Panthers defeated the aforementioned Saints and pushed themselves to the front of the NFC South line at 4-5. Next up on the Panther’s schedule are the Lamar Jackson-less Ravens— A game they’ll likely be favored to win. The Buccaneers still have plenty of time and division games to go in order to make up ground, but with the season rapidly barreling towards Thanksgiving, Tampa’s remaining season is running shorter and shorter.

title: Titans changed their offensive philosophy after Colts game
summary: Robert Saleh said at his Monday press conference this morning that the Tennessee Titans changed their offensive philosophy after the game against the Indianapolis Colts. You can see the whole answer here: The changes they have made have certainly paid off. The Titans are averaging almost 28 points per game in that span. Cam Ward […]
full_text: NASHVILLE, TENNESSEE - NOVEMBER 15: Cam Ward #1 of the Tennessee Titans reacts during the first half against the Jacksonville Jaguars at Nissan Stadium on November 15, 2026 in Nashville, Tennessee. (Photo by Justin Ford/Getty Images) | Getty Images Robert Saleh said at his Monday press conference this morning that the Tennessee Titans changed their offensive philosophy after the game against the Indianapolis Colts. You can see the whole answer here: Titans HC Robert Saleh’s full response this morning on changing the team’s philosophical approach to the offense around Cam Ward a few weeks ago (via @Titans ) pic.twitter.com/GwxUG4z1k4 — Buck Reising (@BuckReising) November 16, 2026 The changes they have made have certainly paid off. The Titans are averaging almost 28 points per game in that span. Cam Ward has looked much more comfortable. He wasn’t that good in the loss to the Cleveland Browns, which was the first game they made the switch, but he has been really good since. There are probably a couple of reasons they made the switch. The first is that running the offense up-tempo benefits Ward because it fits his style of play. He is better out of structure than in structure. You can’t always play out of structure as an NFL quarterback, but it makes sense to create more of those opportunities. The other reason is that the defense, which was already bad, lost its two best players over that span. If the Titans are going to have any chance to win games, they are going to have to score a bunch of points. It is going to take another 30-point effort for them to have a chance against the Dallas Cowboys on Sunday. I wrote early on this season that Brian Daboll needed to open things up for Ward. The conservative offense just wasn’t working. It is good to see that they made the decision in-house to do that. Hopefully, it will eventually lead to some wins.

(Photo by Andy Lyons/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Tennessee Titans were defeated 40-23 by the Jacksonville Jaguars in Week 10 . A familiar theme is emerging. The offense is beginning to show real signs of life while the defense flounders following the Jeffery Simmons and Amani Hooker trades. Anyhow, we’ve identified and analyzed the Titans’ five best performances in Week 10. QB Cam Ward It was another strong performance for Titans quarterback Cam Ward. The sophomore No. 1 overall selection completed 28-of-39 passing attempts for 231 yards, two touchdowns, and one interception. He also rushed for a team-high 39 yards. Ward’s 28 completions tied a previous career high, and his 71.8% completion percentage was his best of the season. LB Cedric Gray Cedric Gray finally received an opportunity to play an every-down role with three linebackers sidelined by injury. Gray posted a team-high nine tackles, had two pass breakups, a TFL, and intercepted a tipped Trevow Lawrence pass. He better retain his starting role next weekend alongside Anthony Hill Jr. Cody Barton needs to be benched. RT JC Latham Right tackle JC Latham continues to take the desired steps forward. Pro Football Focus credited him with allowing two pressures and zero sacks. Latham has allowed two sacks all season long. He was downright dominant at times versus the Jaguars while providing Ward with clean pockets. RB Tony Pollard The Titans decided to retain Tony Pollard beyond the trade deadline despite having offers. He struggled to run the football effectively versus the Jaguars, being limited to 33 yards via nine carries. But Pollard made an outstanding individual effort on a 32-yard TD pass from Ward, and totaled 66 receiving yards on eight checkdowns. WR Elic Ayomanor With Carnell Tate sidelined, the supporting cast of receivers possessed an opportunity to shine. Though he wasn’t perfect, Elic Ayomanor was the offense’s leading receiver. Ayomanor posted five receptions for a team-high 79 yards, including an explosive 50-yard gain.

title: Washington’s offensive identity is beginning to take shape | Commanders Film Session
summary: The Washington Commanders handled the New York Giants’ pressure packages significantly better than they did in their first matchup in Week 5, and the improvement stemmed from several areas. Offensive coordinator David Blough was more willing to move the pocket, particularly in down-and-distance situations where Giants defensive coordinator Dennard Wilson typically dialed up pressure. Jayden […]
full_text: EAST RUTHERFORD, NJ - NOVEMBER 12: Jayden Daniels #5 of the Washington Commanders celebrates during an NFL football game against the New York Giants at MetLife Stadium on November 12, 2026 in East Rutherford, New Jersey. (Photo by Cooper Neill/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Washington Commanders handled the New York Giants’ pressure packages significantly better than they did in their first matchup in Week 5, and the improvement stemmed from several areas. Offensive coordinator David Blough was more willing to move the pocket, particularly in down-and-distance situations where Giants defensive coordinator Dennard Wilson typically dialed up pressure. Jayden Daniels and Nick Allegretti did an excellent job setting protections, but perhaps most importantly, Daniels consistently identified answers pre-snap and delivered the football within the timing of the offense. According to SumerSports, Washington’s pressure rate dropped from 46 percent (seventh-worst in the NFL) in its Week 5 matchup against New York to 23 percent in Week 10, the third-best mark in the NFL that week. However, Washington’s offensive performance against the Giants was about more than its ability to handle pressure. For an offense that has struggled with consistency throughout the season, Thursday night offered some indication that Washington may finally be developing an identity through the strengths of its personnel. In the film session above, I detail how and why tight end Ben Sinnott was so impactful against the Giants and explore whether his breakout performance is a sign of things to come as a receiving threat in Washington’s offense. Commanders pass protection drastically improved Although the pass was off-target, the protection on this particular rep is exactly what you want to see from Washington in a critical down-and-distance situation. New York presents a double A-gap threat with linebacker Arvell Reese aligned to the offensive left. Given the tendencies of the Giants’ pressure schemes, Daniels and Allegretti have seven potential rush threats to account for. They set the protection toward the more athletic side of New York’s defensive front, implementing a three-man slide to the offensive right. Running back Rachaad White does an excellent job scanning from the inside out before ultimately picking up the seventh potential rusher, a cornerback coming off the edge. The result of the play doesn’t reflect the quality of the execution up front, but Washington’s ability to identify, communicate, and account for New York’s pressure is an encouraging development for an offense that has struggled in those situations throughout the season. Treylon Burks has established himself as a serious deep threat It feels more like a matter of when, not if, Daniels and Treylon Burks connect on an explosive play downfield this season. Hopefully, it begins Monday night against the Cincinnati Bengals. The Giants rotate into a single-high shell pre-snap, allowing Daniels to recognize the opportunity he has with Burks downfield. Aligned in the slot, Burks does an excellent job accelerating off the snap, quickly closing the cushion between himself and the defender before blowing past him with pure foot speed. What stands out about this rep is that both Daniels and Burks appear to recognize the touchdown opportunity before Burks even gets level with the defender. Post-snap, the Giants settle into Cover 3, and with the middle-of-the-field safety positioned toward the opposite hash, there is little opportunity for him to recover had Daniels delivered a more accurate pass. The connection hasn’t consistently materialized yet, but Burks’ ability to threaten defenses vertically is becoming an increasingly valuable element of Washington’s offense. Stefon Diggs mental processing is creating trust between him and Daniels Stefon Diggs’ savviness consistently shows up on film, and the chemistry between him and Daniels appears to be developing at a critical juncture in Washington’s season. The Commanders initially align in a 4×1 formation before motioning Diggs across the formation to create a 3×2 look. In response, the Giants rotate into a two-high shell, with their safeties gaining additional depth. Recognizing another zone coverage, Daniels knows he has an opportunity to target Diggs on a slant for a quick gain. What makes this rep impressive, however, is how Diggs creates his separation. Rather than immediately breaking inside, Diggs recognizes the cornerback’s technique while also understanding the timing constraints of his route. He sells the vertical threat by working into the cornerback’s blind spot before suddenly breaking inside on the slant. His ability to manipulate the defender creates both the separation and the sizable throwing window Daniels needs to deliver the football. The play ultimately fell a yard short of the first down, but it illustrates how Diggs’ understanding of leverage, coverage, and route timing can make life easier for his quarterback. Washington has an opportunity to build on its offensive performance against the Giants. It wasn’t all pretty. The run game remains a season-long concern, and Daniels’ two interceptions left a blemish on what was otherwise an efficient night. However, between the improved protection and the intentionality behind incorporating Washington’s playmakers, the Commanders may be beginning to show how the individual strengths of their skilled players can complement one another. In the film session below, I dive into the elements of Washington’s offensive performance that must become staples moving forward if the Commanders hope to make a legitimate postseason push over their final eight games. Comment and let us know what you are seeing from Commanders Offense. Don’t forget to also subscribe to the Trap or Dive Podcast.
