title: Seahawks' Mike Macdonald 'optimistic' QB Sam Darnold returns after bye week
summary: Seahawks coach Mike Macdonald is "optimistic" QB Sam Darnold will return to his starting role after the team's bye week.
full_text:
After a tumultuous first half of the season, quarterback Sam Darnold is on the verge of returning to the Seattle Seahawks' starting lineup.
While acknowledging how well Drew Lock has played in his absence, coach Mike Macdonald said Monday that Darnold is still the team's starter when healthy, and that he's on track to play next week against the San Francisco 49ers following Seattle's bye.
"I think the best way to put it right now is we're optimistic that he's going to be able to get a full week's worth of reps next week and play the game," Macdonald said. "But you're a week out and we're projecting that, so there's some things that we need to get over hurdle-wise for him to be able to do it. He wouldn't be able to do that right now, but you're assuming that it's going to progress to that point."
After helping the Seahawks win Super Bowl LX last season, Darnold's start to 2026 has been marred by injuries and interceptions.
He hurt his glute on the fifth play of Seattle's win over the New England Patriots in Week 1, which sidelined him for the remainder of that game and the following week. He's missed the last two weeks due to a quad injury he suffered near the end of a loss to the Chicago Bears in Week 8, when he played through a cracked rib he sustained on his first dropback of the night.
In the six games from Weeks 3 through 8, Darnold threw 10 touchdown passes and nine interceptions while posting a Total QBR of 50.0 that ranked 23rd in that span. The Seahawks went 2-4 in those games, with losses to the Washington Commanders , 49ers, Denver Broncos and Bears, and wins over the Los Angeles Chargers and Kansas City Chiefs .
Lock, meanwhile, has thrown seven touchdown passes and zero interceptions in four games. He ranked second in Total QBR over the first two weeks at 79.8, and he's second over the last two weeks at 90.4. Lock's only turnovers in those four games were the two fumbles he lost Sunday in Seattle's 21-13 win over the Las Vegas Raiders , one of which was the result of running back Zach Charbonnet bumped into him while he was beginning his delivery.
Lock had already been dealing with a right elbow injury for the last month when he hurt his quad last week against Arizona. Playing through both injuries against the Raiders, he completed 14 of 17 attempts for 240 yards, two touchdowns and the two lost fumbles.
While the Week 1 win officially goes on Darnold's ledger because he started the game, Lock is effectively 4-0 this season as Seattle's quarterback, with two wins over Arizona and one apiece over New England and Las Vegas.
"Drew's been fantastic," Macdonald said Monday on Seattle Sports 710-AM. "He's been phenomenal, but Sam's our quarterback. We saw what Sam's been capable of both last year and -- the beginning of the year for Sam has been a tough road ... Sam's our starting quarterback. I can't wait for him to be fully healthy probably for the first time, or minimal times it's happened this year, and get a full week's worth of work and we'll rock and roll from there.
"But to have Drew as our backup and to play the way he has has just been awesome. So we're blessed ... I think we have three really good quarterbacks and Sam's our starter."
At 6-4, the Seahawks are 2.5 games behind the 49ers in the NFC West standings. San Francisco beat Seattle at Lumen Field in October.
Macdonald said Monday that none of the Seahawks who went down against the Raiders appear to be hurt badly enough to require stints on injured reserve. Right tackle Abe Lucas (ankle sprain), running back George Holani (knee) and tight end Nick Kallerup all left the game.
A source told NFL Network's Ian Rapoport that Holani -- a backup to Zach Charbonnet and Jadarian Price -- has an MCL sprain and is considered week-to-week.
Macdonald said the team is also optimistic that left tackle Charles Cross will return next week from the ankle sprain that has sidelined him for the last three games. He did not know if left guard Quenton Nelson , who's missed the last two games, will return to practice next week. Nelson is recovering from a knee procedure he had after aggravating an injury he was dealing with before the Seahawks acquired him in an Oct. 27 trade with the Indianapolis Colts .

title: 49ers WR Mike Evans' Achilles tendinitis injury explained
summary: ESPN spoke with a medical professional for a better understanding of Evans' diagnosis. When could he return? And will the injury completely resolve itself?
full_text:
COLORADO SPRINGS, Colo. -- As wide receiver Mike Evans works his way back from Achilles tendinitis , nobody in the  San Francisco 49ers ' locker room knows better how frustrating that injury can be than running back Christian McCaffrey .

 In 2024, McCaffrey missed the first eight games of the season with bilateral Achilles tendinitis  -- tendinitis in both legs, though the issue was more concentrated to one of his legs. The injury still makes him wince at the mere mention of it.

 "It's tough," McCaffrey said. "It's a compounding thing that can get worse really quickly and then it can be really debilitating. I had my own experience with it. I hated everything about it."

 While Evans isn't dealing with the bilateral version of the injury -- his tendinitis is in his right leg -- the issue has been enough to keep him out of three-plus games. His last play came in the second quarter of the 49ers' Week 6 win over the Commanders, and he had missed practice all week leading up to that game with Achilles soreness and a rib issue.

 There's still no definitive return date for Evans, though coach Kyle Shanahan said before Week 10 that Evans has progressed well and has "a chance" to return as soon as Sunday night against the Minnesota Vikings in Mexico City.

 

 "I'm hoping to, just not sure yet. Still too early," Shanahan said Monday when asked if Evans will be back at practice this week. "He's flying in tonight with the guys who were left behind who didn't travel with us to Dallas. So we'll let these next few days go and see if he can get out there sometime this week."

 While the 49ers' offense has still been good without Evans, averaging 6.4 yards per play without him, it's been downright dominant with him. The Niners are averaging 7.2 yards per play with Evans on the field this season.

 Without Evans, the 49ers are Super Bowl contenders. With him, they could be the favorites.

 "Everybody on the field, their life is easier because of how good he is and how much of a threat he is," tight end George Kittle said. "I've actually never been more confident in an offense than when I look out and I see Mike Evans ... I'm excited to get Mike back, hopefully."

 For the Niners, it's not just about getting back their No. 1 receiver. It's about getting Evans back and keeping him back upon his return.  

 ESPN spoke to Dr. Daniel Kaplan, an orthopedic surgeon at NYU Langone Hospital, to discuss the nature of Evans' injury, the timeline for him to return, and whether the injury can be completely resolved so he's able to finish the season without issue. Dr. Kaplan has not treated Evans' injury specifically nor does he work with the Niners.

 (The conversation has been edited for brevity and clarity.)

 

 Mike Evans is dealing with Achilles tendinitis; can you explain what it is and any potential causes? 
 Kaplan: Tendinitis is in the family of overwork usage injury. It's not like a tear or something like that. It's usually a chronic ongoing inflammation of the tendon. It's about load and load management.

 Usually when it becomes persistent, it goes slightly from tendinitis to tendinosis, which is not just inflammation but when some of the tissue is a little bit less healthy. It's not necessarily at risk for rupture, but it just means it takes a little bit longer for things to heal. And he's probably -- given the fact that he has been out for a couple weeks now -- in that territory.

 You mentioned it's not necessarily at more risk of rupture, but what are the risks of attempting to play through it or push it before it's fully healthy? 
 Kaplan:  The biggest risk is really more that you let this thing perpetuate and just not actually cool down. So instead of getting 100% better, you're 75% better and then you play and now you're 70% better. That's the bigger risk.

 Theoretically, whenever a tendon is not working optimally or a tendon around it, you are just in general at slightly higher risk. It's not that he's at no increased risk, but that's just not the primary concern.

 Generally speaking, what is the recovery timeline for Achilles tendinitis? 
 Kaplan: It totally depends on the severity. Also, timing in the season. If it's like the Super Bowl, he's playing because it's mostly about a pain thing as opposed to necessarily a function aspect. We usually assume it's in the two- to four-week range for tendinitis. That's about what I would expect. Longer than that sometimes, but a lot of it has to do with how much he's actually shut down. It sounds like they did the right thing by actually shutting him down, as opposed to the other option is trying to play through it and letting it drag on and then it's just never going to resolve.

 

 So, it's an injury that if you treat it properly, it can resolve in that time and not linger all season? 
 Kaplan: Exactly. It is like an overuse workload thing. He's a wide receiver. Explosive. He's running a million sprints in practice every day type of thing. You don't just purely shut them down and just have them sit on the couch. There's a physical therapy component where you're doing certain types of strengthening and stretching and things like that. You are trying to reduce the inflammation. So that's anti-inflammatories, that's cold baths, that's massage. It's not that you're just purely saying, "Don't play for three weeks and you'll be fine." There is an active treatment component to it, but the most important thing is giving the tendon a break.

 McCaffrey had bilateral Achilles tendinitis a couple of years ago, and he missed eight games. Does bilateral versus one leg make a difference in recovery or does it depend on how they handled recovery more? 
 Kaplan: I wouldn't think so. That timeline was way longer for McCaffrey than I would expect for this problem. I would expect it wasn't necessarily that the problem was bilateral, just more the severity.

 Once Evans' injury resolves, is he then at higher risk for it to return or is that solely dependent on usage? 
 Kaplan: Mostly just depending on usage. Now, if he's prone to it for some sort of biomechanical reason, I suppose it's possible. But to my knowledge, it's not like that's something that he has been battling over the course of his career.

 So, I don't think so as long as it does resolve. And that's where the secret sauce comes in about really determining when it's safe for him to go back because you obviously don't want to keep him out any longer than you have to. But if you send him back too soon, then you restart the clock and now all of a sudden, it's another two weeks here, another week there. It's kind of like when people have hamstring tears and you follow those; it's the same idea.

title: Titans getting more after adding more to QB Cam Ward's plate
summary: The Titans offense has functioned better since putting more on quarterback Cam Ward's plate, even if it hasn't led to more wins yet.
full_text:
NASHVILLE, Tenn. -- The Tennessee Titans decided to shift their philosophical approach on offense to put more on second-year quarterback Cam Ward 's plate, according to coach Robert Saleh. The coaching staff wanted to give Ward more command of the offense by getting him the playcall quickly so he could get the offense to the line of scrimmage and be a field general.
The shift started after the Titans' 26-20 win over the Indianapolis Colts in Week 6 with a specific goal in mind.
"We've said from the beginning that we're going to give him every opportunity to prove that he's the franchise quarterback of the Tennessee Titans," Saleh said Monday. "So philosophically the change was how are we going to evaluate whether or not he's capable of being our franchise quarterback if we don't give him the opportunity to prove it? I think over the last three weeks he's done that or at least doing it."
Ward responded by posting his first 300-yard passing performance and throwing four touchdown passes over the past three games, matching his total from the first six weeks. Saleh said the coaching staff likes what they've seen from Ward recently. The staff feels Ward seems more comfortable in the offense and with the verbiage, and coaches believe he's gaining confidence with the protection. Ward's footwork has improved and he's working through his progressions faster as he gets more time on task in the offense.
As a result, he's playing quarterback more efficiently and that's without reigning AFC Offensive Rookie of the Month Carnell Tate over the past two games. Tate has been out with a shoulder injury. Ward and Tate connected five times for 69 yards in Tennessee's 27-24 loss to the Cleveland Browns in Week 7, the first game after the philosophical shift.
Offensive coordinator Brian Daboll utilized more no huddle in the Browns game to get Ward to the line with more time on the clock and give him freedom to change the play.
"He's given me the keys to the kingdom," Ward said of Daboll. "It doesn't matter what I go to, but I always got to have an explanation of what I'm going to and why. And he's a true quarterback coach.
"He and [quarterback coach] Shea [Tierney] prepare me the right way every week."
Wide receiver Elic Ayomanor said the players lobbied for Daboll to use more no huddle on offense in hopes of getting a spark. It worked. The no huddle helped them get off to a fast start against Cleveland by scoring a touchdown on their opening drive for the first time all season. The Titans jumped out to a 14-0 lead in that game. The Titans built a 10-0 lead over the Cincinnati Bengals on the road the following week.
Tennessee went no huddle 21 times against Cleveland, 29 times against the Bengals and 28 times in their 40-23 loss to the Jacksonville Jaguars on Sunday. It's not a coincidence that Ward is playing better after the shift. Tierney said he thinks Ward is comfortable working no huddle because of his experience with it in college. Ayomanor agrees.
"I think Cam is a lot more comfortable doing tempo," Ayomanor said. "Being able to be at the line of scrimmage with a lot of time left on the play clock, being able to see everything clearly, make changes at the line if he needs to. I think that's something that he did in college quite a bit."
